News.title: Will the lunar eclipse be visible from my area? UK weather forecast for the Blood Moon – and best time to see it
News.content:
STARGAZERS across the UK are gearing up for a spectacular celestial show this week as a stunning “Blood Moon” takes to the skies.

Those who set their alarms for the early hours of Friday, August 28 will be in for a treat as the UK experiences a partial lunar eclipse – with over 93% of the Moon’s face plunging into the darkest part of Earth’s shadow.



It will look almost identical to a total lunar eclipse, and you can even leave the specialist eyewear at home.

A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth positions itself directly between the Sun and the Moon, stopping sunlight from directly reaching the lunar surface.



During a near total lunar eclipse, the Moon is bathed in a dramatic red, copper-like glow caused by the Earth’s atmosphere – hence the nickname “Blood Moon”.

It’s a sight you won’t want to miss, but to fully appreciate it, you’ll need a decent break in the clouds.



When is the best time to see the lunar eclipse?

The eclipse is an hours-long event, but the action kicks off at 2.23am on Friday, August 28, as Earth’s outer shadow first touches the Moon, causing a subtle dimming.

The partial eclipse officially begins at 3.33am, when a distinct dark “bite” will appear across the lunar disk as it enters the Earth’s main shadow.

The peak of the eclipse will arrive at 5.12am, when maximum coverage will cause the Moon to glow in dramatic reddish-orange hues – the “Blood Moon” effect.

Around 6.15am, the Moon dips below the horizon, wrapping up visibility across the UK.



What is the weather forecast where you live?

The Met Office has issued its latest update, but it says that “weather conditions are expected to be challenging for many hoping to see the eclipse.”

If you live in the South or East of England, you have drawn the lucky ticket, at least to start with.

The Met Office says: “The best initial viewing opportunities are… likely to be across southern and eastern England.

“These areas are expected to remain relatively cloud-free from around 2am, potentially allowing observers to see the opening stages of the eclipse.”

But for many others, the start of the eclipse is going to be hidden behind a blanket of grey.



“At the beginning of the event,” says the Met Office, “cloud is forecast across Cornwall and Devon, Wales, the Midlands, parts of northwest England, and most of Scotland and Northern Ireland.”

But “cloud amounts are also expected to build elsewhere across the UK, meaning conditions may become increasingly unfavourable before the eclipse reaches its maximum at 5.12am.”

There is slightly better news if you live in the North East of England, where “patchier cloud is expected,” meaning you might just get lucky and spot the red Moon peeking through the gaps.

The Blood Moon weather forecast where you live:

Cornwall & Devon: Cloudy from the start of the event, creating generally challenging early viewing conditions.

Cloudy from the start of the event, creating generally challenging early viewing conditions. Midlands & Northwest England: Overcast skies expected early on, with cloud amounts building as the night progresses.

Overcast skies expected early on, with cloud amounts building as the night progresses. Northeast England: Patchier cloud cover, offering a fair chance of catching glimpses of the Blood Moon through gaps in the sky.

Patchier cloud cover, offering a fair chance of catching glimpses of the Blood Moon through gaps in the sky. Scotland & Northern Ireland: Mostly blanketed by cloud at the start, though brief temporary breaks may still afford quick views.

Mostly blanketed by cloud at the start, though brief temporary breaks may still afford quick views. Southern & Eastern England: Best initial viewing opportunities, remaining relatively clear from around 2am before cloud cover gradually increases ahead of the 5.12am peak.

Best initial viewing opportunities, remaining relatively clear from around 2am before cloud cover gradually increases ahead of the 5.12am peak. Wales: Cloud-heavy at the beginning of the eclipse, leading to increasingly unfavourable conditions into the early morning.

The Met Office says that though “the greatest chance of seeing something is likely to be across southern and eastern England during its earlier stages… there may not be one location offering ideal conditions throughout.”

There is some hope, with the service reminding us that the Great British weather can change at the drop of a hat.

“Cloud cover can vary over relatively short distances,” it says, “so those planning to watch should check the latest local forecast before setting out.”

News.title: Brits would get £30 tax break if left on hold by HMRC for 30 minutes under Reform plans
News.content:
PAY PER WAIT Brits would get £30 tax break if left on hold by HMRC for 30 minutes under Reform plans

TAXPAYERS would get £30 knocked off their tax bill if they are left hanging on the phone to HMRC for more than 30 minutes under Reform plans.

The payout would be capped at twice a year and only available to people who owe tax.



The party’s Treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick announced the move at a press conference this morning, saying: “Last year, MPs were accusing HMRC of deliberately degrading its own services to force people onto the website. It’s a disgrace.

“Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough.



“So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

“I’m announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, well, they can repay.

“And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we’ll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance.”

Callers waited an average of 23 minutes in 2023/24 – compared with just five minutes five years earlier.

Nearly 50,000 calls were reportedly cut off without help after hitting HMRC’s 70-minute limit.

Reform claims taxpayers lost 14 million hours on the phone that year, costing the economy £275million in wasted time.



The party expects the tax credits to cost £70million annually but says the bill would fall if HMRC answered calls faster.

Officials would be ordered to improve services without extra departmental cash, including by letting small firms arrange debt repayments in writing.

At the press conference, Mr Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a “light-touch” approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash “red tape” for businesses.

News.title: Brits to be told ‘stock up on bottled water & tinned food to prepare for threats including cyber attacks & weather’
News.content:
HOME FRONT Brits to be told ‘stock up on bottled water & tinned food to prepare for threats including cyber attacks & weather’

BRITS are reportedly to be told to stock up on water and tinned food to prepare for threats posed by cyber attacks and weather.

Andy Burnham’s government is understood to be preparing a campaign to warn households how to be ready for severe disruption.



It comes after it was revealed that a cyber attack on a UK energy facility, thought to be linked to Iran, shut down the facility.

Work on a government “war book” is said to have been accelerated after ex-PM Keir Starmer said there could be an attack by Russia against Nato as soon as 2030.



The “war book” is a detailed manual for the defence of the UK from external threats.

Amid the rising tensions, people are believed they will be told to ensure they have emergency supplies like canned food and water on hand.



The Financial Times reports that a focus has been put on national resilience after Russia threatened the UK with “consequences” when British drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes.

Seperately, the attack on a UK energy facility, allegedly by Iran, has prompted claims that the country’s infrastructure is vulnerable.

Dieter Helm, professor of economic policy at Oxford university, said the UK’s energy system was “very vulnerable” to cyber attacks.

He added that it was time for ministers to “wake up and smell the coffee.”



Downing Street has insisted that Britain had “One of the most resilient energy systems in the world”, however.

Officials confirmed that Andy Burnham is making preparations for the country to face severe disruption.

Darren Jones, former Cabinet Office minister, announced at the end of Keir Starmer’s premiership that work was being sped-up on “updating the government ‘war book.'”

The manual was last updated in 2004.

A social media campaign is now reportedly being prepared to tell people how to prepare for disruption caused by weather, hostile state action or cyber attacks.



A source told the Financial Times: “There will be practical advice on things you can do to improve domestic resilience, like having some bottled water and tinned food.

“It will be common sense, not scaremongering.”

The Cabinet Office said: “Safeguarding national security is the first priority of any government.

“We’re committed to raising awareness of simple steps households can take to make themselves more resilient, as well as driving forward the Home Defence Programme to build our country’s preparedness for various threats.”

News.title: Buc-ee’s confirms ‘visible’ tattoo ban in strict nationwide policy for all 56 stores
News.content:
NEW STORE POLICY Buc-ee’s confirms ‘visible’ tattoo ban in strict nationwide policy for all 56 stores

ROAD trip stop Buc-ee’s has forbidden their staff from sporting “visible tattoos” in a nationwide ban.

Famed across the US for the squeaky-clean bathrooms, Buc-ee’s has announced that staff at all 56 stores are also not allowed to wear “torn or faded clothing”.



Other dress code decrees include a ban on “unnatural coloured hair, open toe shoes, and body piercings.”

But what they must wear, according to their website, are “tan/khaki/black pants and a clean, professional, solid red shirt with a collar.”



“In cooler weather, employees may also wear a red sweater or coat.”

The Texan convenience chain has developed a cult-following in the US over the years.



Fans have said that they have transformed “necessity into an adventure.”

The world’s largest in Sevierville, Tennessee, offers a wide selection of bagged jerky with an eye-watering amount of flavours and even a brisket station.

Another part comes from the cleanliness of their bathrooms, even winning awards for being spotless.



The first store opened in Clute, Texas, in 1982.

Over 45 stores remain in Texas but the chain has expanded outside the Lone Star State and into places like Alabama, Florida, and South Carolina.

On Buc-ee’s website it says: “Ever since our inception in 1982, we have been committed to providing clean, friendly, and in stock experience for our customers.”

“Regardless of where you may find us, if the store is big ore small, near or far, the mission remains the same.”

News.title: Moment reckless driver mounts pavement to deliberately ram four men after being booted out of casino
News.content:
THIS is the moment a driver deliberately mounted the pavement to mow down four men after being booted out of a casino.

Nadeem Khan, 49, was captured hurtling towards the group in his Nissan Juke as they stood outside Napoleon’s Casino in Bradford, West Yorkshire.



The driver then miraculously missed the men and instead smashed through a line of bollards.

A judge later told Khan: “You could have killed those men.”



The thug has now been jailed for 47 months and banned from the roads for four years and 11 months.

He must also pass an extended re-test before he can legally drive again.



Bradford Crown Court heard Khan had been ushered out of the casino after becoming involved in an altercation.

He drove away but instead of heading home, Khan returned to the scene and deliberately sped towards the men.

Khan was later arrested at home after police found the damaged car abandoned.

The yob was initially charged with four counts of attempted murder but he admitted four alternative offences of attempting to cause grievous bodily harm with intent, as well as dangerous driving.



Judge Sophie McKone told him: “Whatever happened before your offending is absolutely no excuse for what you did.”

She added: “You mounted the pavement. You crashed through bollards and it was clearly your intention to cause those four men really serious harm.

“At the time none of the men posed any sort of risk to you.

“Whatever had happened has finished.

“You could have got in your car and driven away, but you made a decision to do that.”

News.title: Shocking moment ‘machete brawl’ erupts in UK city centre in broad daylight – as two men arrested and three injured
News.content:
THIS is the moment an alleged machete brawl erupted in broad daylight, with three men rushed to hospital.

Armed cops rushed to the scene at 1.45pm Monday following a report of a violent disturbance.



Footage shows one man lying on the floor being kicked by a group.

Video also appears to show one person brandishing a long blade in the air before running after a man.



Police said violence broke out in Truro, Cornwall, at around 1.45pm.

The force added that one man suffered a “potentially serious injury” in the fracas.

Two others were left with minor injuries.

The force said those involved are believed to have known each other.



A number of witnesses told CornwallLive there was an extremely large police and ambulance presence in the area.

One person said: “[The road is] all cordoned off around Burger King, around 30 coppers, 12 police cars”.

Sinjar Zurel, 27, and Seyin Zurel, 24, have been charged with two counts of causing grievous bodily harm with intent.

Sinjar Zurel has also been charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm and possession of a knife blade/sharp pointed article in a public place.

They have been remanded in custody to appear at Truro Magistrates’ Court today.

News.title: Did CIA have intel on plot to attack Nato? Spy chief ‘rushes to Moscow on secret trip to warn Putin to back down’
News.content:
CIA chief John Ratcliffe’s top secret visit to Moscow could have been to warn Vladimir Putin not to launch a daring attack on Nato, experts fear.

The spy boss’ unprecedented trip has raised concerns the Russian tyrant could be plotting to test the alliance after worrying US intelligence reports.



It is the first time since Putin invaded Ukraine that the CIA has publicly visited Russia. The last time was in November 2021, when CIA head William Burns warned Putin not to attack.

Neither the US or Russia has made any official comment on Ratcliffe’s bombshell visit – but the urgency and rare nature of the trip has sparked speculation.



It comes amid concerning claims US intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a mass military mobilisation and could attack Nato.

Ukraine has been warning for weeks that Putin is ramping up plans to deploy 300,000 troops to the frontline and try to gain further territory.



US intelligence has now received similar information, sparking Ratcliffe’s “unprecedented” trip, according to the Wall Street Journal.

They also claim the CIA has uncovered rumoured Russian plans around testing the Nato alliance in the Baltics in the coming months.

Former Deputy Director of US National Intelligence Beth Sanner said she believes Ratcliffe may have told Russia: “We know what you are thinking about doing, and you better not.”

Experts told The Sun they agree the most likely reason for the trip would be the US delivering a stark warning to Putin based on intelligence.

Bob Seeley, former MP and author of The New Total War which focuses on the war in Ukraine, said: “The main suggestion is that the CIA have gone to tell Putin, ‘don’t do anything stupid in the Baltics because we’re ready for you’.



“They are clearly on the alert, and picking up stuff if they’ve gone there like this.”

Bob added: “When the CIA turn up and say don’t do it, you’ve got to take that pretty seriously.”

A CIA director has not stepped foot in Moscow for almost five years making Ratcliffe’s trip a major moment in US-Russian relations.



The last time was just three months before Putin’s invasion of Ukraine when Bill Burns directly warned the tyrant a full-scale assault would be a disaster for him and his country.

Burns claims he said the US knew what Russia was planning and issued a defiant plea for Putin to halt any invasion.

It fell on deaf ears as Putin sent tanks into Ukraine in February 2022 and continues to fight on several fronts today.

His military has suffered 1.4 million battlefield casualties – including an estimated 77,000 deaths in 2026 alone.

Hamish noted: “When Burns went there in 2021 it didn’t really have an impact, but we’re in a different position now.”



“In 2021 when Putin looked West, he didn’t see a conventional deterrence and he didn’t see something that would affect him.

“In the five years since that visit, Europe has re-energised its military capability and spent billions building up defences.

“I think the Kremlin will realise the Russian military has been absolutely hammered over the last five years, whereas the European armies and the US armies are pretty much intact.”

US attempts to achieve peace in Europe have so far relied heavily on Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Both men are close to the US leadership but have little to no experience in military situations or real world conflict.



Hamish believes the use of a powerful CIA director is a clear sign the US is taking the latest intelligence reports seriously.

“This is pretty extraordinary. These things do not happen very often.

“So it shows a sort of step up, as heads of CIA tend to be fairly undemonstrative.



“I’m sure this would have been a non-political, non-diplomatic type of meeting which was very much about the facts.

“I should think it was a very straightforward laying down and perhaps saying what the consequences of any actions the Russians might be thinking of taking.

“And perhaps also the CIA just showing their hand a little bit and revealing a little bit of what they know.”

“If you’re thinking about doing anything, just be aware, we know what you’re thinking about, so don’t do it.”

Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed Ratcliffe and Putin did not meet yesterday and that the chats were between intelligence services only.



It comes despite the Russian leader reportedly clearing his schedule for a “major event”.

Kremlin propagandist Alexander Yunashev claimed a major event involving the president had been scheduled for Tuesday but was scrapped “a couple of days ago”.

A source also told Axios the US had warned Ukraine to pause strikes on the capital, telling it a senior delegation was travelling to Moscow.

Former CIA Senior Operations Officer Sean Wiswesser told The Sun: “I hope the meeting represents a warning.

“Russia respects strength and we have not shown enough of that as an alliance, let’s hope the CIA visit will help change that.”



Hamish added: “If the boss of the CIA has managed to turn the dial towards peace, then I think everybody would really appreciate and welcome.it”

Wiswesser continued saying that while the CIA appearing to put their foot down with the tyrant is a positive sign, it remains just a verbal threat.

Should Putin mobilise troops and attempt to smash through Ukraine’s defensive lines then the US must come down hard on Russia, Wiswesser said.

“Deterrence cannot be a one-way proposition with escalation going unanswered,” he said.

If the US wanted to ramp up pressure even more, they should begin to send more Patriot, Taurus and other long-range missile systems to Ukraine so they “have the tools they need to finish the job”.



In the aftermath of the eight-hour CIA trip, the appearance of several “doomsday planes” spotted circling above the US sparked concerns on Tuesday.

At least five Boeing E-6 Mercury aircraft were seen on the West Coast and in the central US, according to aviation enthusiasts.

The giant jets are designed to withstand electromagnetic pulses and even nuclear and thermal blasts – hence the doomsday moniker.

Top US military commanders would be aboard the aircraft if fears of a catastrophic disaster broke out so they can plan Washington’s next move.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

President Donald Trump has his own special jet for the same reasons – the impervious US Air Force E-4B “Nightwatch” aircraft.



E-6Bs do routinely fly in the region for training making their appearance not unprecedented.

News.title: Do I need eclipse glasses to watch the lunar eclipse? Why you can see the Blood Moon safely without eye protection
News.content:
IF you spent the recent solar eclipse scrambling for some ISO 12312-2 certified glasses, you might be wondering if you need to pull them out for the upcoming lunar eclipse.

Stargazers across the UK are in for a treat in the early hours of Friday, August 28.



The UK will experience a deep partial lunar eclipse, with over 93% of the Moon’s face plunging into the darkest part of Earth’s shadow. It will look almost identical to a total lunar eclipse.

Thankfully, you can leave the specialist eyewear in the drawer and look directly at the Moon with your bare eyes.



Why is a lunar eclipse safe to look at directly?

During a solar eclipse, you are looking directly at the Sun.

Even when the Sun is partially blocked by the Moon, its remaining rays unleash intense ultraviolet (UV) and infrared radiation.

Because the human retina has no pain receptors, looking at the Sun without specialised filters can cause silent, permanent damage – known as solar retinopathy.

During a lunar eclipse, Earth moves directly between the Sun and the Moon.

You are not staring at the Sun, you are looking at the Moon as it passes into Earth’s shadow.

The Moon generates no light of its own – it simply reflects sunlight.



During a lunar eclipse, instead of bright, direct rays, the Moon receives only indirect sunlight filtered through Earth’s atmosphere.

This atmospheric filtering scatters shorter blue light waves and lets longer red wavelengths pass through, casting a deep crimson or copper glow across the lunar surface – the “Blood Moon” effect.

Because the light reaching your eyes is far dimmer than even a normal full Moon, looking at it poses no risk to your vision.

How to see the lunar eclipse in the UK

You’ll want to set your alarm for the early hours of Friday, August 28 if you want to step outside and enjoy the show.

The action kicks off at 2.23am, as Earth’s outer shadow first touches the Moon, causing a subtle dimming.



The partial eclipse officially begins at 3.33am, when a distinct dark “bite” will appear across the lunar disk as it enters the Earth’s main shadow.

The peak of the eclipse will arrive at 5.12am, when maximum coverage will cause the Moon to glow in dramatic reddish-orange hues – the “Blood Moon” effect.

Around 6.15am, the Moon dips below the horizon, wrapping up visibility across the UK.

To get the best view, face west-southwest in the early hours before dawn.

Because peak coverage happens low in the sky, heading to high ground with an open view is your best bet.



Avoid spots blocked by tall buildings, dense trees, or steep hills.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

You don’t need to bring any special gear, but if you’re lucky enough to own a standard pair of binoculars or a camera with a modest zoom lens, you should be able to get a closer look at the crimson-lit craters.

Remember of course, that the visibility of anticipated celestial events can also rely on the mercy of the Great British weather…

News.title: Middlesbrough fire live: Two house fire 'murders' may be linked to organised crime
News.content:
Police are at the scene of a house fire in Middlesbrough

Seven fire engines were called to Birchington Avenue and Leighton Road, which are closed, after a house fire in Grangetown - two people have died and a murder investigation has been launched

Middlesbrough fire live: Two house fire 'murders' may be linked to organised crime

Two people have died following a devastating house fire in Grangetown, Middlesbrough.

A murder investigation has been launched, and police say links to organised crime cannot be ruled out.

Cleveland Police said officers were called to a house on Birchington Avenue at 5:23am, where two people died. A woman remains in the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI) in a critical condition, and a further three people have suffered non-life-threatening injuries and are in hospital.

Seven fire engines were called to Birchington Avenue and Leighton Road, which are closed, while crews deal with the incident. Armed officers are at the scene.

The fire occurred about two miles from the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers, on Saturday morning.

News.title: Man jailed after dumping body of dad-of-five arson killer inside wheelie bin
News.content:
Man jailed after dumping body of dad-of-five arson killer inside wheelie bin

Steven Wales reported the death of father-of-five Paul Smith to police, two days after the 40-year-old is believed to have overdosed in a bath

View 3 Images Paul Smith killed an elderly couple during his arson attack but died before he could be brought to justice (Image: LIVERPOOL ECHO)

A man who dumped the body of a dad in a wheelie bin was branded a "scumbag" in court as he was jailed today.

‌



Steven Wales, 61, reported the death of father-of-five Paul Smith two days after the 40-year-old is believed to have overdosed in a bath.

‌



The report was made on July 22 last year, when Wales, of Pope Street in Bootle, Merseyside, called the police to say Smith “had died in the bath”.

‌



Once at the scene, officers found the dad’s body in a bin at the back of some derelict properties. The discovery was made a week after Smith had carried out a revenge arson attack that turned fatal on South John Street in St Helens, killing an elderly couple.

Wales, a convicted killer, allegedly “panicked” when he found his friend, Smith, dead while Wales was on licence out of prison. This supposedly led to his decision to "violate the most fundamental of dignities to be afforded to someone" and leaving his friend’s body in the bin.

Wales told officers he had moved Smith's body to a wheelie bin in a nearby overgrown garden, where attempts were discovered to have been made to conceal the body under litter, green waste and furniture. When he was arrested on suspicion of murder, Wales told officers that Smith had asked to use his flat to bathe and wash his clothes.

‌



When Wales returned home, he said he found his friend dead in the bath and "was worried about going back to prison", leading to him placing the body in the bin.

When he was jailed at Liverpool Crown Court today, Smith’s brother shouted “you little scumbag” from the public gallery while Wales was taken to the cells.

View 3 Images Steven Wales (Image: Liverpool ECHO)

‌



Wearing glasses and a black and grey Berghaus coat over a black Monterrain t-shirt in the dock, Wales showed no reaction as he was jailed for 28 months, Liverpool Echo reports.

Smith, who had been a "working family man" but developed a class A drug dependency in late 2024. He led a "chaotic lifestyle" after he was released from prison, the court also heard.

Christopher Hopkins, prosecuting, said: "It appears that he was with this defendant at the defendant's home on the weekend of July 19 and 20 last year. At some point, they had taken drugs together.

‌



"Mr Smith's mother spoke to him daily. She last spoke to him in the late afternoon of Saturday, July 19. His brother reported him missing on Monday evening. It was at 9.22am the next morning that the defendant dialled 999 and reported that a man had died of a drug overdose in his bath two days previously."

Mr Hopkins added: "[Wales] has violated the most fundamental of dignities to be afforded to someone. His actions were deeply disrespectful."

A trial earlier this year was told Eric Greener, 77, and Sheila Jackson, 83, died following an arson attack at their home on July 15, 2025. The proceedings were told the man who carried out the attack was Smith.

‌



Kevin Weetman, Kylie Maynard and Lee Owens were all convicted. Smith, known as Smigger, and Owens went to the property together and intended for the victim of the attack to be Ms Jackson’s son, George Jackson, who sometimes lived at the house.

Weetman was said to have planned the attack after Mr Jackson refused to sell drugs for him. Weetman was jailed for life with a minimum of 25 years, "trusted lieutenant" Maynard was jailed for 23 years and Owens was sentenced to 13 years and six months.

View 3 Images The wheelie bin containing Smith's body was found at the back of some derelict properties in July last year (Image: Liverpool Echo)

‌



Smith had been reported missing on July 21 by his brother, Michael, having last contacted a family member on July 19. The father, who lived on Lower Breck Road, was said to have spent July 20 at a house on Coniston Street in Everton, where he took a range of drugs such as heroin, cocaine and several sedatives.

An inquest in July this year was told Smith is then believed to have overdosed in the bath, with water being found in his lungs. Smith's medical cause of death was given as mixed drug toxicity.

Wales pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Smith when he appeared at Liverpool Crown Court earlier this month. He has a total of 32 previous convictions for 64 offences, including receiving eight years for manslaughter in 2009 and five years for possession of heroin and cocaine with intent to supply, affray, possession of a bladed article in a public place and being in charge of a dangerous out of control dog causing injury in 2023.

‌



He was recalled on licence for nine months in relation to the latter sentence as a result of his arrest in connection with Smith's death, having been released in October 2024.

Joanne Maxwell, defending, said on Wales' behalf that when Wales returned home, he found Smith with a needle close by. He felt "immediate, significant shock" and Ms Maxwell said he "clearly did not think properly, he panicked".

He had taken cocaine and diazepam and was fearful of going back to prison. Ms Maxwell said: "He knows that he should have contacted the emergency services immediately, and certainly before he moved Mr Smith's body.

Article continues below

"He has accepted full responsibility for his actions, and he is only too aware of the seriousness of those actions. He feels great shame, and he is, of course, aware of the impact it must have had and the distress he has caused to Mr Smith's family.

"He also says that, by carrying out those actions, it has had a significant and lasting psychological impact on him and is something that will live with him for the rest of his life. He asks me to mitigate on his behalf that he did not cause or play any role in the death of Mr Smith."

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan 'arrive in UK' as they make bombshell return to Britain
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan 'arrive in UK' as they make bombshell return to Britain

Prince Harry and Meghan are said to have travelled privately from California to the UK with their two children - just days after it emerged they planned to relocate back to Britain

View Image The Sussexes are moving back to the UK today, it is claimed (Image: The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan have arrived in the UK with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet today, it has been claimed.

‌



The Sussexes reportedly landed in the country after privately travelling from California to start their new life in Britain.

‌



They are to settle themselves in the UK for an “extended period”, with the children enrolled in British schools ready to start in September, it emerged just days ago.

‌



The duke and duchess decamped to California more than six years ago amid the turbulent Megxit crisis, which was followed by ongoing family fallouts and a barrage of accusations the couple fired at the Prince and Princess of Wales and the King and Queen.

Rumours have abounded as to where Harry and Meghan will choose to settle, with suggestions including rural locations in the Cotswolds in Oxfordshire or Gloucestershire, amid speculation over which schools they have chosen for their children. The couple are understood to have secured a home outside of London, which is a non-royal residence.

According to The Telegraph, the family landed at Birmingham Airport at lunchtime. A source close to the Sussexes told the publication: “How long will they stay? I don’t know, but it will be for an extended period. Whether that’s six months, a year, two years… who knows.” The Mirror has asked the Sussexes spokesperson for comment.

‌



News of their return sent shockwaves through the royal households, with insiders revealing how the royal family remain intensely wary of the Sussexes swapping their California base to set up home in the UK, six years after leaving their royal roles behind.

Sources close to the King and the Prince of Wales have confirmed the monarch and his heir are “in complete lockstep” in terms of not allowing Harry and Meghan to have a “half in, half out” role within the royal family.

The decision to relocate to the UK comes just weeks after Harry secured a meeting with his wife and children with the King and Queen at the monarch’s Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.

‌



While the Sussexes are believed to be bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them to Britain, their 10 pet chickens, which live in a coop called ‘Archie’s Chick Inn ’, will stay at their Montecito home. The couple are keeping their home in the US, with household staff set to look after the birds when Harry and Meghan are away.

The decision to keep on their house across the Atlantic and their beloved chickens there is being seen as a sign that they will still spend time in California.

Meanwhile, it has been claimed that Meghan is still in talks for a potential role in Netflix show The Gentlemen, which is filmed in Britain.

‌



Last week, it was reported that she could be poised to land a part in the Guy Ritchie crime caper, which was confirmed by Netflix on Monday to have been renewed for a third season. The show is about a British Duke who unexpectedly inherits his father’s country estate and discovers it is home to a cannabis empire run by notorious criminals.

Talks are said to be at an early stage, with a role being written for Meghan, who previously appeared in Suits, meaning it is unclear how many episodes she would appear in.

News.title: Andy Burnham gives defiant Ukraine warning after CIA chief makes secret Russia trip
News.content:
Andy Burnham gives defiant Ukraine warning after CIA chief makes secret Russia trip

Prime Minister Andy Burnham stood firm on his backing for Kyiv, saying 'We are supporting them, and that won’t change' amid fears over further Russian aggression

View 2 Images Andy Burnham looks at debris from a recent strike on Lukanivska market in Kyiv (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham issued a defiant message about the UK’s support for Ukraine amid fears of fresh aggression from Russia.

‌



The Prime Minister stood firm on his backing for Kyiv, saying: “We are supporting them, and that won’t change.” It comes as the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe, flew to Moscow for unannounced talks on Tuesday, triggering widespread speculation that it could pre-empt new military action by Vladimir Putin.

‌



"There were contacts with the intelligence services," Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov, told reporters. "There were no meetings with the president of Russia. That's all I can say on the subject. Naturally, President Putin is briefed immediately about everything," he added.

‌



One of the last known times a CIA chief travelled to Russia was in the months ahead of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Recent US intelligence reports have reportedly warned that Putin may attempt to test Nato's resolve by mounting a small land incursion in the next few years.

Andy Burnham hits back after Russia accuses UK of 'participating' in war over missile blueprints READ MORE :

Andy Burnham arrives in Kyiv to share long-range missile blueprints with Ukraine READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham travelled to Ukraine to reassure President Volodymyr Zelensky of the UK's support (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The Kremlin appears to have been emboldened by stalled peace talks as Donald Trump's attention is fixed on his disastrous war with Iran.

‌



Asked if Brits should be worried that the talks herald the possibility of attacks by the Russians on the UK, Mr Burnham said: “It’s a challenging situation when we look around the world right now.

“But from what we’re doing, people need to be sure of this: We’re doing what we’ve done since the start of this conflict, which is to provide that back-up support to Ukraine to be able to defend themselves, because they do need to do that.

“They are obviously in an impossible situation, so challenging, but Britain needs to be there and be a constant as they go through this illegal invasion that they’re facing.

‌



“So, we will continue to do that. Prime ministers before me gave that assurance and I visited Ukraine to send a really clear message to the Ukrainian people that Britain isn’t changing course. We said we would support them. We are supporting them, and that won’t change.”

The Prime Minister travelled to Kyiv on Monday for his first visit to Ukraine since coming to office, where he told President Volodymyr Zelensky there would be “no change in the UK’s steadfast support”.

In a move that angered the Kremlin, Mr Burnham agreed to share top-secret blueprints to help Kyiv build long-range Scalp missiles, which can hit deep into Russia.

Article continues below

A spokesman for Putin said Britain "methodically and regularly pours fuel on the fire". But Mr Burnham shot back: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

Mr Burnham also appealed to Ukraine's allies to send more interceptor missiles to Kyiv at his first coalition of the willing meeting. He said he hoped to use a trip to the US in September to lobby Donald Trump for more support for Ukraine.

Mr Burnham signalled he would attend the UN General Assembly meeting in New York, with officials preparing the ground for a potential meeting with the US President.

News.title: Trump asked Ukraine to halt attacks on Russia during CIA chief’s secret Moscow mission
News.content:
Trump asked Ukraine to halt attacks on Russia during CIA chief’s secret Moscow mission

Ukraine suspended strikes on Moscow and other Russian cities at Washington’s request while CIA director John Ratcliffe made a secret visit to the Russian capital.

View 3 Images A US military C-17 transport aircraft was tracked flying into Moscow as CIA director John Ratcliffe made his secret visit to Russia (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ukraine was ordered to hold its fire on major Russian cities after America’s CIA director John Ratcliffe flew into the country for secret talks.

‌



Washington contacted Kyiv last week and asked it not to strike Moscow, St Petersburg and a swathe of northern Russia while a plane carrying the senior US intelligence official was flying into and out of the capital. The request covered Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and was made to protect Ratcliffe and the US delegation during the highly unusual visit.

‌



Ukraine complied, before resuming strikes early on Wednesday following Ratcliffe’s departure. Russia later claimed its forces had shot down at least 426 Ukrainian drones overnight. Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow on Tuesday for unannounced meetings with Russian officials, marking the first known visit to Russia by a serving CIA director in almost five years.

‌



View 3 Images CIA director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow for highly sensitive talks as Ukraine was asked to suspend strikes on major Russian cities (Image: AP)

Andy Burnham gives defiant Ukraine warning after CIA chief makes secret Russia trip READ MORE :

Neither the White House nor the Kremlin disclosed the purpose of the trip, who Ratcliffe met or what was discussed.

Flight-tracking data showed a US military C-17 transport aircraft travelling from the US to Latvia before continuing to Moscow. The aircraft left Riga airport at 5.50 am and appeared to land at Moscow’s Vnukovo International Airport at around 7.04 am. It returned to the Latvian capital shortly before 5 pm.

‌



Video posted on social media appeared to show the C-17 approaching Vnukovo, while separate footage purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow. The CIA, White House and Pentagon did not immediately give details of Ratcliffe’s mission.

The trip is believed to have been his first to Russia since becoming CIA director and was one of the highest-level visits by an American official during Donald Trump’s second term. Ratcliffe has, however, maintained contact with senior Russian intelligence officials.

Former British military attaché to Moscow John Foreman suggested the trip could be linked to efforts to manage the risk of a wider confrontation between Russia and the West. He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high-ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

‌



There was also speculation that Ratcliffe’s visit could have involved negotiations over Americans being detained in Russia. The CIA director previously played a role in talks which secured the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina after she spent more than a year imprisoned in Russia, accused of providing support to Ukraine.

The agency was also involved in the major 2024 prisoner exchange, which secured the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, former US Marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.

Ratcliffe's journey came against the backdrop of deeply strained relations between Washington and Moscow following Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

‌



Russia has since faced sweeping Western sanctions and widespread diplomatic isolation, although the Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to reopen negotiations with Moscow.

View 3 Images Ukraine held back attacks on Moscow at Washington’s request while a senior US delegation was inside the Russian capital (Image: GAVRIIL GRIGOROV/SPUTNIK/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump met Putin during a summit in Alaska last year in an attempt to push forward efforts to end the war. The talks failed to produce a breakthrough, however, and subsequent US-led negotiations involving Russia and Ukraine have largely stalled.

Article continues below

Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit represented a rare direct channel between two governments whose relations have remained hostile despite Trump's attempts to negotiate with Putin. The last known visit to Moscow by a serving CIA director was made by Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, in November 2021, just months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Burns travelled to the Russian capital as the Biden administration sought to warn Putin against launching an attack on Ukraine. The latest visit came as Kyiv continues to use increasingly sophisticated long-range drones to strike military sites, oil facilities and other targets deep inside Russian territory.

News.content:
Met Office urges Brits in 73 areas to prepare 'emergency' kit on Thursday – list

More heavy rain and thunderstorms are on the cards on Thursday as Met Office weather forecasters urge Brits to gather essential items and prepare an 'emergency' kit

View Image Weather models show heavy rain moving across the UK on Thursday (Image: Met Office)

The Met Office is urging people across large swathes of England and Wales to consider preparing an “emergency” kit for Thursday.

‌



It comes after the Met Office issued two weather warnings for thunderstorms, one for today and one for Thursday.

‌



Today’s warning is in force until 10pm and covers parts of southern, eastern and central England as well as parts of Wales. Cities including London and Birmingham are all impacted.

‌



However, a larger warning is due to come into force at 6am on Thursday, lasting until 10pm. Again it covers parts of England and Wales, and warns as much as 75mm of rain could fall across 12 hours.

It also warns there is a risk of lightning strikes, hail, floods and power cuts, and people in the warning area are urged to consider preparing for the extreme weather.

‌



If your area is prone to flash flooding, the Met Office says: “Consider preparing a flood plan and an emergency flood kit.”

The Met Office recommends including the following items in any flood kit: insurance documents and list of contact numbers; torch and spare batteries; first aid kit and any prescription medicines; warm waterproof clothes and blankets; bottled water and snacks; battery or wind-up radio; supplies for looking after your baby or pet.

‌



The warning also states people should “ensure moveable objects or temporary structures are well secured” before strong winds arrive, including bins, garden furniture, trampolines, tents, gazebos, sheds and fences.

Finally, the Met Office urges people to prepare for potential power cuts by gathering torches, batteries, a mobile phone power pack and other essential items.

News.title: Meghan Markle shares telling joke in first Instagram post since UK return bombshell
News.content:
Meghan Markle shares telling joke in first Instagram post since UK return bombshell

Meghan has made her first personal social media posts since it was revealed that she, Prince Harry and their children were moving back to the UK by the end of the month

View 6 Images Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex (Image: Getty)

Meghan Markle has returned to Instagram for the first time since the explosive news she and Prince Harry are moving back to the UK - with a joke about chickens.

‌



The Sussexes and their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are to settle themselves in the UK for an “extended period” of time by the end of the month, with the children enrolled in British schools ready to start in September.

‌



So far, neither Meghan nor Harry have spoken publicly about their surprise plans that come six years after they dramatically quit their royal roles, which emerged a week ago, but the Duchess of Sussex has posted on her Instagram account for the first time since then.

‌



Prince Harry and Meghan to leave pet chickens in California amid telling sign on UK move READ MORE :

6 View 6 Images The Sussexes are moving back to the UK in the coming days (Image: The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Meghan Markle shared a joke about chickens on Instagram

She posted an Instagram story in which she chuckled at what appeared to be a tea towel with the message: “People who take care of chickens are literally chicken tenders”. It follows news that the Sussexes’ brood of chickens are remaining at their home in California to be cared for there - while their pet dogs Mia and Pula will travel to the UK and live with them in their new home.

Meanwhile, Meghan has also unveiled the latest addition to her As Ever range – Spiced Apple Butter. On Monday, she sparked mystery when her As Ever Instagram page posted a video of Meghan picking apples from an orchard and collecting them in a basket.

‌



The jar of “orchard apples and fragrant spices” is being launched today, “just in time for fall”, with Meghan’s brand saying the product captures the season’s “promise of crisp mornings and changing leaves just around the corner”. It comes as some reports have suggested the Sussexes’ stay in the UK could last as little as anything from just the autumn to six months, or even a year or so, with the family retaining their houses in Montecito and Portugal.

6 View 6 Images Meghan could be seen picking apples from an orchard for a new As Ever product (Image: aseverofficial/Instagram) 6 View 6 Images Meghan will continue to run As Ever from the UK (Image: aseverofficial/Instagram)

‌



Rumours have also swirled around Meghan’s plans to return to acting, with speculation that she is in talks to star in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix gangster series The Gentlemen. The Sussexes, who are remaining as non-working royals, stepped away from the monarchy six years ago for a new life in the US, from where they criticised the royal family and the institution.

Meanwhile, it has emerged that Harry has joined actors Sir Stephen Fry, Sharon Stone and Alyssa Milano in guest-curating a Ukraine photography exhibition in Los Angeles. The collection of images is set to go on show in California on September 11, by which time Harry is expected to have set up home in the UK.

Former soldier Harry will miss the unveiling of Postcode Ukraine: Diary of a Volunteer, which has been put together to raise funds for frontline grassroots aid as Russia ’s full-scale invasion nears its fifth year. The duke selected a moving black-and-white picture by photographer Mark Neville of a schoolboy in a blazer and shorts standing in the rubble of a destroyed farm in the Kyiv region in October 2022 for the exhibition.

‌



View 6 Images Harry on a trip to Ukraine last September (Image: Emmi Korhonen/Lehtikuva/Shutterstock)

Harry, who travelled to Kyiv in April and made a direct appeal to Russian President Vladimir Putin to “stop this war”, personally chose the image for the display by British Kyiv-based artist Neville. News of Harry’s involvement followed a message from the King to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in which Charles shared his “sincere and special wishes” on the 35th anniversary of the war-torn country’s independence from the Soviet Union.

Article continues below

The photography exhibition, which focuses on Ukraine’s children, families and volunteers, opens at Westwood Contemporary Gallery in LA from September 11 to 30, and is the first major presentation of Neville’s Ukraine photography work. Each guest curator, including Harry, separately selected a photograph by Neville that resonated with them personally and also contributed a reflection on the importance of that image.

Others who helped curate the display included comedian and author Sir Stephen, who is a friend of the King, as well as activists Stone and Milano; Oleksandra Matviichuk, who heads the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Centre for Civil Liberties; and Ukrainian poet Kateryna Babkina.

News.title: HRT shown to reduce dementia risk as study reveals best age to start taking it
News.content:
HRT shown to reduce dementia risk as study reveals best age to start taking it

Biggest ever study of HRT following 183,000 post-menopausal women in Britain shows how the treatment appears to boost cognitive health and cut dementia risk

View 3 Images Woman taking HRT (stock) (Image: Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RF)

HRT appears to reduce women’s risk of developing dementia by 10% according to the largest ever study of the treatment.

‌



Landmark research following 183,000 post-menopausal women in Britain for 13 years identified a "window of opportunity" for women to start taking HRT (hormone replacement therapy) between the ages of 46 and 56. Overall women taking HRT for at least a year were 10% less likely to go on to develop dementia and 16% less likely to get Alzheimer's.

‌



The research by the University of East Anglia (UEA) and the University of Exeter appears to show which women can benefit from HRT and at what point in their lives. It comes after previous research linked HRT to a very small increase in breast cancer risk which had deterred some women.

‌



View 3 Images Woman having hot flush at home (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

Menopausal women to get ‘vital’ new pill for hot flushes and night sweats on NHS READ MORE :

Women taking certain HRT drugs could be at slightly higher risk of heart attacks READ MORE :

Study leader Professor Anne-Marie Minihane said: "Dementia affects millions of people worldwide, with women making up almost two-thirds of Alzheimer's disease cases, the main form of dementia. In addition to living longer, the reason behind the higher female prevalence is thought to be related to the effects of menopause on brain metabolism.

"We wanted to better understand how HRT could prevent dementia and to assess if particular groups of women may respond differently. The protective association between HRT and dementia was not the same for all women."

‌



Researchers analysed health data on 183,450 women from the UK Biobank database. Over a 13-year period 4,000 of them were diagnosed with dementia. Those who started HRT aged 46 to 50 had a 13% reduced risk of dementia, while those who started taking HRT when they were aged 51 to 56 saw a 23% reduced risk.

View 3 Images Menopause symptoms can be debilitating and are linked to reduced cognitive health (Image: Getty Images)

Commenting on the study, Prof Aimee Spector, of University College London, said: "This supports the `window of opportunity' hypothesis, suggesting that HRT use during the menopause transition phase - where symptoms are typically more problematic - is important."

‌



The strongest benefit was identified for women who took HRT after surgical menopause such as a hysterectomy. These women had a 26% lower risk of being diagnosed with dementia. Women with the gene variant APOE4 - a risk factor for Alzheimer's - who also took HRT, had a 13% reduced dementia risk.

Prof Minihane said: "We also found that women whose bodies naturally produced less oestrogen over their lives - because they started their periods late or hit menopause early - seemed to get more help from HRT. Their risk of dementia was around 16% lower with HRT."

Prof David Llewellyn, from the University of Exeter Medical School, said: "These findings represent a significant step forward. Rather than asking simply whether HRT affects dementia risk, we've been able to identify which women are most likely to benefit, and when.”

Article continues below

Prof Minihane added: "While HRT has long been prescribed primarily to relieve menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats, this work suggests it may also play a role in long term cognitive health for some women."

News.title: Murder probe as two people dead in house fire in Middlesbrough
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after two people died in a house fire.

The blaze in Grangetown, Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating what had happened but was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area as this investigation progresses, and to provide reassurance to local communities, who will no doubt be impacted by this tragic incident."

Patrols have been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

The Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.

King Charles was told of the move earlier this month. The family visited the King at his Highgrove home in July this year, but it is understood the move was not discussed.

Before that visit, Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.

News.title: From 'dirt poor' to philanthropic superstar - the life of Dolly Parton
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Ex-chief constable investigated over ban on Israeli Maccabi Tel Aviv fans
News.content:
The former chief constable of West Midlands Police is being investigated by the police watchdog for gross misconduct over the banning of Israeli Maccabi Tel Aviv fans from a match against Aston Villa.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has given notice that it is investigating Craig Guildford, as well as three police officers and a staff member.

The IOPC launched an independent investigation in January to examine the involvement of West Midlands Police officers in the planning and preparation of the match at Villa Park on 6 November 2025.

The ban attracted national and international debate, with the government saying it would do everything in its power to have it overturned.

The IOPC said evidence indicated that Guildford "may have had oversight on an intelligence briefing document presented to the safety advisory group (SAG) that was later reported to have contained inaccuracies and misleading information".

It is alleged the briefing document "gave an imbalanced view of the risk away fans posed", contributing to the decision to ban the supporters.

The police watchdog added: "We consider Mr Guildford may have failed to ensure due diligence and the highest level of scrutiny over such an influential document."

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged people would find the increase "difficult" but highlighted his move to cut VAT from electricity bills, which he said would help from October.

He said the government would "continue to look... at how we get energy prices down in the long term".

As well as the VAT cut, the government said the warm homes discount would take Â£150 off bills for six million households this winter.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government must "put cheap energy first", saying while it had promised to cut bills by Â£300 they had "gone up by nearly Â£400 instead".

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said Burnham needed to "wake up to the scale of the challenge" and make bold changes to lower bills.

Reform UK treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick said households faced a "difficult period ahead" and said Labour's "net zero ideology" is driving up bills.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed in, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use proceeds to help those struggling with bills.

Longer term, he said Burnham should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting," he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

He said the gap between gas and electricity bills meant it would be cheaper for households to transition to heat pumps.

News.title: At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire
News.content:
At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire on a hospital ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad.

The fire broke out on the third floor of the mother and child unit of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital, one of the main state-run hospitals in the city, on Wednesday morning.

An air conditioning unit caught fire, a spokesman for the hospital told the BBC.

The fire killed 14 of the 15 babies who were in the ward at the time, a spokesperson said. Seven other babies, two men and 10 mothers were also rescued from elsewhere in the hospital, according to Pakistan's minister of state for interior.

The babies in the ward were either in incubators or hooked on oxygen equipment, Pakistan's Health Minister Mustafa Kamal told Geo News. Oxygen is not flammable on its own, but it can accelerate a fire, making materials burn hotter and faster.

Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has suspended Federal Secretary of Health Aslam Ghauri, a top official in the health department, removing him from his post.

The PM has been chairing a high-level meeting on the hospital fire, and has expressed "deep anger" at some officials, the information ministry said.

Some families recognised their deceased babies through their wristbands, while others could identify them based on their ages, Pakistan's Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry told the BBC. Some of the babies were only three hours old, he said.

Eyewitnesses described chaotic and harrowing scenes at the hospital, including intense smoke and broken glass, with some complaining that rescuers were slow to respond.

One of them, Khurram Mehmood, told the AFP news agency his three-day-old daughter died in the fire and claimed that rescuers took hours to arrive: "We were sitting on the road waiting for help."

Another witness, Abdul Ghafoor, told AFP the fire spread "very quickly".

He said he went into the hospital to try to help save patients but could not reach the maternity ward: "There was thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped... rescue teams arrived after almost two hours."

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: CIA chief met Russian intelligence services but not Putin, Kremlin says
News.content:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) John Ratcliffe has met Russia's intelligence services during his visit to Moscow, the Kremlin has said.

Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday in a rare and unannounced visit.

"There were contacts with the intelligence services," Vladimir Putin's press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters.

"There were no meetings with the president of Russia. That's all I can say on the subject. Naturally, President Putin is briefed immediately about everything," he added.

Peskov made the comments in response to a question at his daily press briefing from a reporter at the Russian newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta, who asked if Vladimir Putin was informed about the CIA chief meetings and "at what level" they were held.

Putin's spokesman was also asked by the BBC's Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg what was the topic of the CIA talks.

"I have nothing to add to what I've already said on the subject," Peskov replied.

It was too early to say what impact this meeting would have over repairing bilateral US Russian relations, he said.

"How much this will impact the overall process of recovering our bilateral relations from the profound crisis they're currently in, it is premature to say."

But contacts between intelligence agencies are "a positive phenomenon, a positive process," Peskov added, saying they often continue "even during the most difficult moments" in relations between the two countries.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit Russia during President Donald Trump's second term.

In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021 - when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine. Weeks later, the Kremlin launched its full-scale war on Ukraine.

Since then, the US has had strained relations with Russia, which has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attachÃ© to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.

News.title: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
News.content:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

News.title: Yellow warnings remain in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid until 22:00 BST, and was amended on Wednesday morning to cover northern and eastern Wales, as well as north-west England, the Midlands and parts of eastern and southern England.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

Another Met Office yellow warning is in place for Thursday, when more thunderstorms are expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: 'Ironing board' seats to be replaced on Thameslink
News.content:
"Ironing board" seats on some commuter trains will get extra cushioning, the transport secretary has said, more than a decade after the government spent Â£1.6bn of public money building the fleet.

Heidi Alexander announced that more than 60,000 seats on all 115 Thameslink trains would get new cushions and backrests, replacing much-criticised thin and hard seats.

She said the work, set to begin in 2027 and last two years, was "public ownership of our railways in action" as part of the new Great British Railways programme.

However, some have criticised how the Department for Transport (DfT) awarded a Â£1.6bn contract for the trains despite being warned of the seat discomfort at the time.

The seat upgrades are part of wider improvements planned for the Thameslink network after Greater Thameslink Railway came into public ownership in May 2026.

Other measures included an increase in Gatwick Express services from December and a programme to refurbish train toilets and remove graffiti across the fleet.

Alexander said: "We'll start getting rid of the dreaded 'ironing board seats' so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes."

She said wider rail reforms would continue under the planned Great British Railways organisation, which is intended to oversee rail services across England.

The class-700 Thameslink trains were heralded by the DfT as "state-of-the-art" and "a fantastic deal" for taxpayers when they were rolled out between 2016 and 2019.

That followed the DfT spending Â£1.6bn of taxpayers' money for German manufacturer Siemens to build the trains in 2013, following a bidding process which began in 2008.

DfT's own procurement guidance document for the fleet, seen by the BBC, stressed that they should be "high capacity" and "reduced weight".

It said the new electric fleet would have a design that "must cater for [about] 1,000 people to board or alight at one time" and a "2+2 seat layout to ease flow and provide standing space".

Some have claimed that this aim to maximise capacity and standing space for commuters led to the seats being so thinly cushioned.

Responding to Alexander's post on X praising the new re-cushioning project, Graeme Pickering, senior correspondent at Railway Magazine, wrote: "Might have been wise not to frame this as 'public ownership fixes private sector mess' when it was the DfT which procured said trains."

Two years before the Thameslink trains were rolled out to the public, a prototype was unveiled at London's Excel centre in 2014.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims in adulthood, say psychiatrists
News.content:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discrete episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support â many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

News.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
News.content:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost Â£6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) â with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says, external the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

News.title: Major Scottish gangland figure Steven Daniel arrested in organised crime raid
News.content:
One of Scotland's most high-profile gangland figures has been arrested during an early morning police raid.

Steven 'Bonzo' Daniel, 46 was taken into custody at around 06:00 from his home in Robroyston in the north of Glasgow.

Daniel is understood to be the head of the notorious Daniel crime family which has been engaged in a violent feud with the rival Lyons family for 25 years.

He was arrested in connection with serious and organised crime, firearms and drugs offences as part of Operation Ventetic, a major UK-wide operation which has dismantled several gangs.
