A tenured professor at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point claims he was fired after pushing back on a presidential directive to “defy science” and stop teaching cadets that climate change had “primarily human causes, something contrary to the ideology of the Commander in Chief and forbidden at West Point.”

Last September, Dr. Adam Kalkstein, a professor of geography and the only climate scientist at the United States Military Academy, says higher-ups “expressly forbade” him from talking about anthropogenic climate change, according to a federal lawsuit reviewed by The Independent.

“At the time, [Kalkstein] was teaching two sections of Climatology in which he taught that humans were responsible for much of the current planetary warming trend and presented the scientific evidence, consequences, and military impacts,” the complaint states. “Learning how humans affect the atmosphere was a fundamental component of his course which he had been teaching for many years, and the concept that humans can alter Earth’s climate is a plainly established scientific fact.”

The order had come from the White House, Kalkstein was informed, his complaint says. Its intent was to “chill and suppress speech and censor viewpoints contrary” to those promulgated by the Trump administration, the complaint goes on.

However, Kalkstein – a conservative Republican, according to his lawyer – spoke out against the decree, telling West Point brass that misrepresenting reality “violated the mission of the academy as it required professors to hide scientific truth,” according to the complaint.

“We’re only telling cadets part of the story,” Kalkstein told his bosses. “We’re lying to them, deceiving them. It would be like trying to teach the law without being able to even mention the Constitution. The guiding principle of any school should be to the truth… I’m supposed to be an educator and a scientist upholding Army values, but… right now, I’m a liar and a fraud.”

open image in gallery A climatologist on the faculty of the US Military Academy at West Point says Donald Trump forced him and others to mislead cadets in the classroom ( Getty Images )

In response, Kalkstein was stripped of his tenure and put on a contract – which has since been canceled. It is set to expire in December, the complaint states.

Attorney Michael Sussman, who is representing Kalkstein, told The Independent that he is presently battling two types of cancer but felt this case was too important to pass up.

“This is not someone who is a radical or a progressive or anything close to that,” Sussman said on Tuesday. “He is a scientist though, and he’s trying to inform the cadets on what is true. But they told him, ‘If you teach that, you’re out of here.’”

Sussman said Kalkstein even wrote a letter to Trump-appointed Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, pointing out that climate change is a recognized threat to the military itself, but that the missive never reached its intended destination.

Ignoring the human factors that are accelerating climate change is “counterproductive from the perspective of people who are deeply concerned about the military and its challenges,” Sussman argued.

“What’s going on there is a form of censorship, which is just shocking,” he said. “And it's not being defended based on any intellectual principles. It’s being defended on the basis of power, that, ‘I have power over you.’ When my client made clear his consternation, that was it.”

The only other civilian faculty member laid off was a professor who researched bias, Sussman said, citing Kalkstein’s complaint.

A West Point spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

open image in gallery Dr. Adam Kalkstein is a West Point professor who is now suing over a new rule that forbids teaching cadets about anthropogenic climate change ( United States Military Academy )

In January 2025, exactly one week after Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office, he issued an Executive Order requiring the military to “carefully review the leadership, curriculum and instructors of the United States Service Academies and other defense academic institutions.” Trump famously never served, being granted at least five draft deferrals during Vietnam for “bone spurs.”

West Point touts its academic program as one that aims “to establish the intellectual foundation for service as a highly educated commissioned officer,” with the ability to “collect, analyze and interpret data to inform evidence-based conclusions and evaluate outcomes,” according to Kalkstein’s complaint, which was filed August 24 in White Plains federal court.

Kalkstein, one of about 100 civilian professors at West Point, joined the faculty roughly 17 years ago, his complaint states.

His annual reviews were “outstanding,” with top ratings in each category, according to the complaint. It says Kalkstein was also one of West Point’s biggest recipients of external research grant funding.

Then, in May 2025, Kalkstein was suddenly informed by Geography and Earth Sciences department head Col. Mark Read that he was one of two professors being let go as part of a “reduction in force,” the complaint states.

Although Read insisted the move had nothing to do with his teaching the only climatology course at the academy, Kalkstein did not believe his claims, according to the complaint. Still, it says Kalkstein was allowed to stay on as a contract employee, with his salary coming from his existing grant money. But, in order to make it happen, Kalkstein’s superiors told him he would have to give up his tenure.

“With no options and significant obligations, [he] accepted this offer,” the complaint states.

open image in gallery In January 2025, exactly one week after Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office, he issued an Executive Order requiring the military to 'carefully review the leadership, curriculum and instructors of the United States Service Academies and other defense academic institutions’ ( AFP via Getty Images )

That September, Kalkstein was called into an “emergency meeting” by geography program director Lt. Col. Joel Radunzel, according to the complaint. Radunzel said no one was to teach students about human-caused climate change, and relayed a “clear threat” that if anyone leaked news of the directive to the media, the entire department would be eliminated, the complaint alleges.

Later that day, Kalkstein told Read that the administration’s demands “crossed a red line for him as a scientist.”

Yet, Kalkstein’s misgivings about the order were ignored. He went to the Department of Defense Inspector General’s Office, without success, the complaint states. So, Kalkstein tried West Point’s legal department, which responded by sending him a sheaf of cases “supposedly supporting the legality of the order.” Kalkstein “studied the cases, which clearly showed the exact opposite,” according to the complaint.

“Despite his profound misgivings, [Kalkstein] continued to obey the order,” it says.

In early November, Kalkstein presented his research to “plaudits” from Brig. Gen. Shane Reeves, dean of West Point’s Academic Board, the complaint states. When he was finished, one of Kalkstein’s fellow professors presented a PowerPoint deck that “affirmed the department’s compliance with the directive not to mention human causes for climate change,” according to the complaint.

Kalkstein, for his part, explained that the directive “violated the mission” of West Point, as it “required professors to hide scientific truth.” Reeves, who is now retired, became incensed, and angrily reminded Kalkstein that the president sets the academic agenda for West Point, the complaint says. While that may be true, Kalkstein replied, the president was still required to abide by the Constitution.

open image in gallery Trump's antipathy about climate change is at the center of a new lawsuit by the West Point climatologist who says he was forbidden to teach settled science to cadets ( Getty Images for Climate Power 2 )

“Defendant Reeves suggested that [Kalkstein] resign from his position,” the complaint states. “[Kalkstein] indicated that his personal responsibilities precluded that. Continuing to yell, Defendant Reeves stated that he had seen enough and stormed out of the meeting, again threatening the entire Department if its members did not comply.”

This past May, Read told Kalkstein that his contract would not be renewed when it expired in December. Read claimed Kalkstein was being let go over his supposed “poor character and temperament,” which contradicted nearly two decades of glowing performance reviews, according to the complaint.

West Point, the complaint maintains, “clearly terminated [Kalkstein] because he expressed his opposition to the directive to purge human causes as one of the bases for climate change.”

Kalkstein is suing West Point, Reeves, Read, and Lt. Gen. Steven Gilland, now retired, who served as the academy’s superintendent and commanding officer until this month.

His lawsuit follows one filed last year by a West Point law professor who said the academy’s restrictions on lesson plans violated his First Amendment rights.

Kalkstein is now seeking a court order to enjoin West Point from “imposing or enforcing baseless restrictions on academic freedom and the capacity of a professor to fairly represent the state of scientific research and knowledge,” to reinstate him to his tenured position, and is demanding compensatory damages for material losses and emotional distress, plus attorneys’ fees and court costs.

Professor Jason Arday was found unresponsive by family members days after resigning from his post at the University of Cambridge, an inquest has heard.

The 41-year-old was discovered at his home in Battersea, south London, on 14 August after facing intense scrutiny over accusations of plagiarism.

An inquest at London Inner South Coroner’s Court, which opened on Wednesday, heard an investigation has been launched into his “unnatural death”.

Senior coroner Dr Julian Morris said: “The various reports have given me reason to suspect that Professor Arday died an unnatural death 12 days ago.

“It therefore follows that I must open an investigation. I will be setting out further directions for the coroner officer.”

open image in gallery A vigil was organised by campaign group Stand Up to Racism for Prof Arday in Trafalgar Square last Monday ( PA Wire )

Despite resuscitative efforts, he was pronounced dead and the Metropolitan Police said the scene was not suspicious, the inquest was told.

Prof Arday resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education at the university earlier this month following the accusations.

Sir Patrick Vernon, who played a leading role in the successful campaign to establish a national Windrush Day, set up a GoFundMe crowdfunding page following Prof Arday’s death to help support the academic’s family – with £224,474 raised through more than 7,900 donations.

In a message on the page on Tuesday, Prof Arday’s family said: “We are deeply moved by the extraordinary support we have received.

“The response to this appeal reflects the number of people whose lives were touched by our beloved Jason and the affection, respect and admiration in which he was held.

“Jason devoted his life and career to advancing education, widening participation, tackling race and inequality, and championing autism and neurodiversity.

“It means a great deal to us that so many people wish to celebrate his life and remember the difference he made to others.

“We are still grieving the loss of our beloved son, partner, father, brother, uncle and friend. We hope you will understand our need for time and space as we come to terms with this devastating loss and consider how best to move forward.”

Accusations of plagiarism were initially made against Prof Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest Black professor in 2023, by academic Nathan Cofnas.

Mr Cofnas, who has advocated for “race realism”, was last week suspended from his post at Ghent University.

The Belgian university announced a preliminary disciplinary investigation has been launched after saying Prof Arday’s death “should prompt reflection”, adding the institution “opposes discrimination, hatred and racism”.

Prof Arday’s memoir, Great And Unfortunate Things, is due to be published in the UK on Thursday.

Publisher Simon & Schuster announced on Monday that his book will be released as planned, with his family saying: “It is only right that we honour his wishes.”

Last week, organisers said more than 30,000 people had attended a vigil for Prof Arday in Trafalgar Square, central London.

Speakers at the vigil criticised the press coverage of Prof Arday, with MP Diane Abbott saying he had been the subject of a “vicious” and “bitter” campaign by people who did not believe a Black man should be a Cambridge professor, and Lord Woolley describing it as a “public execution” and a “lynching”.

India has rejected a UN watchdog’s report highlighting ethnic and caste discrimination in the country and asking the government to protect its tribals and disadvantaged groups from extrajudicial killings.

The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), following a periodic review, expressed "grave concern" over reports of law enforcement agencies targeting ethno-religious groups, indigenous and tribal people, including those from the lower rungs of the archaic Hindu caste system, and non-citizens.

The report said that India urgently needed to tackle hate crimes and targeted operations against Rohingya refugees, Bengali-speaking Muslims from the state of West Bengal and asylum seekers.

The caste system is a rigid social stratification structure that goes back thousands of years and is still critical in Indian life and politics. It divides Hindus into a hierarchal system by birth, with those on the bottom rung, the 200 million Dalits formerly known as the "untouchables", facing social, religious and economic discrimination.

The watchdog said on Tuesday that large-scale violations perpetrated by law enforcement officials in India included "racially motivated violence, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary and prolonged detention without due process, torture, ill-treatment and sexual violence".

It urged Narendra Modi’s government to investigate the claims and bring those responsible to justice.

The Indian foreign ministry on Wednesday rejected the report, calling it "politically motivated and highly malicious".

An Indian delegation led by solicitor general Tushar Mehta appeared before CERD earlier this month for the first time in almost 20 years. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said it was a routine treaty-body review in which Delhi participated in the spirit of constructive engagement.

He said India underscored its constitutional safeguards, comprehensive legal framework, pluralistic ethos, and continuous efforts directed at safeguarding disadvantaged communities.

While Delhi would respond to the watchdog’s observations “through the established procedure”, the spokesperson said, its “delegation had already rejected the sweeping generalisations, unsubstantiated allegations, or tendency to exceed the convention's mandate during the review meeting”.

The report alleged that police stops and identity checks involving racial profiling had led to arbitrary arrest and detention without due process. A Human Rights Watch report from July 2025 found that Indian authorities had forcibly pushed hundreds of Bengali-speaking Muslims into Bangladesh without due process.

The watchdog also flagged deportation and forced return of individuals, such as the Rohingya refugees, requiring international protection. Human rights groups and the UN raised alarm in May last year after Indian authorities allegedly forced dozens of Rohingya refugees off a naval vessel into the sea near the coast of Myanmar after providing them with life jackets.

India has routinely rejected reports critical of its treatment of minorities and disadvantaged people. Last year, it dismissed a report from a US panel on religious freedom highlighting the “deteriorating” treatment of religious minorities in the South Asian country.

Downton Abbey legend Dame Maggie Smith left an estate worth almost £16m to her two sons following her death, new records reveal.

The star of the stage and screen, who also famously played Hogwarts professor Minerva McGonagall in the Harry Potter films, died aged 89 in September 2024.

Probate records show Smith left £15,977,325 to her children Christopher and Toby Stephens, who she shared with her first husband, fellow actor Robert Stephens.

Both of the couple’s sons followed them into acting, with Christopher – who goes by the stage name Chris Larkin – landing roles in Doctor Who and Holby City, while Toby’s credits include the James Bond film Die Another Day and the BBC’s mid-noughties Jane Eyre adaptation.

Smith and Robert Stephens divorced after almost eight years of marriage in 1975 and the former married Half a Sixpence playwright Beverley Cross just months after her divorce was finalised. They remained together until Cross’s death in 1998.

open image in gallery Maggie Smith in ‘Downton Abbey’ ( ITV )

Smith’s will states that copyright, royalties and unpublished works she inherited from Cross after his death should be split equally between the actor’s two sons and her late husband’s two children, Philippa Maughan and Shaun Cross, The Telegraph reports.

Smith’s estate, which included her five-bedroom West Sussex home, was worth a total of just over £16m. Debts and expenses of just over £25,000 were deducted to give the final figure.

Smith’s death was announced by her sons, who said via a publicist at the time: “An intensely private person, she was with friends and family at the end.

“She leaves two sons and five loving grandchildren who are devastated by the loss of their extraordinary mother and grandmother.”

open image in gallery The actor won two Academy Awards and four Emmys ( PA )

In a decades-spanning career, Smith won two Oscars – being named best actress for The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie in 1969, before winning in the best supporting actress category for California Suite in 1978 – and four Emmys, including three for her portrayal of Violet Crawley in Downton Abbey.

Her death sparked tributes from many of the stars she shared the big and small screens with. Harry Potter star Daniel Radcliffe said: “I will always consider myself amazingly lucky to have been able to work with her, and to spend time around her on set. The word legend is overused but if it applies to anyone in our industry then it applies to her. Thank you, Maggie.”

The King and Queen also shared their condolences, saying in a joint statement: “As the curtain comes down on a national treasure, we join all those around the world in remembering with the fondest admiration and affection her many great performances, and her warmth and wit that shone through both off and on the stage.”

Under normal circumstances, Senator Darline Graham should not have won the Republican primary to replace her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. But then President Donald Trump stepped in.

Graham scored a narrow win in South Carolina Tuesday night. With 99 per cent of the vote counted, Graham had 52.5 percent of the vote over Representative Ralph Norman with 47.6 percent, according to The Associated Press.

Her political fortunes had looked rocky ahead of Tuesday’s runoff during a debate with Norman, when she was asked about the South China Sea and Taiwan. Her late brother — a China and Russia hawk who had visited Ukraine shortly before his sudden death last month — would have argued that defending them was vital to American interests.

Instead, his little sister said simply: “I’m not that informed on national security.”

The gaffe was also a black eye for Trump, who had passed over a surefire candidate to endorse Graham as her brother's successor — first to finish out Lindsey Graham's term, then to serve a full term of her own.

MAGA Inc., the super PAC affiliated with Trump, poured money into the primary, and the president traveled to Myrtle Beach to campaign with Graham last Friday.

The gamble paid off.

Trump has been particularly sensitive about his endorsement track record as of late. Earlier this week, he pushed back against the idea that he had lost his winning touch.

“My Endorsements are stronger than ever — Not to mention the fact that good people are getting elected who never had the chance!” he insisted on Truth Social.

In the past, the nod from Trump used to be a lock. His endorsements of Ron DeSantis in Florida and Brian Kemp in Georgia catapulted them to become governors of their states in the 2018 midterms.

In 2022, JD Vance was languishing behind other Republican candidates for Senate before Trump gave his imprimatur, which set Vance on the course to be Ohio’s senator and ultimately, Trump’s vice president.

That same year, he endorsed TV doctor Mehmet Oz, helping him become the Republican nominee for Senate in Pennsylvania. Trump cleared the field in the 2022 Georgia Senate race for Herschel Walker, and in Arizona, he backed Blake Masters for Senate.

But the last three fell flat. More recently, Trump’s endorsement has failed to do the trick elsewhere.

In Georgia, he backed Lt. Gov. Burt Jones to succeed Kemp as governor, only for him to lose to Rick Jackson. He offered a last-minute endorsement to Rep. Randy Feenstra in Iowa in the primary for governor. But Feenstra lost to Zach Lahn.

Earlier this year in South Carolina, he endorsed Lt. Gov Pamela Evette to be governor. But Trump would then double-endorse Evette and Attorney General Alan Wilson before the runoff to save face.

The president had less-than-stellar luck in the Minnesota gubernatorial primary when Mike Lindell lost and Minnesota Republicans criticized Trump’s endorsement. He also whiffed his endorsement of Megan Degenfelder to be governor of Wyoming.

Republican Rep. Andy Ogles lost his primary in Tennessee’s 5th district despite Trump’s endorsement ( Getty )

He also struck out recently in congressional endorsements. In Tennessee, he endorsed Rep. Andy Ogles, a firebrand with a history of Islamophobic and bigoted remarks who would lose to a more mainstream Republican named Charlie Hatcher.

Trump endorsed Catalina Lauf, who would place second in Florida’s 19th district.

And Representative Cory Mills, whom Trump also endorsed, lost his primary as he faces a House Ethics Committee investigation into whether he violated campaign finance law, misused congressional resources and whether he engaged in dating violence or sexual misconduct. Trump would subsequently try to wash his hands of Mills despite the endorsement.

“I told Congressman Cory Mills of Florida, a friend of mine, to get out of the Race, but he wouldn’t listen. He thought he could win, so who can blame him?” he said.

Trump still has the ability to motivate crowds - but seems to know that his voters are low-propensity.

“They say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come and they don’t vote for senators, congressmen and other Republicans,” he told the South Carolina crowd who had turned out to see him campaign for Graham. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote.”

What’s more, the president doesn’t not seem all that motivated to save his majority in Congress. Save for an event in Georgia and another in Michigan, Trump has not barnstormed swing states for his political allies the way he did in the 2018 midterms.

His allies have not deployed MAGA Inc., which has roughly $400 million in cash to save endangered Republicans. Even in Texas, where his endorsement of Attorney General Ken Paxton saddled Republicans with a vulnerable candidate, Trump has mostly sat on his hands.

Rather than focus on the long-term health of the GOP after he leaves office, Trump seems consumed with refurbishing Washington monuments, construction projects and trying to find a way out of the Iran war.

And that might keep him from holding onto a majority that can insulate him politically in his final two years in the White House.

News.title: How Dolly Parton redefined Glastonbury’s Legends slot
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

From Kylie Minogue’s long-awaited performance to Lionel Richie leading thousands in a synchronised dance routine, Glastonbury’s Legends slot has become known for providing some of the most memorable moments in the festival’s history. But it wasn’t always this way.

For almost two decades, the Sunday afternoon spot had varying success. Until a certain five-foot-nothing southern trailblazer charmed the farm and raised the bar. Who? Dolly Parton, of course.

As I packed for Glastonbury in 2014, I counted myself as a slightly-above-casual Dolly fan; excited for her set and aware of her obvious cultural significance, but with no proper grasp of what was to come. By the time we were dismantling the tents on the Monday morning, like many of the 100,000 people who saw Parton perform that weekend, I was a born again, fully paid-up member of the Dolly fan club.

As Glastonburys go, it was a blokey one. The festival was headlined by indie faves Arcade Fire (who do have one female member out of five), heavy metal band Metallica and Leicester lads Kasabian. But the rhinestone-clad Parton outshone them all.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton raised the bar with her gamechanging Legends performance ( Alamy/PA )

After years of inviting veteran acts to grace the Pyramid Stage on Sunday afternoons, Glastonbury made the Legends Slot an official occasion in 1998 when jazz crooner Tony Bennett stopped by at Worthy Farm.

In the years that followed, the likes of Godfather of Soul James Brown(!), Dame Shirley Bassey – wearing diamanté Wellingtons and a £50k dress, naturally – and Pet Shop Boys visionary Brian Wilson performed in the mid-afternoon spot.

But when Parton, then aged 68, was announced for Glastonbury in February 2014, you got the sense that something special was brewing. The festival’s founder, Michael Eavis, threw aside any concerns of picking favourites and tweeted: "We are delighted to say that Dolly is coming to Glastonbury ... It really doesn't get much better than this!"

Fast forward four months and by the time soundchecks were underway and the tinnies opened, there was only one act anyone at Worthy Farm wanted to talk about. Just as her death has sparked genuinely heartfelt tributes from an eclectic range of musicians, figures from across the political spectrum (Trump and Obama!) and institutions including NASA, Parton’s Legends appearance was the ultimate Glastonbury leveller.

open image in gallery Wigs, costumes and singing along: Parton inspired the crowd ( PA )

Whether fellow festivalgoers were most hyped for Metallica, itching to hear Lana Del Rey perform from the newly-released Ultraviolence, or hoping to catch a Fatboy Slim secret set, every conversation with a stranger ended in the same agreement: country powerhouse Parton was the act you simply couldn’t miss.

The “9 to 5” singer was midway through a global arena tour at the time, and even performed at London’s O2 Arena the night before her Glastonbury set, but of course, she understood the assignment – and provided a blueprint for all of the Legends who have performed at Worthy Farm since.

Rather than trotting out a slimmed-down version of her tour show, Parton carefully constructed a special, one-time only gig. On paper, her custom-made outfit (head-to-toe white and sparkles, topped off with an astonishingly tall, platinum blonde wig) was wildly unsuitable for the muddy Somerset fields, but this is Dolly Parton we’re talking about. Obviously she pulled it off with ease.

Arriving on stage to the biggest cheers of the weekend – and in front of the biggest crowd ever recorded at the festival – Parton kicked off her hour-and-10-minute set with a fiery medley of “Baby I’m Burnin’”, “Great Balls of Fire” and “Girl on Fire”, before the catchy “Why'd You Come in Here Lookin' Like That” and Rolling Stone’s picks for greatest country song of all-time, “Jolene”.

open image in gallery A young fan getting into the spirit of things ( PA )

Parton’s unrivalled storytelling abilities were displayed both in her performances and the anecdotes she told between. “I got rid of that redheaded woman in a hurry!” she quipped after Jolene, before adding: “But had it not been for her, I wouldn’t have written ‘Jolene’ and I wouldn’t have made all that money... so thank you!”

I am not ashamed to say that, having had minimal sleep for four nights, I sobbed through both her explanation of “Coat of Many Colours” and the rendition of it that followed, before Parton switched the mood up again, by delighting the crowd with “Mud Song”, a track she’d written especially for Glastonbury.

She aced it with her choice of special guest too, going for something a little different by welcoming former Bon Jovi guitarist Richie Sambora, who assisted with a cover of “Lay Your Hands on Me”. By the time she closed her set with an emotional rendition of power ballad “I Will Always Love You”, even the hardiest of naysayers would have been won over. Parton herself was pretty pleased, too. "They seemed to enjoy it,” she later said of the crowd. “And that made me feel good because I've never done the festival before.”

As well as winning over thousands of new fans, Parton made the Legends slot “cool”, paving the way for the likes of fellow country legend Shania Twain and Scottish rocker Sir Rod Stewart to follow in her footsteps.

The rest of that Sunday at Glastonbury is a blur to be honest. I know I interviewed Kasabian in the run-up to the festival, but I couldn’t tell you whether I saw them perform or not (sorry, Serge). What we do know is this: the Legends slot hasn’t been the same since – as she did through so much of her career, Parton effortlessly raised the bar and set the standard for those who would follow her. Thank you, Dolly.

News.title: Josh Tongue reveals Joe Root’s no-nonsense message to England players after Brydon Carse arrest
News.content:

Josh Tongue has revealed that direct-speaking England captain Joe Root left the squad under no illusions regarding expected behavioural standards as they attempt to clean up their public image.

Root was clearly annoyed on Tuesday while responding to the latest off-field controversy surrounding the squad, describing himself as "hacked off" following an incident where fast bowler Brydon Carse was briefly arrested outside a venue in Derby on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly.

Carse was dropped from the squad pending an inquiry by the Cricket Regulator, leading Root to hold a ‘robust’ team discussion prior to Thursday’s second Rothesay Test against Pakistan, setting out his expectations just a fortnight after making his return as skipper.

Tongue insists that the message was received loud and clear following ten months regularly disrupted by unwelcome stories concerning team discipline off the pitch.

"We had a chat before training yesterday as Joe said. It was a very good conversation and he made it clear what he expects from us," he said.

open image in gallery Josh Tongue revealed Joe Root spoke to the England squad about the standards of behaviour he expects ( PA Wire )

"He’s been around the England dressing room for plenty of years now, he knows what it takes to be the top professional and I think we’ve just got to do the best we can moving forward.

"I think we’ve just got to make sure we’re as professional as we can be. Obviously things have happened and we need to try and move on from them to show all the youngsters growing up wanting to play for England that it’s an amazing place to be.

"Playing for England is obviously a privilege. We want to give the next generation the best place that they can be really."

Tongue is one of eight centrally contracted players who have been present during or involved with late-night incidents in recent times.

He was present with white-ball captain Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell in Wellington when the former was hit by a bouncer the day before an ODI, though the Cricket Regulator ultimately cleared Tongue of any wrongdoing because he was not in the matchday squad.

In the time since, the 28-year-old fast bowler has become one of England’s most reliable figures, offering a bright spark in a difficult Ashes campaign and cementing his place across all three formats during the current summer.

"I just tried to move on from that (Wellington) situation really and focus on the cricket. It’s an absolute privilege to play for England, especially walking out and thousands of people watching you," he said.

"Things have been happening off the field but I’ve been personally trying to sort of forget about it and try and play as best cricket as I can for England and try to put England in best positions to win games of cricket. That’s why we’re here and that’s what we want to do for the fans."

open image in gallery Brydon Carse was briefly arrested earlier this week ( PA Wire )

England have failed to secure a multi-match Test series victory since visiting New Zealand in December 2024, drawing at home against India before enduring a 4-1 loss in Australia and a defeat to the Kiwis that ended the Bazball era led by Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum.

Consequently, Tongue is still waiting for a first series success, despite a personal record showing 65 wickets in 13 Tests at an average of 27.38. The upcoming five days at Lord’s represent a major opportunity to put that right against a visiting side dominated in every area at Headingley last week.

"Yeah, it’d be amazing to win a series," said Tongue.

"Obviously it would be my first one in the red ball stuff. We’ve just got to focus, make sure we play our best cricket just be nice and relaxed out there and hopefully we get over the line."

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.
