World.title: Why women’s voice should be heard, By Sam Akpe
World.content:
It started with visible empty seats. Then, suddenly, the rotunda of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs — designed for elite class activities — got thronged with quality audience. It was a well-planned, well-attended, and brilliantly executed event, with a theme that spoke to the moment.

The audience comprised ambassadors, top government representatives, technocrats, seasoned policy makers, tested security experts, confirmed women leaders, development specialists, civil society groups, young leaders, partners, and representatives of everyone connected to the issues that formed the centre of discourse.

Coordinating the events, with her trademark diplomatic finesse, was the ever-elegant veteran broadcast journalist, author, mentor, and event compere extraordinaire, Mrs Eugenia Abu. She did what only Eugenia can do — from the introduction of guests to a full grasp of the issues that summoned them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Noisy, active politicians seemed to have been deliberately excluded. A select few who were invited conveniently sent representatives. This created rooms for exclusive focus on key security and development issues, instead of politics disguised as patriotism.

Hosted by a non-governmental organisation: I Teach Africa, the summit was themed: Empowering Her for Governance: Advancing Women’s Leadership for Inclusive Governance and Security.

It aimed at discussing the importance of inclusive governance and women’s meaningful participation in leadership, peace, security, and national development.

With well-applauded keynote addresses, panel discussions, leadership conversations, stakeholder engagement, and strategic perspectives on strengthening inclusive governance and building more resilient and secure communities, it drew some conclusions on vital issues concerning security.

Host of the conference, Mrs Ebi Elezieanya drew impressive applause in her opening remarks. She said armed conflicts anywhere affect women and girls differently, stressing the imperativeness of participation of women in security decision-making, and their inclusion in conflict prevention strategies.

Citing certain international agreements, she observed that women inclusion in security policy-making is not simply a gender issue, but an absolute incontrovertible necessity, because while security protects a nation, inclusion gives every citizen a reason to defend the nation.

Two heart-wrenching documentaries on how terror activities affect women and children were shown. Tears rolled down several cheeks as the visuals and sounds of the well-scripted and beautifully delivered audio wrapped the hall in total silence, with the caption: The Woman’s Voice Must Be Heard.

In an explosive speech, Dr Otive Igbuzor informed the audience that the issue of national security is fully connected to sustainable stability which on its own cannot be achieved without inclusive governance, which would also remain a mirage without transformational leadership.

His view was that national security cannot be guaranteed where a large section of the population, especially women, young persons, the disabled, the poor and the marginalised, are excluded from the political and economic decision-making process.

In all, he noted that inclusion is a development imperative, because it determines whose voice is heard, adding that security embodies inclusion, good governance, development, credible elections, and strong institutions.

The highly cerebral retired national security expert whose life-time involvement in ensuring a conflict-free Niger Delta and Nigeria at large has been archived, His Majesty, Dr Ferdinand Ikwang — the Mkpisong Ekid Afid — was a part of the panel discussion.

Ikwang said, in response to a question, that the starting point for any national security discourse is the community where everybody grew up, and that avoidable negligence of institutional memory has been the reason for failures in security architecture in Nigeria.

In a presentation entitled, “Inclusion as Security: the Niger Delta Model and the Imperative of Empowering the Nigerian Women,” Chief Ndutime Alaibe told the audience that his experience in the Niger Delta has taught him one belief: People are more likely to protect a system in which they have meaningful stakes.

He revealed that over the years, Nigeria has seen and treated the Niger Delta substantially as a security problem, but a better understanding has revealed that beneath the security drawbacks were questions of development, justice; and a profound crisis of belonging.

His conclusion, arising from this realisation, was that inclusion is not merely a social policy, but a national security policy. He explained that for too long, Nigeria’s understanding of security has been dominated by the instruments of safety such as soldiers, police officers, intelligence agencies, weapons, checkpoints, and surveillance.

‘Timi confirmed that while these remain necessary because any responsible state must possess the capacity to enforce its laws, defend its territory and protect its citizens, sustainable security goes beyond absence of violence to include the presence of conditions that make violence less attractive, less legitimate and less sustainable.

He said this boils down to: Justice — where citizens believe in fair treatment; then opportunity — which connotes that gains such as jobs, businesses, education, and hope, are derived from stability; and belonging — which implies that citizens see themselves as participants and not spectators outside the national project.

‘Timi was categorical that where these variables are absent, security institutions would be repeatedly asked to manage the consequences, but where they are present, citizens themselves would become stakeholders in stability.

As someone who has repeatedly been involved in the management of security issues in the Niger Delta, ‘Timi recalled that for decades, communities have watched enormous wealth leave their environment while many remained without adequate roads, electricity, clean water, employment opportunities and environmental remediation.

He said young people have seen sophisticated industrial infrastructure criss-cross their ancestral lands while struggling to see any meaningful pathway for themselves in the prosperity which their land represents, and that the widening gap between what they see and what they can access most times ignited violence based on frustration.

Whenever this happened, he said the Nigerian state always responded with security operations. However, could that be the solution? This is what ‘Timi thinks: “force can contain violence. It cannot, by itself, resolve the grievance that produces violence.”

This implies, in his words, that a checkpoint cannot create employment, a gunboat cannot create political belonging, a military operation cannot substitute development, and intelligence gathering cannot permanently compensate a community that has lost confidence in the system.

Accordingly, “the lesson was not that security operations were unnecessary. The lesson was that security without political, developmental and economic inclusion could never be sufficient.”

As he spoke, certain initiatives introduced to control this awkward situation came to mind. They included the framework called the Niger Delta Regional Development Master Plan, dreamt to provide a comprehensive development charter for the region.

Then, the Presidential Amnesty Programme which introduced disarmament, demobilisation, rehabilitation and reintegration as an alternative to endless military confrontation; and the Nigerian Content framework which significantly opened more space for Nigerian businesses, professionals and workers within the oil and gas value chain.

Also, in the inclusion package has been the Petroleum Industry Act which created Host Communities Development Trusts, in formal recognition of the fact that communities hosting petroleum operations must have an institutional stake in development.

The community-embedded pipeline surveillance, working alongside soldiers, intelligence agencies, regulators and operators, is another initiative that has demonstrated the value of local knowledge and community participation in protecting critical national assets.

‘Timi noted that though these initiatives were different and imperfect, a common principle runs through them: “Move people from the margins of the economy into the architecture of the economy. That is stake-holding.”

He continued: “When communities participate in protecting national assets, local knowledge becomes national intelligence; employment becomes a security instrument; and infrastructure protection becomes a shared interest.

“This is what I mean by inclusion as security. Not the abandonment of the state. Not the privatisation of national security. But the intelligent integration of communities into the security and economic architecture of the state.”

Then he moved from the general inclusion to the specific. ‘Timi said one of the clearest weaknesses of the Niger Delta peace architecture was the insufficient inclusion of women — the same women who have been the most victimised gender whenever there was environmental crisis or security conflict.

The technocrat reminded the audience that women have variously suffered from environmental degradation, lost livelihoods, lost husbands, sons and family members, sustained households during periods of instability, and participated in community advocacy and grassroots peacebuilding.

He said, “Yet when formal structures of negotiation, disarmament and reintegration emerged, women were overwhelmingly on the margins. Now, we must acknowledge an obvious fact: Niger Delta women were not generally the ones who took up arms against the state, so one would naturally expect fewer women in a disarmament programme. But that is precisely the point.

“We defined peace too narrowly around those who carried weapons, rather than around all those who carried the consequences of the conflict — and all those who could help sustain the peace.

“That is a lesson we must not forget. And the problem extends far beyond the Niger Delta. Women constitute approximately half of Nigeria’s population, yet they occupy only about four per cent of the seats in our National Assembly. Nigeria is yet to elect a woman as Governor of any of its 36 States.

“This is not simply a women’s issue. It is a national capacity issue. It is a democratic legitimacy issue, and yes, it is a national security issue, because no country can sustainably secure itself while systematically underutilising the intelligence, experience, economic capacity and leadership potential of approximately half its population.”

Suddenly, ‘Timi waxed spiritual. He cited the Holy Book. First, he cited Galatians 3:28 which says “there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Then Acts 2:17 where we are reminded that “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” The hall erupted in applause.

Then the preacher declared: “The message is profound: talent, capacity, calling and responsibility are not the exclusive preserve of one gender. So, we must change the language. Women must not appear in our national security framework merely as victims to be protected.

“They must be recognised as agents of security — as intelligence professionals, police officers, military officers, mediators, community leaders, entrepreneurs, legislators, policymakers, negotiators and peacebuilders.”

He went ahead to dwell on women economic inclusion, political inclusion, security-sector inclusion, and inclusion in the community peace architecture, adding that women-led organisations, traditional institutions, youth organisations and community networks should be integrated into early-warning systems, mediation structures and local security dialogue.

His thinking is that the woman in a rural community who detects the early signs of radicalisation may be contributing as much to national security as the analyst sitting before multiple screens in a command centre, and that Nigeria’s security architecture must learn to connect the two.

His conclusion pulled the hall to its feet in approval. He said every constituency represented at the summit had a lever to pull. Government must, “make gender-responsive budgeting measurable. Let appropriations demonstrate our priorities more loudly than communiqués.”

To the National Assembly, he advised, “history has again placed the question of women’s representation before you. Let this generation be remembered for opening the door” while the security agencies should, “move beyond recruitment numbers. Build deliberate pathways into command and strategic leadership.”

He told the industry operators to “apply the discipline of Nigerian Content to women’s participation — in procurement, contracting, employment, technical training and executive leadership,” while development partners and civil society must “help us measure what works,” because inclusion without measurement and economic power is mere rhetoric and tokenism.

The take home from the summit as captured by ‘Timi was that when citizens are given justice, they build faith in the system. When given opportunity, they acquire a stake in the system. If given a sense of belonging, they acquire a reason to defend the system.

Ultimately, the most secured Nigeria will not simply be the Nigeria with the strongest security forces. It will be the Nigeria in which the greatest number of its citizens believe that the country belongs to them—and that they belong to the country.

The concern of participants at the summit was mainly whether government would listen, consider, and implement the ground-breaking suggestions put forward by experts on the burning issues of development, national security, and inclusion.

Sam Akpe writes from www.wordsworthglobal.com

World.title: How Adeleke thwarted APC’s bid to reclaim Osun
World.content:
The defeat of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Osun State’s 15 August governorship election was more than another change in the state’s political map. It marked the failure of the party’s attempt to return to the Government House four years after its candidate, Gboyega Oyetola, lost the seat to Ademola Adeleke in the 2022 election.

For Mr Adeleke, the victory was the culmination of a political journey that began less than a decade ago and was shaped by a powerful family name, an upset senatorial victory, a bitterly contested governorship election, a year of litigation over credibility of the 2018 election and, eventually, two successful bids for the state’s highest political office.

In the 15 August governorship election, Mr Adeleke, the Accord Party candidate, defeated his closest challenger, Bola Oyebamiji of the APC, to secure another four-year term. Mr Adeleke polled 511,067 votes against Mr Oyebamiji’s 444,815, according to the results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The governor was presented a certificate of return on Wednesday in Osogbo by INEC National Commissioner representing the South-west, Kunle Ajayi. At the event, Mr Adeleke announced plans to establish a N500 million endowment fund for victims of election-related violence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the victory has taken Mr Adeleke from a politician whose emergence was initially closely associated with the influential Adeleke family to an incumbent governor whom Osun voters have chosen to retain.

But that victory also fits into a broader pattern in Osun politics, where incumbency and party structures have repeatedly failed to guarantee political survival.

From family influence to political contender

Mr Adeleke did not enter Osun politics from an ordinary political background. He is the younger brother of Isiaka Adeleke, Osun’s first civilian governor and later a senator representing Osun West. Their father, the late patriarch of the Adeleke family, Ayoola Adeleke, served as a Nigerian senator during the Second Republic (1979–1983), representing the old Oyo State Senatorial District. The Adeleke family has since remained influential in the state’s political and social landscape.

Mr Adeleke’s political breakthrough came in 2017, following the death of his brother, which created a vacancy in the Osun West senatorial district.

To join the contest, he had initially sought the APC ticket but defected to the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) after failing to secure the ruling party’s nomination. He subsequently contested the July 2017 senatorial by-election on the PDP platform.

The election outcome immediately established him as a political force to reckon with. He polled 97,480 votes to defeat APC candidate Mudashiru Hussein, who secured 66,116 votes, winning nine of the 10 local government areas in the senatorial district.

The victory was particularly significant because the APC controlled the state government under Governor Rauf Aregbesola at the time. It showed that the Adeleke name could still translate into electoral support decades after the family first left its footprints on the political landscape of the state.

Mr Adeleke soon turned that momentum towards the big prize: the Osun governorship.

Osun voters and the want of changing governments

Mr Adeleke’s rise cannot be fully understood without examining Osun’s electoral history.

Since the return to democratic rule in 1999, the state has moved between political parties and administrations, producing one of the most competitive electoral landscapes in the South-west.

Bisi Akande of the Alliance for Democracy governed the state from 1999 to 2003 before Olagunsoye Oyinlola of the PDP defeated him in the 2003 governorship election. Mr Oyinlola subsequently secured a second term in 2007.

But Mr Oyinlola’s second term was cut short by a prolonged legal battle. Rauf Aregbesola of the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN) – one of the legacy parties of today’s APC – who had lost the 2007 election, challenged the result in court. The Court of Appeal in 2010 declared him the rightful winner, overturning the earlier result.

The 2010 ruling fundamentally altered Osun’s electoral calendar, making it one of the Nigerian states where governorship elections are held off-cycle. During Mr Aregbesola’s first term, PDP was the ruling political party at the federal level under former president Goodluck Jonathan.

Mr Aregbesola subsequently won a fresh mandate for a second term in 2014 after his party, ACN, merged with other political parties in 2013 to form the APC, and governed the state until 2018, when his party’s candidate, Gboyega Oyetola, succeeded him after defeating his closest challenger Mr Adeleke of the PDP by a razor-thin margin.

Before Mr Oyetola was declared winner, the September 2018 governorship election was first pronounced “inconclusive” after the 353-vote margin separating Mr Adeleke and Mr Oyetola was lower than the 3,498 votes cancelled across seven polling units. Mr Adeleke had polled 254,698 votes, narrowly ahead of Mr Oyetola of the APC, who scored 254,345.

The supplementary rerun election held on 27 September, 2018, however, swung the contest in Mr Oyetola’s favour, leading to his declaration as winner. Mr Adeleke and the PDP challenged the result through the courts, but after a prolonged legal battle, the Supreme Court delivered the final verdict and affirmed Mr Oyetola’s victory.

Mr Oyetola’s tenure, however, lasted only one term after voters returned power to the PDP and elected Mr Adeleke in 2022. He defeated Mr Oyetola, then the incumbent, in a rematch that marked a decisive shift in the state’s political direction.

The pattern is significant: Osun voters have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to change political control of the state. Sometimes that change has happened at the ballot box; in Aregbesola’s case, it followed a successful legal challenge to an election result and then by a ballot for his second term.

The next test for Adeleke

Once again, Mr Adeleke’s re-election has truncated the APC’s immediate attempt to reclaim Osun, but it has also created a new political obligation for the governor.

His first term was defined by visible infrastructure projects, interventions in workers’ welfare, debt reduction and increased revenue mobilisation, but also by unresolved questions over education spending, healthcare sustainability, local government administration and the completion and quality of some major projects.

There were concerns raised about lopsidedness of projects favouring his Ede axis of the state and proclivity to award government appointments to relatives.

The second term will therefore be judged less by campaign promises and more by whether the administration can convert its first-term interventions into lasting improvements and be fairer in its distribution of projects and appointments.

‘Osun election was a demonstration of people’s power’

Prince Gutap, an election expert at Yiaga Africa and its consultant on democracy, said the outcome of the Osun election should also be understood as the willingness of voters to assert their choice at the ballot box.

He said the people’s active participation was one of the clearest lessons from the election, particularly their determination to ensure that their votes counted.

Although Mr Gutap cautioned against using Osun’s experience as a direct template for the entire country, noting that voter participation differs across Nigeria’s regions. But he said the state offers an important example of how an engaged electorate can shape political outcomes.

“The willingness of voters to participate actively in the election was to ensure that their choice at the poll determines who governs them. And that is an important element of democratic development,” he said.

He pointed to an incident during the election in which citizens alerted the police after allegedly identifying a man they suspected was attempting to buy votes. According to him, police responded and arrested the individual.

“That’s the level of trust we want to have in our security agencies, that when we see a problem or when we see an issue, we can be able to walk to them and tell them, ‘There’s a problem here,’ and then they will quickly respond to it,” Mr Gutap said.

He noted that Osun State’s political history shows that voters can reward incumbents, but they can also withdraw that support when they decide to change direction.

“We have seen how voters have voted out incumbent governors at some points and, at other times, re-elected governors. What that tells us is that voters respond to leaders who address their problems and improve their welfare,” Mr Gutap added.

Also, public affairs journalist and analyst, Dayo Akintobi, expressed that the outcome of the recently concluded Osun’s governorship election demonstrated the growing power of Osun voters to determine electoral outcomes.

READ ALSO: Osun constitutes committee to disburse N500m fund to election violence victims

Speaking on Channels Television, Mr Akintobi said the outcome reflected the will of voters who remained engaged throughout the electoral process, despite concerns over violence, intimidation and alleged vote-buying ahead of the election.

According to him, voters’ determination to protect their ballots made it difficult for any political or institutional force to subvert their choice.

“What happened in Osun was what we call people power. People’s power showed its capabilities, and nobody rested on their laurels and allowed themselves to be trampled over by juggernauts, by political opposition, by even federal might,” he said.

The analyst also pointed to the reported prevalence of vote-buying during the election, arguing that if voters collected money but still voted according to their conscience, politicians could eventually begin to question the value of spending huge sums to influence voters.

World.title: Emaduku’s “Colours of My Mind”: Memorialising the paradoxes of a beloved landscape
World.content:
Emaduku’s “Colours of My Mind” is a product of experience and expression, which bestride different facets of the Nigerian society. The different sections of the book weave together relatable sociopolitical and cultural episodes in Nigeria. The author’s social and socialist vision reflects patriotic and transformative commitment in the Niger Delta and Nigeria. With the urgency to communicate realities, Emaduku deploys simple and rhythmic language, which occasionally infuses literary flavour. The mosaic of literary tools adds a striking sophistication to the book.

The ideas that drive and rejuvenate human communities are products of the mind, conveyed through language. In the biblical account of creation, God’s declaration, “Let’s there be light,” evidently carries a thought-process that privileges creativity and innovation. It is apt to draw a connection between this background and the assortment of ideas in Austin Emaduku’s anthology, Colours of My Mind. Spanning 2016 and 2022, the essays and commentary featured in the book reflect contemporary realities in Nigeria, underscoring the author’s vision of an improved social order.

Published by Premium Times Books, Abuja, in 2025, Emaduku’s Colours of My Mind is a 275-page volume of essays and poems on homeland and national realities. The book is logically structured into six parts captioned as chapters, which bear distinct but related thoughts about human and societal development. The systematic structuring of the book into different sections makes it easy to locate the issues that trouble our humanity and the regenerative thoughts of the author, as he desperately craves a healthy society that eschews any manifestations of abnormalities. It is, therefore, easy to trace the colours of the author’s mind as the reader follows his thoughts from page to page, chapter to chapter!

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The first section of the book, “Thoughts on the Niger Delta,” features 15 essays that diagnose the socio-cultural and politico-economic condition of communities in the oil-rich Niger Delta region of Nigeria, highlighting the neocolonial repression, connivance tactics, indigenes’ naivety and some redemptive measures. From the themes of the essays that constitute this section, it is evident that the author is enthusiastic about human and community development. The opening essay in the book, “Preserving Udu History and Culture,” anchors on cultural history, and accentuates the writer’s quest for cultural reclamation. Here, Emaduku draws on mythical and legendary characters to reflect on the heroic prowess of the Udu people, which now seems denigrated as a result of the current trend of sycophantic and manipulative politicking. The thesis of this essay anchors on the urgent need to resuscitate the eroding gallantry and unifying spirit of the Udu people. In another essay, Emaduku plays with “Udu-Ovo,” the symbolic rhetoric of unity and oneness in Udu Kingdom, to demonstrate his patriotism to his cultural space.

Most of the essays in the first section of the book reflect the author’s unbiased stance on the vexatious issues in Niger Delta, especially the hooliganism that drove away investors from different parts of the region. In “The Tragedy of an Unthinking Agitation,” Emaduku laments how the insecurity created by thoughtless agitations crippled the economic state of Niger Delta communities. Decrying how insecurity “chased away the companies that would have employed our teeming unemployed youths” (p. 6), Emaduku reminisces over the lost glory of Warri metropolis, which was an economic hub in Delta State: “I can recall the mid 1980s to the early 1990s when Warri, the economic hub of Delta State, was home to hundreds of oil companies” (p. 6). This essay sends a cautionary note to Niger Delta youths who manifest aggression, educating them about the ruinous consequence of such acts of violence. Here is a takeaway for our youths: “Until we create a conducive atmosphere for investment to thrive, we will continue to be jobless” (p. 7). This idea is further broadly echoed in the next article, “Youth Restiveness, Militancy and the Intractable Problems of the Niger Delta.”

Some essays in the first section of the book dissect the disunity among ethnic nationalities in Delta State as a major hindrance to development. Here, Emaduku decries disunity and advocates for inter-(intra-) peaceful coexistence within and among language groups. The essay, “The Itsekiri and their Neighbours” conveys the author’s distaste for the thoughtless and avoidable ethnic crises in Delta State, which continue to hinder development in Warri and its metropolis. The essay indicts the Itsekiri for most of the crises in Warri, noting that, “To maintain the false sense of domination, the Itsekiris have fought and continue to fight against anything that benefits the other ethnic groups or areas which they occupy” (p. 33). This indictment arises from the author’s thorough attempt to diagnose a condition before administering therapeutics. Drawing on biblical allusion, Emaduku emphasises how neighbourliness and the love for one another is a universal law for humanity.

A significant part of this essay is the celebration of the Wado City Advocacy Movement, which, according to Emaduku, offers a “a creative, almost magic-like solution to the issue of identity that has been the underlying cause of tensions and crises which rocked the city and led to avoidable deaths in the past” (p. 33). The next essay, “Vice President Yemi Osibanjo’s Visit and the Place of the Urhobo Nation in Delta State and the Niger Delta Question,” typifies the anger of the Urhobo people, who despite being the most peaceful and major language group in Delta State, is undermined by its neighbours. The essay bitterly recalls the denigration of Urhobo kings during the visit of President Yemi Osibanjo in the years 2017, and recommends the need for the Urhobo nation to carry itself with dignity and valour. Emaduku’s consistent call for peace in the Aladja-Ogbe-Ijoh crisis reflects his quest for unity. In his words, “Well, I was on the side of peace then as I remain now” (p. 80). This is a reflection of the quality of his mind — a fertile, dignified and a dispassionate mind that desperately craves peace and its offsprings.

The episodes of disunity captured in the book also underline intra-ethnic division among the Urhobo people. Emaduku notes that the strength of a people lies in their unity and image modelling. He emphasises that the Urhobo nation should look inward, dignify itself and build a formidable stance and voice in the nation. In “Urhobo Youths, Social Media and Unthinking Criticism,” Emaduku blames the growing sycophancy and thoughtlessness among Urhobo youths who are quick to insult their leaders and ethnic nationality online, for political gains. He asserts that “constructive criticism is good and can serve as a wake-up call from lethargy for the leader(s) but criticism for criticism’s sake is ‘pull downism’” (44). He, therefore admonishes Urhobo youths to be thoughtful and discerning.

In “Leave the Urhobo Progress Union (UPU) Out of Your Partisan Politics,” Emaduku censures the deep-seated sycophantic politics that continue to defame the Urhobo nation, which has badly inferiorised the exalted image of its apex body, the UPU. This thesis is also depicted in the essay, “The Need to Separate Partisan Politics from the Upcoming UUC Elections,” underscoring a consistency that highlights Emaduku’s quest for unity and cultural dignity in Urhobo. Emaduku’s vision for societal improvement and revulsion against hypocrisy is what he allegorically portrays as Colours of My Mind. That is, the book is a representation of his mental quality; a liberated mind that seeks the redemption of other minds. That consistency inheres in the articles.

As the past President General of Union of Udu Communities (UUC), Emaduku’s interventions on electric power supply are captured in some of the essays. He understands the import of stable electricity for the industrialisation of any human community. This is why he resents the injustices manifested by BEDC in Udu, captured in reprimanding lament with the essay, “Help! BEDC is Returning Udu 30 Years Back to the Days of Rural Electrification Boards (REBs).” As a patriotic leader driven by the vision to develop his communities, Emaduku recommends steps to be taken by the incoming President of UUC, for the advancement of Udu.

The second section of the book, “Restructure or Rupture,” engages the Nigerian federation, dissecting intractable challenges and rescuing measures. The essays featured in this section advocate for total restructuring of the Nigerian federation as a panacea for peace and development in Nigeria. Emaduku submits that “what the nation needs is the return to a true federal structure with minimum central might” (p. 93). He advises Nigerian leaders to “make the centre less attractive and the tensions will cease” (90). Illustrating further, he notes that “Each federating unit will become more acutely aware of its strengths and weaknesses and will consequently respect the strengths of other regions over its own weaknesses” (pp.90-91).

These submissions emphasise his deep knowledge of the Nigerian political experience. In “The Conflagration Will Come from the North,” Emaduku advises that, as a nation, we must eschew every ethnic and religious sentiment and solve the raging issue of poverty in the Northern part of Nigeria. Evidently, the issues of terrorism and banditry were triggered by poverty and lack of education, which are now affecting every part of the country.

The third and fourth sections of the book, “When Democracy Insults” and “Nigeria, We Hail Thee,” feature essays that dissect the Nigerian political situation. Emaduku’s disgust towards the manifest sycophancy and docility in the Nigerian society is captured in the essay, “Our ‘Mumu’ Our Fears?” which challenges Nigerian citizens to eschew fears and hypocrisy, and hold their leaders to account. The pidginised word, ‘mumu,’ which translates to ‘idiocy,’ reflects the author’s disdain for foolhardiness and hypocritical loyalty in the Nigerian political landscape. Other representative essays that resent the growing stupidity and absurd conducts of the Nigerian masses are “Gullibility and the Average Nigerian,” “The Self-Devaluation of the Nigerian Electorate,” and “The Stomach is the Leader.”

Emaduku’s political orientations and activistic ideological inclinations are expressed in a good number of essays featured in section three and four, including “Human Right and Minority Opinion,” “The Arrest and Release of Journalist, Chido Onumah,” #EndSARS,” “The Injustice in the Nigerian Prison System” amongst others. His essays on electoral malpractice in Nigeria and his insights on free and fair elections are compelling.

The fifth section of the book reflects on religious and cultural experiences. Aptly captioned as “Of Culture and Religion,” Emaduku decries the destructive manifestations of religious sentiments in Nigeria. In “The Familiar Spirits of the Nigerian Nation,” he identifies religion as one of the main causes of the Nigerian predicaments. He declares that “of all the familiar spirits, religion is the one that has been mostly deployed, sometimes with devastating effect, due to its emotive nature” (p.229). Emaduku does not merely narrate the damages caused by ethno-religious sentiments in Nigeria, he stimulates a conversation and orientates the public to shun the destructive fanaticism caused by religion in Nigeria, which include political docility, sycophancy, violence and terrorism. Some of the essays in this section ridicule religious hypocrisy, while others interrogate our dwindling mores and values.

The sixth and last section of the book, uncovers the author’s creative inclination. This section, titled “Colours of My Mind,” highlights Emaduku’s literary forage into poetry and narratives. The poems and autobiographical narratives in this part of the book embody related sociopolitical and cultural realities in Nigeria and elsewhere. They attest to Emaduku’s social vision and transformative fervour.

Emaduku’s Colours of My Mind is a product of experience and expression, which bestride different facets of the Nigerian society. The different sections of the book weave together relatable sociopolitical and cultural episodes in Nigeria. The author’s social and socialist vision reflects patriotic and transformative commitment in the Niger Delta and Nigeria. With the urgency to communicate realities, Emaduku deploys simple and rhythmic language, which occasionally infuses literary flavour. The mosaic of literary tools adds a striking sophistication to the book. This is a great and resourceful compendium that every Nigerian, especially indigenes of the Niger Delta, should have. It memorialises different experiences in the Nigerian sociocultural and political landscape. I, therefore, enthusiastically recommend this book without any reservations whatsoever.

Stephen Kekeghe (PhD) is a Senior Lecturer at the Department of English and Literary Studies, Delta State University, Abraka.

World.title: Rockson A. Igelige: A tireless labourer’s death just before harvest time!, By Ogaga Ifowodo
World.content:
Everyone who encountered Rockson knew how passionate he was about intellectual property rights and entertainment law. Long before these emergent areas of law became familiar, even to lawyers here in Nigeria, he had gone to the University of Westminster in the United Kingdom and obtained a Master’s in the field. His zeal was almost missionary and soon we were talking about how to popularise IPR beyond the courtroom. He had, in fact, gone as far as conceiving a non-governmental organisation for the purpose. He was the moving spirit behind Friends of the Creator (Artistic) Foundation, the first (and, to my knowledge, only) Nigerian NGO to be accredited by the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), with him as founding Executive Director and I as chairman, board of trustees.

Friday, morning, 21 August. As soon as I switched my phone back on, it began to ring. It was a call from a childhood friend of Rockson’s, bearing the worst news of the year, guaranteed to be an instance of the worst news I will ever hear in my life, however long God grants that I remain on earth. “Rockson is dead!” he said, barely holding back tears, apologising for being a bearer of bad news. The caller whom I know very well and his tears, which he could no longer stop, did not permit the false hope of “You’re joking, not so?” or “Tell me it is not true.” I brought the phone from my ear, as if to distance the tragic news from me, stared at the screen, and wished I hadn’t powered it back on.

As a rule, I switch off when going to bed. Nothing is ever so urgent it cannot wait a few hours till dawn. There was life before the invention of the telephone, before the tyranny of mobile cell phones. In short, for a moment, I wished the telephone had not been invented, and while my caller sobbed and spoke his grief, mine welled up slowly, looking for something that might arrest its progress. Finding none, it drifted to a poem I last read over twenty years ago. I saw now the morbid dread the late English poet, Ted Hughes, expressed so feverishly in his poem, “Do Not Pick Up the Telephone.” Even in those by-gone days of bell telephones crouched like crabs on the table or wall, fixed to a point, Hughes claimed that “Death invented the phone,” that it looked ‘like the altar of death,” with the “cosmetic breath of the gravestone.” After a long list of the evils that the telephone does, he ended on the note of strict admonition with which he began: “Do not pick up the detonator of the telephone/A flame from the last day will come lashing out of the telephone/A dead body will fall out of the telephone.” That Friday morning, there was nothing quite as apocalyptic, straight from a horror movie, but I had gone to Hughes for something on which to hang this tragedy.

“Rockson dead? How? I spoke with him four days ago. I’m expecting his follow-up call with respect to our conversation, the meeting in Port Harcourt he proposed…” I got the details of his death, in his bedroom, apparently from a heart attack, as he seemed to have risen to either plug his phone — the telephone! — to charge or to unplug it, the power cord still in his hand. But however death had surprised him, it didn’t really matter now. My caller apologised again for the news he had brought me and we hung up, to grieve separately or jointly with others we would call or who would call us; grief, as happiness, ever needing to be shared.

Rockson was like the younger brother I never had. And like a younger brother, he looked up to me, rebelled against me, then made peace with me. It couldn’t have been otherwise, for he was nothing if not strong-willed. The peculiar circumstances of growing up in a polygamous family large enough to found its own village, town in due course, had taught him very early on the necessity of standing up for oneself, of being heard, even if one would be damned. Even if it meant standing alone, so long as one had found the ground to stand on. To be against the crowd, to keep the company of one was, thus, an old suit in which he felt comfortable. He had worn it from childhood. I had to bear this and other attenuating circumstances in mind whenever we had our arguments, sibling rivalries, as it were. For that same trait made him a dependable ally. You couldn’t wish for someone to go to battle with more reliable than Rockson. Let me explain.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

When an urgent family need required that I take leave of my teaching position in the United States and come home, and once back my village blood called for a full return, Rockson’s enthusiasm alone was enough to make it immediate. A year later when I did return, now with the intention of dipping my toe in the rather hot waters of politics, he was all in with me. He had been a local government councillor and speaker of its parliament. He was a card-carrying member of the Peoples Democratic Party, but was ready to openly work with me, newly registered in the All Progressives Congress, towards the goal of unseating the sixteen-year occupant of the Isoko Federal constituency seat, with little to show for all that time.

For him, electing the right representative of the people, a knowledgeable and competent legislator, one with a voice, was a matter that transcended partisan loyalties, especially for an oil-and-gas-producing ethnic minority gladly exploited but hardly acknowledged as part of the nation. He endorsed, whole-heartedly, my joining APC, certain that I would not come a thousand miles close to getting the PDP’s ticket. He became my adviser and campaign manager, even before the tricky race of party primaries began. And, predictably, accusations of disloyalty, of working against his own party, were rained on him. Still, he did not budge. He would, he said, recount the countless instances of anti-party activity, from top to bottom, to his accusers whenever he would be formally charged.

As it happened, we had been working together since 2015 in a loose legal partnership of him, a law faculty mate of his from the Oleh campus of Delta State University (now a magistrate in the Federal Capital Territory), a retired Assistant Inspector-General of Police who was like an uncle to both of us, a Lagos-based homeboy who combined practice with law reporting, and my good self. It began when we took on the case of Omenuwoma Okson Dovie, a musician professionally known as Baba 2010, for the enforcement of his copyright against MTN, which had without authorisation used four of his songs as caller or ring-back tunes.

Wish such courage and commitment had found just reward! I got my first lesson of politics or, I should say, of running for political office, at the party primary stage. An unknown opponent, surprisingly with money to spend, had appeared. And even though arrested by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission a few days before the primary election, he managed to be released and escorted out of jail just in time. It was quite a spectacle watching his convoy enter the election venue, the absurdity notwithstanding. Needless to inform you, he beat me to the ticket. I returned to my teaching post in the United States, but shortly after received a call from the local leader of the party to please come back home as the winner of the primary election had disappeared into thin air! Knowing I had no money, the plot of my putative opponent in the general election had been simple: sponsor a puppet, fund him to snatch the ticket, after which he would disappear, for a virtually unchallenged fourth tenure. It was a scenario that Rockson had anticipated but which I had thought too obvious and ridiculous to succeed.

There was some consolation, however. A year-and-a-half after, I was appointed as the Delta State representative on the board of the Niger Delta Development Commission. Without hesitation, I named Rockson my special assistant. Although the board was, as all previous boards, sadly, dissolved before the end of its tenure, in this case, midway, I had the benefit of a close working relationship with him for two full years and saw him manifest, in varying circumstances, the qualities of forthrightness and public spiritedness that I already knew he possessed. The even more telling part was his total lack of desire for material acquisitions. We shared a common passion for a redress of the plight of the Niger Delta and any opportunity to work towards that end was not to be compromised. But in Nigeria, dreams die first and where they survive, are soon dampened. The untimely dissolution of the NDDC board soured him greatly on politics. He announced to me his decision to quit that terrain and focus entirely on legal practice henceforth.

As it happened, we had been working together since 2015 in a loose legal partnership of him, a law faculty mate of his from the Oleh campus of Delta State University (now a magistrate in the Federal Capital Territory), a retired Assistant Inspector-General of Police who was like an uncle to both of us, a Lagos-based homeboy who combined practice with law reporting, and my good self. It began when we took on the case of Omenuwoma Okson Dovie, a musician professionally known as Baba 2010, for the enforcement of his copyright against MTN, which had without authorisation used four of his songs as caller or ring-back tunes. The case was settled without trial but the “partnership” successfully instituted and won yet another copyright violation suit against MTN and a record label, the case going all the way to trial and judgement.

A suit against a publishing company for the unauthorised publication of a young playwright’s work and appropriation of his copyright was settled out of court. Another, against a television house for the unauthorised broadcast of a cooking show, was settled after trial was almost completed. One more suit, this time for the publication without permission by The Sun newspaper, of a young lady’s photograph as a Page 3 Girl, went to trial with the court finding for our client. Such a successful special area collaboration deserved a more formal platform, hence Remedium Law Partners was found.

Everyone who encountered Rockson knew how passionate he was about intellectual property rights and entertainment law. Long before these emergent areas of law became familiar, even to lawyers here in Nigeria, he had gone to the University of Westminster in the United Kingdom and obtained a Master’s in the field. His zeal was almost missionary and soon we were talking about how to popularise IPR beyond the courtroom. He had, in fact, gone as far as conceiving a non-governmental organisation for the purpose. He was the moving spirit behind Friends of the Creator (Artistic) Foundation, the first (and, to my knowledge, only) Nigerian NGO to be accredited by the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), with him as founding Executive Director and I as chairman, board of trustees.

When in January this year he secured judgement for Veno Marioghae-Mbanefo against the telecoms giants, Airtel, for infringement of copyright to her well-known song, “Nigeria Go Survive,” it was a fitting reward for his tenacity. I had played a nominal role in the case, mostly as a sounding board on aspects of it. I felt certain that the defendants would appeal, even if only on the ground of the quantum of damages. And he prayed they would, for IPR being a new and recondite field, there is a vexing paucity of appellate decisions to help clear a great deal of the muddle in the high courts by the binding power of precedent.

Having turned his back on politics, he was impatient to make his mark. But I had yet to resolve a few issues around my return from the United States, such as whether to go back, the fatherland proving rather hostile and where, if I didn’t, to pitch tent. With him mainly settled in Oleh, and Warri only a temporary address for me, I would have to choose between Lagos and Abuja for personal and professional reasons. While I pondered the issue, he wisely chose to develop a personal legal brand with the goal of name recognition in the IPR domain, deploying every available means to create awareness of IPR: talks, articles, online platforms, conferences.

When in January this year he secured judgement for Veno Marioghae-Mbanefo against the telecoms giants, Airtel, for infringement of copyright to her well-known song, “Nigeria Go Survive,” it was a fitting reward for his tenacity. I had played a nominal role in the case, mostly as a sounding board on aspects of it. I felt certain that the defendants would appeal, even if only on the ground of the quantum of damages. And he prayed they would, for IPR being a new and recondite field, there is a vexing paucity of appellate decisions to help clear a great deal of the muddle in the high courts by the binding power of precedent. The appeal was indeed filed, briefs of argument exchanged but, it seems, death has now cheated the most ardent advocate of IPR that I know in Nigeria, of the final fruits of his labours!

Space and occasion will not permit me to say more about this remarkable individual. Was Rockson flawless? Definitely not! Who is? But even in his less admirable ways, he proved his outstanding qualities. I bear witness. In 2015, he had been an indefatigable champion of my foray into politics. In 2022, however, he was the exact opposite when, at the strong urging of the party, I had accepted to run for the vacant seat of my constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly. For reasons I need not go into here, one of which was totally unfounded and another misconstrued, he stood vehemently against me, even going as far as joining ranks with a younger man who came into my orbit through him to campaign against me.

That other man later confessed the motive for his calumny to me but I didn’t even need that. I had forgiven them both even before the chance to ask why. I don’t bear grudges, have no need of the extra luggage of malice, in addition to life’s neck-twisting load. Let go of it before death, I say. With two exceptions: I know now that as a mortal, I am not allotted enough time to forgive false-star General Sani Abacha — God roast his soul, if he had any, or another false-star general for whom it is yet too early to extend that godly sentiment. Besides, it was easy to overlook my younger brother, for if we must value independence of mind, we must also accept that the mind will not be right all the time.

Yet, I have a regret. Shortly after the Marioghae-Mbanefo v Airtel judgement, Rockson came to Abuja, on what I saw partly as a well-earned victory lap. I met him at Transcorp Hilton, where he had just had lunch with an old friend. He wanted us to go see a DELSU alumnus now a Senior Advocate of Nigeria. Right from when I saw how much the buttons of his jacket strained against his belly and noticed his laboured breathing as he climbed into my car, I felt that he had been too neglectful of his health. I wanted to broach the subject but I had nagged him far too often, so I curbed my tongue. Besides, I hadn’t wanted to cast a pall on the euphoria of a potentially precedent-setting court victory, a case that had all the trappings of a locus classicus. There would always be another time, a better-attuned moment, I thought. Alas, too often, life tells us belatedly, there is no other time. How I wish now that I had nagged, decorum be damned! Maybe he might have been nudged to take better care of himself. But maybe the manner of his death did not matter a hoot, his time being up. Maybe…

Adieu, Rockson. You will be missed.

Ogaga Ifowodo, lawyer, poet and writer is principal partner at Remedium Law Partners. His new poetry book, Why Does God Need a Gun? is longlisted for the 2026 NLNG Nigeria Literature Prize. He may be reached at [email protected].

World.title: SIAT Group celebrates legacy, leadership and people behind the Group’s journey
World.content:
SIAT Group (Société d’Investissement pour l’Agriculture Tropicale NV), a leading African agro-industrial group and majority shareholder of Presco Plc, recently hosted an intimate and thoughtfully curated event to celebrate its legacy, leadership and the people who have shaped its journey at the SIAT Forward event, held on Friday, 21 August, 2026.

Held under the theme “Legacy, Leadership & the Future,” the event brought together SIAT’s founding family, retired Directors, Boardmembers, company executives, financial partners and other stakeholders.

The evening was an opportunity to reflect on the Group’s history, recognise those who helped build and sustain the business, and celebrate the continuity of a legacy that has evolved across generations, countries and communities.

At the heart of the evening was a celebration of the Vandebeeck family, whose entrepreneurial vision was instrumental in establishing SIAT. Incorporated under Belgian law in 1991 under the leadership of Pierre Vandebeeck, SIAT’s journey in Africa began with the acquisition of Presco in Nigeria that same year. The Group subsequently expanded its footprint across the continent, including through the acquisition of Ghana Oil Palm Development Company (GOPDC) in 1995.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Reflecting on the significance of the event, Rasheed Sarumi, Group Chief Executive Officer, Saroafrica International Limited and Chairman, Presco Plc, said ‘’We are gathered this evening not simply to mark an occasion, but to celebrate a milestone. For decades, this Group has grown across borders and generations through the vision of the founding family and the dedication of those who came before us and those who have carried that vision forward. Many of you in this room were part of buildingthat story. Today is about saying thank you to those who built it, stayed, served, and to those who continue to carry it forward. We do not stand as something new, but as something continued’.

Speaking on behalf of the founding family, Marie Vandebeeck said: “When I think of the legacy of SIAT Group, I don’t first think of hectares and tons of palm oil. I think of people, because ultimately, this business was built over many years. Often, in places where building successful companies requires more than capital and ambition, this is the greatest achievement of SIAT. Above all, you need to believe in the future. This philosophy became the DNA of SIAT, and nowhere is it more visible than in Presco. What Presco became today did not happen overnight. It is the result of decades of persistence, investment and the role of exceptional Nigerian organisations. There was certainly risk and uncertainty; that’s part of the entrepreneurial journey. But there was also a fundamental conviction that it was possible to build a world-class agricultural business in Africa. I am proud of the many talented people who joined this company, stayed, developed and assumed great responsibilities.”

The event also provided an opportunity to look ahead, with Adewale Arikawe, Group Chief Executive Officer, SIAT Group, speaking on the responsibility of the current leadership to build on the foundations established by previous generations. He said: “Our responsibility as a team is to take SIAT to the next level — to build something bigger, bolder and more impactful. This is not just a simple vision; it is a call to action. At SIAT, we are fully committed to being an integrated agriculture business, sustainably growing, processing and marketing agricultural resources to create value for our people and shareholders. The Group is growing, and with that growth comes a greater responsibility to our people, our shareholders and all our stakeholders. This is a journey, and our responsibility is to keep building on what has been established, keep growing and make SIAT bigger and stronger.”

The gathering was attended by a cross-section of leaders and stakeholders who have contributed to SIAT’s evolution, including Chief Atedo Peterside, former Board member, Presco Plc; Reji George, Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Presco Plc; Felix Nwabuko, former Group Chief Executive Officer, SIAT NV and Institutional Adviser, Presco Plc; among others.

Today, SIAT operates integrated agricultural businesses across Africa, with operations spanning plantation development, cultivation, processing and downstream activities. Through its businesses in Nigeria and Ghana, the Group employs more than 17,000 people and supports thousands of smallholder farmers and rural communities.

For more information on SIAT Group, Presco Plc., and GOPDC, visit www.siat-group.com, www.presco-plc.com, and www.gopdc-ltd.com

World.title: Police arrest suspected cross-border car theft syndicate members in Oyo
World.content:
The Oyo State Police Command says it has disrupted a transnational criminal network involved in the trafficking of stolen exotic vehicles across Nigeria’s borders for sale in foreign countries,

In a statement on Wednesday, the command said two suspects were arrested and a stolen Lexus RX 350 SUV recovered during an intelligence-led operation along the Ibadan-Ilorin Expressway.

The operation followed information obtained from a suspect already in police custody over an armed robbery case, according to the statement issued by the command’s spokesperson, Olayinka Ayanlade.

The suspect, the police said, disclosed his knowledge of a criminal gang specialising in receiving stolen vehicles and conveying them across Nigeria’s borders.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the command, operatives subsequently allowed the suspect to use his mobile phone under controlled circumstances, during which members of the alleged syndicate sent him photographs of a vehicle they were preparing to steal.

“They instructed him to make proper arrangements for its reception, preparation and movement across the border for sale in a foreign country,” the statement read.

The operation that led to the arrest started when the Oyo Command received a request from the Kwara State Police Command on 24 August to help intercept a 2017 Lexus RX 350 SUV allegedly stolen at gunpoint from a woman at her residence in Ilorin. The vehicle was reportedly stolen alongside other valuables belonging to the victim.

Following the alert, the Commissioner of Police in Oyo, Abimbola Ayodeji, directed the Commander of the Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU) to deploy operatives along the Ibadan-Ilorin Expressway to intercept the vehicle.

According to the Command, VCRU operatives reportedly sighted the Lexus and attempted to stop it at about 4 a.m. on Tuesday. The occupants, however, allegedly abandoned the vehicle and fled into the bush in different directions.

The police said operatives pursued the suspects, arresting two men identified as Adewale Abiola, 33, and Kabiru Abobarin, 36. During the operation one of the suspects reportedly sustained a gunshot wound to his left foot.

A search of the recovered SUV, the police said, led to the recovery of several items allegedly belonging to the victim, including four HP laptops, an iPhone 15 Pro Max, seven wristwatches and jewellery.

Police allege cross-border trafficking network

The command said preliminary interrogation showed that the two arrested suspects allegedly received the vehicle from members of the gang responsible for stealing it in Ilorin, Kwara State.

The suspects also allegedly told investigators that they were transporting the SUV towards the border, where an ECOWAS document was expected to be obtained to facilitate its movement across the border for sale in another country.

The police did not identify the alleged foreign destination or disclose the number of vehicles the network may have previously trafficked.

The command said the investigation had been expanded to identify and arrest other members of the alleged syndicate and dismantle what it described as the wider transnational criminal network.

World.title: Zenith Bank’s 10th International Trade Seminar sets out strategies to scale Nigeria’s non-oil exports
World.content:
Zenith Bank Plc hosted the 10th edition of its International Trade Seminar on Non-Oil Export on Tuesday, 25 August 2026, marking a decade of sustained advocacy for the diversification of Nigeria’s economy. The virtual event brought together policymakers, regulators, exporters, manufacturers, investors and development partners from across Africa and beyond, all focused on one question: how Nigeria can earn more from what it sells to the world.

Held under the theme “Unlocking Value and Harnessing Growth”, the seminar examined how Nigeria can move beyond exporting raw commodities to building competitive value chains, strengthening trade infrastructure and financing, and deepening the sector’s contribution to sustainable economic growth.

In her welcome address, the Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Zenith Bank Plc, Adaora Umeoji, paid tribute to the Bank’s Founder, Dr Jim Ovia, whose vision gave birth to the seminar in 2015, and urged participants to turn Nigeria’s improving export numbers into lasting economic value.

In her words: “Our theme, ‘Unlocking Value and Harnessing Growth’, is not just a slogan. It speaks to the opportunities before us and the need to translate our collective efforts into sustainable economic value.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the Nigerian Export Promotion Council, Nigeria’s non-oil exports reached a record $6.1 billion in 2025, up 11.5 per cent from the $5.46 billion recorded in 2024, and a remarkable leap from the $612 million recorded a decade earlier. Through our partnership with the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, we have commenced the development of the SMARTAfCFTA portal, and our integration with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is making cross-border business easier for our customers. Wherever our exporters need to reach, Zenith Bank will reach with them.”

She commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, for the structural reforms creating a more enabling environment for businesses, and the Central Bank of Nigeria, under Governor Olayemi Cardoso, for reforms that have improved foreign exchange stability and market confidence. “As we build on the progress recorded so far,” she added, “it is important that, as a nation, we accelerate growth by creating more value locally and exporting finished products, rather than just raw materials.”

Delivering the keynote address, the Honourable Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Jumoke Oduwole, called for deeper trade and investment reforms, a better export environment and wider market access within Africa and beyond. “The question before us now is not simply how to export more, but how to retain more value in Nigeria from everything we export,” she said.

“Our focus at the Ministry is straightforward: produce more competitively in Nigeria, process more in Nigeria, connect Nigerian businesses to bigger markets, and ensure that the financing, infrastructure and trade systems exist to help them scale. In July, I assumed the chair of the AfCFTA Council of Ministers, and I see at first hand that the opportunity before us goes beyond the size of the African market of over 1.4 billion people and approximately $3.4 trillion in GDP.

“It is about enabling Nigerian firms to sell more products, reach more markets and deepen regional value chains. Nigeria’s role as an AfCFTA digital trade co-champion further positions us to help shape how this market evolves, particularly as digital trade creates new pathways for Nigerian businesses to reach customers across the continent,” Oduwole added.

She urged financial institutions to go beyond financing export transactions to financing export capability, and encouraged Nigerian businesses to prepare for intra-African trade by investing in productivity, quality and skills.

In his presentation, the Chair of the Board of Directors of the Fund for Export Development in Africa (FEDA) and immediate past President/Chairman of Afreximbank, Professor Benedict Oramah, argued that the moment demands new thinking. “The theme chosen for this 10th edition is both apt and timely,” he said. “The global economy is experiencing unprecedented levels of entropy. I do not raise this to alarm us.

I raise it because a unique opportunity lies ahead of us that may well pave the way to Africa’s ascendance.

The question is no longer whether Africa can attract enough external capital and external demand to power its growth. The question is whether Africa, and Nigeria within it, can build her own internal demand, participate effectively in global supply chains, build the capacity to finance her own trade and industries, and create her own markets.” He commended Zenith Bank and its leadership for advancing Nigeria’s non-oil export agenda over the past decade.

The Founder and Executive Chair of Plot Enterprise Ghana Limited, Mrs Patricia Poku-Diaby, made the case for transformation plainly. “Let us make no mistake: the future of our economy will not be determined simply by what we grow or what we mine, but by what we transform,” she said. “We need to move from being suppliers of raw materials to becoming producers, processors, manufacturers, exporters and owners of strong African brands. Our focus should be on creating more value before our products leave our shores.”

Speaking on the Nigeria-United Kingdom trade relationship, the UK Minister of State at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, the Hon Florence Eshalomi, MP, represented by Ms Mujina Kaindama, Head of Trade Policy for UK Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, commended the Bank for the platform.

“The trade relationship between the United Kingdom and Nigeria is one of immense importance and even greater potential,” she said. “Nigeria is home to extraordinary entrepreneurial talent, innovation and creativity. One of the most promising opportunities lies not simply in increasing exports, but in increasing the value of those exports: moving further up the value chain, processing raw materials, developing branded products and creating higher-value manufactured and agricultural goods. In doing so, Nigerian businesses can unlock greater returns, create jobs and build sustainable economic growth.”

The Secretary-General of the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, Wamkele Mene, placed the private sector at the centre of the continent’s economic restructuring. “The private sector is at the heart of the fundamental restructuring of Africa’s economy that all of us want to see,” he said, “and the seminar Zenith Bank has convened strikes at the heart of that objective: reducing the reliance of exports on unprocessed commodities and accelerating industrialisation and value addition in Africa. The success of the AfCFTA will ultimately be measured not by how many protocols and legal instruments have been signed, but by the extent to which our private sector can leverage the AfCFTA to access new markets, scale their investment and scale their productive capacity to create jobs across the continent.”

The seminar featured two panel sessions. The public sector panel brought together Mr Abubakar Bello, Managing Director of the Nigerian Export-Import Bank (NEXIM), represented by Mr Hope Nyongo, Technical Adviser; Mr Adewale Adeniyi, MFR, Comptroller-General of the Nigeria Customs Service; Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, Managing Director/CEO of the Nigerian Ports Authority, represented by Mr Adebowale Lawal, Ports Manager, Lagos Ports Complex; Ms Aderinola Shonekan, Director, Trade and Exchange Department, Central Bank of Nigeria; Mrs Nonye Ayeni, Executive Director/CEO of the Nigerian Export Promotion Council; and Mr Adekunle Ajai, General Manager, Neroli Technologies. The panellists committed to improving trade facilitation, customs efficiency, logistics reform, trade advocacy and exporters’ access to funding.

The private sector panel featured Adeniji Adeyemi, MD/CEO of Starlink Global & Ideal Limited; Alhaji Sada Ladan-Baki, Group Executive Director, International Trade and Export, Dangote Group; Mr Bamidele Ayemibo, Senior Consultant, 3T Impex Trade Centre; Mr Mobolaji Salako, Managing Director, Terra Aqua Environmental Consultancy Nigeria Limited; Mr Ramzi Taher, Managing Director, RMM Global Company Limited; Mrs Oluyemisi Iranloye, Founder/Managing Director, Psaltry International; and Chief (Mrs) Chinwe Ezenwa, MD/CEO, Lelook Nigeria Limited. Their discussions centred on trade barriers, value creation and addition, competitiveness, product certification, market intelligence and the structured financing needed to scale non-oil exports.

The Zenith Bank International Trade Seminar on Non-Oil Export was launched in 2015 to drive dialogue and action around Nigeria’s non-oil export potential. Ten years on, the Bank continues to champion the sector’s growth by opening up market opportunities and backing exporters with financing, incentives and practical support.

The 2026 edition streamed live on Zoom, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, X and TikTok, drawing thousands of participants from 97 countries. The tenth edition closed the way the first began a decade ago: with a commitment to give Nigerian businesses the tools, partnerships and capital they need to compete in regional and global markets.
