World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Parliament’s Culture committee rejects opposition candidates to public media authority
World.content:
Parliament’s culture committee has not backed the opposition parties’ candidates to the Independent Public Media Authority. Zoltán Moys, nominated by Our Homeland, Zoltán Márti of the Christian Democrats and Beatrix Siklósi, who was nominated by Fidesz, each received four votes in favour and seven against.

At their (separate) hearings ahead of the vote, the candidates highlighted the importance of credibility, professionalism and creating cultural values. They also stressed that public media must stand above party politics.

Committee head Alexandra Szentkirályi of Fidesz said after the meeting that the fact that none of the nine members of the body were elected by the deadline was “autocratic” and “cinema”.

Chairwoman Szentkirályi speaking at the session. Photo: MTI

Central bank probe is to start

An ad hoc parliamentary committee established to investigate the use of public monies by the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) for non-core activities aims to determine political responsibility, the committee’s chair said ahead of its inaugural meeting on Wednesday, MTI wrote.

Attila Csőszi, an MP of the governing Tisza Party, said the committee would not take over the role of the judiciary. He added that recommendations would be made to improve transparency and accountability when the probe finished. The committee will probe the management of assets in the NBH’s foundation and the renovation of the central bank headquarters.

World.title: Fundamental changes in Hungary’s foreign policy reflected in new UN guidelines
World.content:
Hungary condemns Russia’s military aggression, fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while urging negotiations towards sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees, according to the guidelines set for the Hungarian delegation participating in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, published in Tuesday’s issue of the official gazette Magyar Közlöny.

According to the supplement to the resolution signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, the Hungarian delegation participating in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is tasked with acting in accordance with the government’s objectives and upholding Hungarian national interests.

Russia’s behaviour poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also places the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger, the document said, adding that the government supports all efforts aimed at initiating negotiations toward sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees.

Péter Magyar and Volodimir Zelensky at the EU Summit on 18 June 2026. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

War in Gaza, Iran, USA

On matters relating to the war in Gaza, the delegation is to present Hungary’s position that lasting peace can be achieved on the basis of resolutions adopted by the UN Security Council, by ensuring the protection of civilians, respecting Israel’s right to self-defence, disarming Hamas and improving the humanitarian situation in Gaza. It added that direct negotiations between the parties formed the basis for Israeli–Palestinian reconciliation.

The long-term settlement of the Israel–Hezbollah conflict likewise required the protection of civilians, recognition of Israel’s right to security, the restoration of Lebanon’s sovereignty and the disarmament of Hezbollah, it said.

The resolution stressed that the Government highly valued the efforts of the United States and regional mediators to bring conflicts in the Middle East to an end.

Under the resolution, the delegation is also required to represent Hungary’s position on the conflict involving Iran: rather than resorting to military escalation, the parties should resolve their disputes at the negotiating table while keeping diplomatic channels open. It stressed that Iran must not be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons under any circumstances.

It noted that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the disruption of maritime trade posed a global risk to energy security. Hungary therefore supported every effort aimed at restoring stability in the region.

EU, migration, water issues

The guidelines also state that Hungary – working closely with the International Energy Agency and the European Union – will constructively support all measures capable of safeguarding Europe’s and the world’s energy supplies, while easing the supply-security challenges caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

The delegation must pay particular attention to advancing the Hungarian Government’s position on migration within the framework of the United Nations. It must also make clear that border protection and the rules governing residence on their territory fall within the national competence of member states, while drawing attention to the immediate security risks posed by migration.

Péter Magyar reveals how long he plans to be prime minister as Viktor Orbán’s party falls apart

In another section, the delegation was instructed to continue paying close attention to international processes aimed at implementing goals and targets relating to water and sanitation, to help promote the institutional reforms required for their implementation and, accordingly, to reaffirm Hungary’s commitment to establishing a permanent UN water process. It must also monitor preparations for, and the proceedings of, the UN Water Conference to be held in December, and ensure that Hungary’s position is properly represented.

The guidelines further call on the delegation to support the work of the International Court of Justice and other generally recognised international dispute-resolution bodies, and to back the general recognition of the ICJ’s jurisdiction. It is also expected to oppose the politicisation of international legal and judicial forums in order to preserve their impartiality.

The delegation is tasked with reaffirming Hungary’s support for the UN Secretary-General’s proposals to reform the organisation’s governance. Hungary also intends to continue contributing to the renewal of the General Assembly’s role and to reforms of the UN’s development and environmental systems, the resolution said.

World.title: Péter Magyar reveals how long he plans to be prime minister as Viktor Orbán’s party falls apart
World.content:
It appears that Péter Magyar and the Tisza Party he leads will continue to shape Hungarian public life for some time to come. Yet the country’s current prime minister is making remarkably modest claims in this regard, while his intended involvement in public affairs appears strikingly limited. Viktor Orbán has always planned for the long term; Péter Magyar’s ambitions extend much less far into the future.

Orbán and the longue durée

As prime minister, Viktor Orbán invariably set out lengthy time horizons for his tenure in office. Although, during the past four years, he regularly spoke of eventually having to hand over the baton to the next generation, the last person to seriously question his position as leader was perhaps János Lázár, before the 2018 election. That challenge ended with Lázár being sidelined. This April, Lázár suffered a major defeat alongside his former boss, having served as one of the faces of the campaign.

Orbán always planned at least as far ahead as 2030. In his telling, that was how long it would take to put the country right after the “social-liberal” rampage. Those deadlines, however, were repeatedly pushed back. During the latest campaign, for example, Lázár regularly described Hungary as a half-finished country, implying that much remained to be done before their work – whatever it might have been – could be completed.

Péter Magyar has adopted a far more modest outlook as prime minister, although he threw himself into even the first few months of his first term with extraordinary energy and a punishing workload. He says he sleeps little and values the time he spends with his family and children, but that there is no time for rest at present. “Perhaps there will be time for a little rest in seven years and eight months,” he wrote in a Facebook post yesterday. In the accompanying photograph, he can be seen leaping up two steps at a time while holding a national flag – suggesting, among other things, that slowing down is not currently an option.

Péter Magyar at Paks NPP during the energy and water crisis. Orbán did not even Photo: Facebook/Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz

Could Péter Magyar become Hungary’s next, powerful President?

Among the Tisza government’s first measures was a constitutional limit stipulating that a prime minister may serve no more than two terms – eight years in total – at the head of the Hungarian Government. The calculation above is therefore easy to understand. Although many questioned whether Péter Magyar genuinely intended to honour the restriction, he appears to be standing by his promise.

That said, the new constitution that Tisza intends to draft by next autumn could establish a semi-presidential republic, with a directly elected president enjoying a strong mandate and correspondingly broader and more powerful powers. Nothing currently prevents someone from moving directly from the office of prime minister to that of president, although there has been no such example – in either direction – since the collapse of communism.

Could Hungarians directly elect a much stronger president next year? This is what one of Tisza’s strongmen now says

For now, at least, Tisza has the power to reshape Hungary’s constitutional order as it sees fit. It holds 141 seats in Parliament – comfortably more than the two-thirds majority required. More importantly, if an election were held today, it would receive an even stronger mandate, with roughly two-thirds of the vote.

Tisza has an overwhelming majority in the Hungarian Parliament. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

Meanwhile, Fidesz, the party led by Viktor Orbán and Hungary’s strongest opposition force, is showing signs of disintegration. Tibor Navracsics, a former European commissioner and minister, and Orsolya Ferencz have established an independent platform called the Civic Democrats. János Bóka, Fidesz’s parliamentary group leader, welcomed the move. Yet in Hungarian political history, the emergence of platforms within a party has invariably been the prelude to its collapse – as happened with the Hungarian Socialist Party and, more recently, Jobbik.

Orbán and János Bóka. Photo: MTI

Andrea Virág, strategic director of the Republikon Institute, also told Népszava that Viktor Orbán – despite enjoying the support of almost 100 per cent of his party – had remained virtually silent as party leader in recent months, while Hungary was facing an energy crisis, a water crisis and, in her view, a constitutional crisis.

According to Andrea Virág, this suggests that Viktor Orbán has voluntarily withdrawn from the political stage and is looking for someone to whom he can hand over the baton. She argues that he has abandoned his party, has no strategy for a return and that everything around him is now showing signs of collapse.

World.title: Hungarian firefighters and vehicles sent to Serbia to aid the battle against forest fires
World.content:
Hungary is sending 12 firefighters and four vehicles to Serbia to aid the battle against forest fires, Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai said on Facebook late on Tuesday.

The contingent left for Serbia on Tuesday, Pósfai said. He thanked the firefighters working to extinguish fires in Hungary nationwide. Hungary is committed to strengthening international relations and regional safety, Pósfai said, noting that Serbia was one of several European countries facing a “critical situation”.

“We hope that human and technical resources offered will help contain the Serbian wildfires as soon as possible,” Pósfai said. Other foreign units are also assisting in extinguishing the fires in Serbia under the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. Four firefighting helicopters have arrived in Serbia: two from the Czech Republic, one from Romania, and one from Slovakia. Additionally, German and Romanian ground firefighting units have joined the efforts.

Hungarian firefighters in North Macedonia before. Photo: National Disaster Management Authority

Nearly 4,000 hectares have burned in the Deliblato Sands, with over 3,100 hectares of forest affected. The most severe damage has impacted the wildlife and forest ecosystems of the protected area.

Fires continue to burn elsewhere in Serbia, with the most challenging situation in the Stolovi Mountains near Kraljevo, where difficult terrain, strong winds, and dense smoke hinder firefighting efforts. The Serbian Meteorological Service has warned that persistent heat, lack of rainfall, and occasionally strengthening winds continue to favour the outbreak and spread of wildfires.

World.title: Hungary’s ‘winged phallus’ memorial taken down as officials offer strange explanations – video, photos
World.content:
The wooden monument intended to commemorate the Battle of Mohács — but swiftly dubbed a “winged phallus” by the public — has been removed in the Hungarian town of Devecser, with both the mayor and the deputy mayor behind the initiative offering rather curious explanations.

Deputy mayor ‘did not see’ phallus

An unusual monument was unveiled in Devecser on August 20, Hungary’s national holiday marking the foundation of the state. It was intended to commemorate the Battle of Mohács, whose 500th anniversary falls on August 29 — this Saturday.

The deputy mayor claimed the statue had been completed at breakneck speed: officials were still debating the design on August 19, only for the unveiling to follow the next day, complete with a priestly blessing, children’s entertainment and all the usual trimmings.

Check out our previous article in the issue HERE.

This is how the original wooden memorial looked like. The deputy mayor says she learned about the scandalous resemblance only from the social media conversastion. Forrás: Facebook/Nyárs Hajnalka

Speaking to RTL Híradó, Hajnalka Nyárs, the deputy mayor who conceived the project, said that the organisers had not “seen into it” what others immediately did. She accepted, however, that viewers were free to see whatever their individual imaginations suggested in a work of art.

In this case, much of the country saw a winged phallus in the wooden statue, which was supposedly meant to depict a helmeted Turul — the winged bird of Hungarian mythology. It was intended as a memorial to the Hungarian, Czech, Croatian, Serbian and other soldiers who died fighting bravely for their homeland on the Mohács plain.

A nation remembers Mohács

August 29 marks the 500th anniversary of Hungary’s defeat at the Battle of Mohács. On that day in 1526, Louis II, King of Hungary and Bohemia, was defeated by the Ottoman ruler Suleiman on the Mohács plain — and lost his life in the aftermath.

The defeat effectively marked the collapse of the medieval Hungarian state and the beginning of Ottoman occupation across large parts of the country for more than a century and a half. The occupation profoundly altered the ethnic balance of the region, shaping the course of later history. Mohács was therefore regarded by contemporaries — and remains regarded by modern historians — as a decisive historical watershed.

499 years ago: the Battle of Mohács Memorial – photos and video

It is little surprise, then, that Mohács has already been hosting a steady programme of commemorations and cultural events this week. The anniversary itself, on Saturday, will be marked by a major ceremony and a historically faithful re-enactment of the battle.

Mayor says he never saw it

Devecser has nevertheless found a way to make the anniversary rather more distinctive. The deputy mayor has acknowledged her error, and the monument was dismantled on Tuesday — although, according to RTL Híradó, some visitors had travelled to the town solely to see it.

Ms Nyárs said that negative publicity was still publicity, and that if the affair inadvertently attracted tourists to the town, she would be pleased. Locally, however, she has received ample criticism, with calls in some groups for her resignation or removal from office.

Key deal secured for new Danube bridge at Mohács – new photos

It is telling that she responded to the online mockery only several days after it began to spread.

There has been no word on what will replace the work, which formed part of a larger memorial park — making the episode all the more unfortunate.

The current situation. Source: PrtScr/RTL Híradó

In a further twist, Devecser’s mayor, Gábor Ferenczi, a former Jobbik representative, said he had not seen the monument either before or after it was erected, according to 444.hu. If that is indeed the case, the town hall may need to take a rather closer interest in how independent local initiatives are carried out in future.

The statue was carved free of charge by the mayor of nearby Bodorfa.

World.title: New government would uncover the true wealth of the greatest winners of the Orbán era – will it succeed?
World.content:
The government will tighten and clarify the rules for identifying the ultimate beneficial owners of closed-ended investment funds — including private equity and venture capital funds — the Justice Minister said in a Facebook post on Tuesday. In the past, it took the press months—sometimes years—of painstaking work to establish who might really be behind private-equity funds worth hundreds of billions, or even trillions of forints. And even then, such reports were couched in cautious, conditional terms: nobody dared state anything as fact.

Ministers want the real owners and their true wealth

Márta Görög wrote that private equity and venture capital funds had frequently been used in recent years to conceal from public view the true, ultimate owners of substantial assets. “It is in the public interest to know who stands behind these funds,” she said.

Márta Görög and Péter Magyar. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

In a video shared with the post, the Justice Minister said the objective was to make ownership structures more transparent, with particular attention paid to arrangements capable of obscuring either the identity of the ultimate beneficial owner or the nature of the ownership chain itself.

What is a private equity fund for?

Private equity funds can appeal to wealthy businessmen because they allow substantial assets to be separated and invested without it being clear to the public, sometimes for years, who is behind the fund — or, at least, without any news organisation being able to state under threat of criminal liability what may be strongly suspected.

Private individuals, companies and institutional investors can all place money in such funds. The fund manager may then invest the capital in businesses, property or other assets.

In Hungary, the fact that the identity of private equity funds’ beneficial owners was long unavailable to the public became particularly significant. Funds could often be linked to particular businessmen only indirectly — by piecing together connections between fund managers, companies, ownership structures and, in some cases, registered addresses.

NER-linked fortunes dominated

This does not in itself mean that every asset placed in a private equity fund is illegal or derived from tax avoidance. Yet the structure became particularly important under Viktor Orbán because both state and private money entered the same investment world.

Using figures from late 2023, the Hungarian business outlet G7 estimated that assets held in Hungarian private equity funds totalled roughly HUF 2.6 trillion. It calculated that about 95 per cent could be linked to businessmen close to the National Cooperation System, or NER — the political and economic network associated with Mr Orbán’s rule.

G7 estimated that approximately HUF 716 billion in fund assets could be connected to Lőrinc Mészáros, HUF 589 billion to Dániel Jellinek, HUF 323 billion to István Száraz, and HUF 207 billion to István Tiborcz, Mr Orbán’s son-in-law. It stressed, however, that these were not proven personal fortunes but calculations based on business and ownership links.

Private equity funds therefore became an important component of the Orbán system’s economic structure, not least because the state itself invested substantial sums through such vehicles.

If you missed: These secret funds are managed by the richest in Hungary

Transparency International said the Hungarian state had placed at least HUF 1.311 trillion in private equity funds by the end of 2025, while businesses connected to those funds won roughly HUF 2.6 trillion in state contracts between 2021 and 2024.

For years, Hungarian journalists have attempted to establish who the ultimate owners of these multi-trillion-forint fortunes might be. Direkt36, G7, Telex, Válasz Online and 24.hu have, among others, cross-referenced company databases, financial accounts, links between fund managers and official state documents.

Richer than first thought

Direkt36, for instance, analysed state data from which it was possible to infer the identities of several people behind the funds. However, the information was removed from the state database after the outlet’s article was published.

Válasz Online likewise used financial filings and ownership connections to reconstruct the scale of the wealth linked to figures such as Mr Tiborcz. It concluded that the Prime Minister’s son-in-law was far richer than he initially appeared.

That Sisyphean task — fraught with uncertainty and risk — may now become easier as a result of the Tisza government’s proposed transparency reforms.

World.title: Photos: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions
World.content:
The water level of yet another Hungarian lake has fallen to a critical low, meaning visitors to the Bölömbika lookout, which has seen better days, are now confronted with a dispiriting scene of environmental devastation rather than spectacular views and abundant wildlife. Check out the latest photos in our article below.

Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping

Nature horror from Hungarian lake lookout

Nature lovers visiting one of the Tisza Lake’s best-known attractions, the Bölömbika lookout, have recently been met with a deeply disappointing sight. The landscape around the lookout has changed dramatically: areas once covered by water are now dry lakebed, leaving the structure effectively standing on dry land.

The transformation is particularly striking in new photographs taken by the Madárpart Hiking Centre, Rental Service and Campsite. From the images, it is difficult to imagine that the lookout was once surrounded by water. The present condition of the landscape illustrates the dramatic consequences of the Tisza Lake’s water level falling to an exceptionally low point.

The situation is even more pronounced in the Tiszavalk Basin. The area has almost completely dried out, while the lake itself is registering an unusually low water level. Not only has the familiar landscape disappeared; the conditions that once made the area attractive to hikers and water-sports enthusiasts have also been severely compromised.

Historic drought, drying rivers and vanishing lakes

Hungary is enduring a historic drought, with water levels in its lakes, rivers and streams repeatedly falling to record lows. Lake Velence, once renowned for its thriving tourism, sporting events and festivals, is now in its final throes. Even at Lake Balaton, Hungary’s so-called “sea”, swimmers must walk a considerable distance before reaching water deep enough for a swim.

The Danube’s level was so low in July that the Paks nuclear power plant had to be almost entirely shut down. A submerged weir was subsequently built to raise the water level and ensure that sufficient cooling water could be drawn from the river during periods of extreme low flow such as the present one.

The Tisza is also exceptionally low, while one of its tributaries, the Zagyva, has dried up altogether. The same has happened to the Tarna, the Galga, the Bózsva stream, the Morgó stream, the Tápió and the Hajta. Lake Kolon, a strictly protected habitat in the Kiskunság region, had already dried out by the beginning of summer, as had Lake Bicsérd in Transdanubia and Lake Kocs in the Balaton Uplands.

If you missed: Invasive mosquito species conquering Hungary – climate change destroys our echosystem?

Not just a Hungarian problem

Lake Öreg in Tata, like the Tisza Lake, is experiencing exceptionally low water levels; the same is true of Lake Balaton and Lake Velence. The extreme conditions require swift action from the Government, as forecasts suggest that summers in Hungary will remain hot and dry as climate change and global warming intensify.

The exceptionally dry summer is not a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon. Its consequences are being felt across every area of life, from agriculture and tourism to energy production. Romania was forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because of the Danube’s exceptionally low level, while in Italy the Isonzo – a river familiar from the battles of the First World War – has dried up.

World.title: House price growth eased in Hungary – here are the latest prices
World.content:
House price growth eased in July, with the gap between average prices per square metre reaching as much as tenfold across the country, property website ingatlan.com told Hungary’s MTI news agency on Tuesday.

House price growth eased in Hungary

Monthly price growth slowed to 0.1 per cent, while the annual increase fell to 11.9 per cent. In Budapest, prices rose by 0.9 per cent compared with the previous month, although ingatlan.com said this may have represented a correction following June’s 0.1 per cent decline, MTI wrote.

According to the company’s house price index, Budapest property prices were 8.3 per cent higher than a year earlier, despite a substantial increase in supply.

The number of newly built homes listed for sale in the capital rose from 3,742 a year ago to 5,381 this year, ingatlan.com said. The median price per square metre for second-hand homes in Budapest ranges from HUF 942,000 to HUF 2 million, while prices for newly built properties in the most expensive districts are approaching HUF 3 million per square metre.

Regional differences

The housing market presented a mixed picture nationwide. Pest County stood out with a monthly price increase of 1.2 per cent in July, while the Southern Great Plain recorded a 2.9 per cent decline.

Debrecen had the country’s highest median price for second-hand homes among regional centres, at HUF 1.04 million per square metre. Szeged and Székesfehérvár were also approaching the HUF 1 million mark. Salgótarján was the cheapest county seat, with a median price of HUF 312,000 per square metre.

If you missed – Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

Debrecen also led the expansion in the supply of newly built homes, with listings nearly doubling. Across the main provincial cities, supply increased by an average of close to 50 per cent.

The estate agency said current trends pointed to annual house price growth of less than 10 per cent this year. The last time prices rose at such a modest rate was in 2016.

World.title: Fast food chain Popeyes expands in Romania with first restaurant in Timisoara
World.content:
US fast-food chain Popeyes announced the opening of its first restaurant in Timisoara, western Romania.

The chain, which launched in Romania four years ago, currently has 23 restaurants, of which 8 are in Bucharest, 2 in Iasi, 2 in Constanta, 2 in Cluj, and one in Pitești, Craiova, Buzău, Ploiești, Brașov, Sibiu, Oradea, Suceava and Târgu Mureș.

"The inauguration of the first Popeyes restaurant in Timisoara represents an essential step in our 2026 expansion plan in Romania.," said Jakub Aleksandrowicz, Popeyes Marketing Director for Central and Eastern Europe.

Founded in 1972, Popeyes is one of the world's most famous fast-food brands. The brand owns 4,800 restaurants worldwide.

Polish company Rex Concepts, the exclusive master franchisee for Burger King and Popeyes in Poland, Romania and the Czech Republic, debuted on the Warsaw Stock Exchange at a valuation of PLN 1.3 billion (approximately EUR 315.3 million), marking the sixth listing of a Polish company since the beginning of the year, according to Profit.ro.

The company said it would use the funds to expand the network to 850 restaurants in Poland, Romania and the Czech Republic over the next 6 years. Last year, Rex Concepts opened 59 restaurants, 20 of which were in Romania, reaching a total of 159 directly operated locations at the end of December.

World.title: Romania’s First Lady, UNICEF reaffirm commitment to children's rights and participation
World.content:
The First Lady of Romania, Mirabela Grădinaru, met on Tuesday, August 25, with a UNICEF delegation led by Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF Regional Director for Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, to discuss promoting children's rights and strengthening the participation of children and young people in decisions that affect their lives.

The discussions highlighted the progress made by Romania in promoting the views of children and young people in the public decision-making process, including through legislation adopted in 2024, which strengthens children's opportunities to contribute to the development of policies and legislation that concern them.

“I know how important it is for every child to have access to care, protection, education and opportunities to develop. We must never forget that they are our number one priority. The way we care for children today will shape tomorrow's society. I welcome the continuation of cooperation between Romania and UNICEF to support children and families, to ensure that the voices of young people are heard and to make sure that every child can reach their full potential, regardless of where they live or the circumstances in which they were born,” said Mirabela Grădinaru.

In turn, Edouard Beigbeder said that Romania has taken important steps to strengthen children's participation and integrate it into the decision-making process, and its experience can offer valuable lessons both to countries in Europe and to those outside the region.

The meeting addressed Romania's experience in implementing the integrated community services model, as well as the implementation of the European Child Guarantee. Opportunities to promote internationally the lessons learned and good practices developed in Romania were also discussed.

The discussions also focused on continuing cooperation in areas such as children's participation, education, combating climate change, online safety and preventing violence against children.

Earlier this summer, Romania’s First Lady presented the "Romania in Light" project during a panel within the NATO Summit in Ankara. The project focuses on protecting children in the context of technological development and educating them in an environment where the virtual world supports learning and development.

World.title: Social Monitor: Romania exceeds EU average for household internet access but ranks last in digital skills
World.content:
Romania has moved above the European Union average for household internet connectivity, with 95.47% of homes having access in 2025. However, the country ranks last in the EU for the share of people with at least basic digital skills, according to Eurostat data analyzed by the Social Monitor, a Friedrich Ebert Foundation project.

The share of Romanian households with internet access increased by almost 10 percentage points from 86.24% in 2020. Romania now ranks 12th among the EU’s 27 member states and exceeds the bloc’s average of 94.76%.

The Netherlands recorded the highest household connectivity rate at 99.28%, followed by Luxembourg at 99%, and Malta at 97.77%. Croatia ranked last with 87.91%, behind Greece at 88.73%, and Lithuania at 89.35%.

Internet use among Romania’s general population also rose significantly, reaching 93.15% in 2025 compared with 78.46% in 2020, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ireland had the EU’s highest internet usage rate at 99.78%, followed by Denmark and the Netherlands, both at 99.71%. The lowest rates were recorded in Croatia at 85.9%, Bulgaria at 86.85%, and Greece at 89.15%.

“The data also show that the share of Romanians who have never used the internet fell sharply to just 4.91%, compared with 14.05% in 2020. However, Romania continues to perform below the EU average on this indicator,” reads the Social Monitor report.

The highest proportions of people who had never gone online were recorded in Croatia at 10.33%, Portugal at 9.56%, and Greece at 9.14%, while Ireland, the Netherlands, and Sweden had the lowest rates.

According to the same source, despite the improvement in access and usage, only 31.84% of Romania’s population has basic or above-basic digital skills, placing the country last in the EU and well below the bloc’s average of 60.4%.

Bulgaria followed with 38.26%, while Slovenia and Latvia recorded 46.5% and 48.43%, respectively. The Netherlands led the ranking at 83.61%, followed by Ireland at 82.82%, and Denmark at 81.45%.

Digital skills are assessed based on activities performed online or with software by people aged 16 to 74. The evaluation covers information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem-solving.

World.title: L’Étape Romania by Tour de France brings traffic restrictions to Bucharest this weekend
World.content:
The fifth edition of L’Étape Romania by Tour de France will take place in Bucharest on Sunday, August 30, with almost 2,000 cyclists expected to participate. As such, traffic will be restricted on several major streets and boulevards in the city between 7 a.m. and 2 p.m.

The restrictions will affect Unirii Boulevard, Mircea Vodă Boulevard, Splaiul Unirii in the direction of Bucharest, Decebal Boulevard, Basarabia Boulevard, Calea Victoriei, Regina Elisabeta Boulevard, Schitu Măgureanu Boulevard, Știrbei Vodă and Ion Câmpineanu streets, Kiseleff Road, Buzești, Berzei, Vasile Pârvan and Bogdan Petriceicu Hașdeu streets, and Libertății Boulevard.

The organizers said they were working with the Traffic Police to establish alternative routes.

Constituției Square will serve as the starting and finishing point for all three races.

The 14 km City Adventure route, open to participants aged 7 and over, will begin at 7:30 a.m. The 42 km Ride will start at 8:30 a.m. and is open to cyclists aged at least 15, while the 85 km Race will begin at 10 a.m. and has the same minimum age requirement.

The race routes are scheduled to close fully at 1 p.m., followed by the awards ceremony at 1:30 p.m.

Almost 2,000 cyclists from 17 countries and more than 170 cities and towns have registered. International participants include cyclists from Bulgaria, Greece, the United Kingdom, Serbia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany, Cyprus, France, Belgium, and Austria.

The 42 km route is expected to attract the largest field, with approximately 1,200 cyclists at the start. More than 250 children and teenagers under the age of 18 have also registered.

“To make sure race day is exactly what every participant has been looking forward to, my advice is simple: have your bike checked - brakes, tires and gears - and don’t leave this until the last minute. Also, avoid overtraining during this final week: your fitness has already been built, and now it’s all about rest, hydration and sleep. Don’t try anything new on race day, whether it’s equipment or nutrition, and come to the Race Village on Saturday to collect your race kit, so you can enjoy every kilometer on Sunday morning without a worry,” said Răzvan Jugănaru, MTB Academy, event organizer.

Registration is open until the end of August 26 or until all available places are filled. Participants must collect their race kits on August 29, between 10 a.m. and 7 p.m., from the Race Village in Constituției Square.

World.title: Drone fragment discovered on beach in Romanian seaside resort Olimp
World.content:
Video

A drone fragment was found on Wednesday, August 26, on a beach in the Romanian Black Sea resort of Olimp. The fragment was brought onto the beach by waves and was noticed by several people who notified the authorities.

Authorities restricted access to the area, and specialists went to the scene to analyze the object. Around 10:30 AM, they decided to detonate a part of the fragments that contained explosives. A separate drone fragment is still on the beach and does not contain explosives, according to Digi24.

Another drone fragment was discovered on Tuesday, August 24, near the Casino in Constanţa. The object was noticed near the seafront by people walking in the area. They notified the authorities, who recovered the object, which most likely did not have an explosive payload.

Drones on the Black Sea coast

The discoveries in Olimp and Constanța are part of a series of similar incidents reported in recent weeks on the Romanian coast. Fragments or devices that authorities determined came from drones have been found in several coastal areas, including Costinești and Saturn.

Earlier this month, the Romanian Army also recovered drone fragments from other Black Sea resort towns like Port Tomis, Eforie Sud, Eforie Nord, Costinești, and Năvodari. Around the same time, other drone parts were spotted near a Constanţa beach. In all cases, specialized crews intervened to remove the fragments.

According to the Ministry of Defense, Romania has seen 59 attacks near its borders with Ukraine since the start of the year, and 25 unauthorized entrys in its airspace. Four drones were also brought down by Romanian or allied fighter jets after infringing the national airspace.

Increased defense measures

Romania's Senate Defense Committee met yesterday to discuss an incident from the beginning of June, in the Port of Constanţa, when a Ukrainian drone self-detonated after it was lost from control. General Dragoş Iacob, deputy chief of the Defense Staff, said that following the incident, the security of maritime ports had been strengthened, and the warning system was working better than three months ago. Representatives of the Naval Forces, as well as of the Ministry of Defense, SRI and STS, were present at the meeting.

“There are several questions that institutions need to answer in the chain of response. Who detects the drone, who identifies what type it is, who coordinates, who tracks, and who destroys the drone,” said liberal Nicoleta Pauliuc, chairwoman of the Senate Defense Committee, cited by Radio Romania Actualitati.

World.title: Timișoara bans new gambling halls, existing venues to close by 2027
World.content:
Timișoara’s Local Council unanimously approved a citywide ban on gambling halls, mayor Dominic Fritz announced on Tuesday, August 25. Existing venues will be allowed to operate only until their current licenses expire, no later than next year.

“From today, it is official: slot-machine halls can no longer be authorized in Timișoara,” Fritz wrote on Facebook. “The Local Council approved the decision through which we are completely banning gambling halls in the city.”

The only gambling-related activities that will continue to be permitted are lottery services operated by Romania’s National Lottery.

According to the mayor, the gambling halls that remain open will close gradually as the licenses issued by the central authorities in Bucharest expire.

In the spring, 173 locations in Timișoara held gambling authorizations issued by the National Gambling Office, according to Digi24.

World.title: MVM Energie Romania secures permit for EUR 16 mln solar park in Covasna County
World.content:
MVM Energie Romania received authorization from energy regulator ANRE to develop a photovoltaic park with an installed capacity of almost 25 MW in Arcuș, Covasna County. The EUR 16 million facility is expected to be completed and commissioned by mid-2027.

The Arcuș photovoltaic plant will be built on approximately 20 hectares and will have a maximum installed grid capacity of 24.6 MW. Its maximum electricity export capacity will stand at 21.21 MW.

The development of the project began in 2022, while the authorization issued by the National Energy Regulatory Authority marks a key step toward the implementation phase, the company said.

“Romania is a market where MVM is building its presence with a long-term perspective,” MVM Romania CEO Gabriel Garai said. “Obtaining the authorization for the Arcuș photovoltaic project is a concrete step in a development plan that is not limited to a single project but aims to consolidate our activities in both energy production and supply.”

Garai said the company is developing a portfolio of investments intended to gradually increase its contribution to Romania’s energy market and diversify the energy sources available to customers.

The renewable electricity generated by the Arcuș plant will be integrated into MVM Energie Romania’s portfolio and supplied to its customers in the country. Once fully operational, the project is expected to generate the equivalent of the annual electricity consumption of approximately 12,000 households.

The investment forms part of MVM Group’s plans to increase the share of renewable sources in its portfolio and reduce emissions across the region. The group aims to develop more than 3,000 MW of new renewable energy capacity by 2035.

“In Romania, we bring the experience and capacity of a strong regional energy group with an extensive presence in Central and Eastern Europe and a solid foundation built in Hungary,” Gabriel Garai added.

MVM has operated in Romania for more than 15 years and is active in renewable electricity production, as well as electricity and natural gas supply.

The group operates in 23 countries, employs almost 20,500 people, and serves approximately 11 million customers. In 2025, it sold 40 TWh of electricity and 130 TWh of natural gas.

World.title: Romanian prosecutors expand criminal investigation in Nordis case
World.content:
Romania’s Directorate for the Investigation of Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) announced on Tuesday, August 25, that it has expanded the criminal investigation in the case of real estate developer Nordis.

Nordis, a premium developer, allegedly collected money from buyers, embezzled company funds, and misled customers during the signing of pre-contracts and sales agreements, according to investigators. Moreover, the company illegally obtained refunds or compensation from the state budget. In total, the group leaders are believed to have collected EUR 195 million from 2019 to 2024.

According to prosecutors, 50 new criminal complaints filed by more than 100 new victims have been added to the case file, leading to an expansion of the investigation. The additional damages were estimated at over RON 42 million, EUR 14 million, and USD 17,000.

“The measure targets the administrators of a group of companies, defendants in the case, as well as four commercial companies, all under criminal investigation, for committing the offense of fraud with particularly serious consequences,” according to a DIICOT press release.

Moreover, prosecutors ordered the expansion of the criminal investigation for a distinct offense of fraud with particularly serious consequences, following a complaint filed by a commercial company. In this case, damages were estimated at RON 7 million.

The investigated offenses concern the establishment of an organized criminal group, embezzlement with particularly serious consequences, money laundering, tax evasion, fraud with particularly serious consequences, and the bad-faith determination by the taxpayer of taxes, fees or contributions, resulting in the unlawful obtaining of refunds, reimbursements or offsets from the consolidated general budget, all in continued form.

In total, the Nordis case caused damages that exceed EUR 75 million, with 850 victims on record. The first expansion of the investigation took place in October 2025, when 300 victims came forward.

The case impacted much of the presidential campaign at the end of 2024 and the beginning of 2025 due to the political connections of the accused managers of Nordis, particularly their ties with the Social Democratic Party, or PSD.

World.title: North Macedonia Sees Drop in New School Pupils amid Demographic Woes
World.content:
A child near North Macedonia’s capital, Skopje, going to school. Photo: Robert Atanasovski.

In the latest indication of the country’s demographic problems, Education Minister Vesna Janevska said on Tuesday that enrolment for the 2026-27 school year, while still not final, is already sharply below last year’s 17,921 first-graders.

“We expect this trend to continue next year, which is disappointing,” Janevska told media.

The decline is even more striking over a longer period. In the 2016-17 school year, 23,266 children entered first grade (f, data from the State Statistical Office shows. The number fell to 21,656 the following year and, despite occasional slight increases, continued a broadly downward trend.

By 2025-26, it had dropped to 17,921. The current preliminary figure of 14,500 means the country has lost about 8,800 first-graders, or nearly 38 per cent, in just a decade.

The shrinking cohorts are already forcing changes to the school network. Janevska said that around 200 fewer classes will operate in primary education this year, while secondary education will have around 100 fewer classes.

The government also expects 26 rural schools to close during the school year because they have either too few or no newly-enrolled first-graders.

Some have only five to eight pupils in total, Janevska explained, arguing that keeping very small schools open can leave children in combined classes with pupils from several grades, limiting both the quality of teaching and opportunities for socialisation.

She said that pupils would generally be transferred to larger schools, but that combined classes in smaller schools would still remain where necessary, particularly where they are at a significant distance from more populated areas.

Demographer Donco Gerasimovski, a former director of the State Statistical Office, told Meta.mk news website that low birth rates and the emigration of young families are driving the decline.

Gerasimovski noted that many children also disappear from school rolls during a school year as families leave the country.

“According to my calculations, we ‘lose’ between 1,500 and 2,000 pupils in just one school year because of emigration,” he told Meta.mk.

The shrinking number of first-graders is only the clearest visible signs of a demographic decline that has been building for years.

Over the past three-and-a-half decades, the small landlocked country has failed to produce tangible economic and democratic uptick that could have kept people from leaving, or join the EU, in large part due to the former Greek blockade over its name and the current Bulgarian impasse that centres around contested identity issues.

The results of the last national headcount carried out in 2021, showed the country’s population has shrunk by 9.2 per cent over two decades since the previous census, from roughly 2.1 million to just over 1.8 million.

World.title: Plea Deals Reveal Logistics of Smuggling Macedonian Marijuana into Serbia
World.content:
Shortly after midnight on January 15 this year, a truck crossed from North Macedonia into Serbia. Several hours later, having crossed the length of the country, it caught fire near Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad.

According to paperwork, the truck was carrying textiles for export to Britain. In reality, it was stuffed with tonnes of marijuana; the smugglers set it on fire to cover their tracks.

Two weeks later, police seized five tonnes of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, near the central Serbian town of Krusevac.

According to plea bargains reached last week between prosecutors in North Macedonia and two of the smugglers, the January shipment was just one of five carried out between mid-2025 and early 2026.

More people are under investigation. Sources close to the probe say prosecutors in North Macedonia are also looking into the finances of three companies tied to Skopje-based Alfapharm Group, which allegedly served as a front for the drugs production.

The case is the latest to raise questions about North Macedonia’s legal medicinal marijuana industry, legalised in 2016, and whether it is fuelling the smuggling. In recent years, 14 firms have lost their permits to grow medicinal marijuana for failing to comply with the law, the Health Ministry said.

World.title: Riots, Teargas and ‘Gruesome Photos’ Behind Serbian Photographer’s Success
World.content:
An Orthodox priest talks to a young man during street protests in Belgrade. A police cordon faces the crowd in Serbia’s capital, holding plastic shields. A wounded demonstrator lies prone as riot police run past him.

These images date back to March 2011, when protesters packed the streets after the arrest of Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic. They were the first photos that Andrej Cukic sent to EPA Images (European Pressphoto Agency). Now he is set to lead the organization, as editor-in-chief.

“I was in the right place at the right time,” he tells BIRN. “I had some gruesome photos. Somebody thought that they were very good, and they ran them, and the photos were kind of published everywhere.”

The photos led to Cukic gaining regular work from Belgrade for EPA Images, an international news photo agency based in Frankfurt. BIRN has a contract with EPA and regularly uses its images.

World.title: Greek Neo-Nazi Casts Himself as Political Martyr Ahead of Prison Release
World.content:
On the Greek capital’s bustling Omonia Square, a group of young men held Greek flags and chanted: “Ilias, stay strong on the road to freedom” and “Remember Ilias, we are with you”.

It was July 20 and Ilias Kasidiaris - on day release from prison - was inaugurating the offices of a new party he had announced the previous month.

Convicted in 2020 of directing a criminal organisation, Kasidiaris has no legal grounds to lead a political party, but media reports this month suggest a relative of his has submitted a request to do so before the Supreme Court.

Addressing his supporters, Kasidiaris called on them to gather outside Domokos prison come mid-September, when he is due to be released.

Together, he said, they would “send a message of resistance to all those who are selling out Greece”, and vowed to run in the next parliamentary election, expected in the spring of next year.

World.title: Bulgaria Violated Rights of Roma Families by Demolishing Settlement, Court Rules
World.content:
Bulgaria breached the human rights of dozens of Roma families in Sofia by demolishing their homes without giving them a chance to contest the decision, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday.

The government must pay 10,000 euro in damages to each party to the case and reform its demolition procedures.

The demolition took place in Sofia’s Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in August 2023, despite residents insisting that the authorities had not consulted them over the plans. Some of the families said they had lived in their homes since the 1950s.

The authorities insisted that they had carried out a formal process for issuing demolition orders. This was denied by the residents, who said the authorities deliberately concealed their intentions, gave evasive answers to repeated requests for information and refused to engage directly with the community.

The court ruled that Bulgaria had violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects family life and homes. It found that residents had no effective procedure to challenge the plans for demolition based on their personal circumstances, including length of residence, vulnerability and the availability of alternative housing.

The court also ruled, however, that the residents held no property rights in the demolished houses that would be recognized under Bulgarian law.

The ruling is not yet final and Bulgaria has three months to request that the case be referred for further review. The residents may make a similar application.

The flattening of Roma settlements in Bulgaria has become a repeated problem and a source of tension between the ethnic minority and local authorities. Demolitions also took place in the Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in 2017.

The ECHR has now heard four cases involving Roma settlement demolitions since 2012. In 2025, BIRN covered two similar cases: in April 2025, despite an ECHR ruling warning the municipality not to “proceed with the demolition of the homes of the applicants until further notice”, authorities still flattened houses in the enclave which had been there for decades.

A similar operation followed in the town of Stara Zagora in August the same year.

World.title: Serbia Again Requests “Humanitarian” Release of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic has once again called for the release of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic. On Tuesday, he asked the UN war crimes court in The Hague to consider a new request by the family of the former Bosnian Serb military leader.

Vujic made the plea in a letter to Graciela Gatti Santana, the president of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, IRMCT. It follows last week’s decision by the IRMCT to reject a request by Mladic’s defence for conditional early release and transfer to Serbia on health grounds.

Vujic noted a report by the medical officer at the detention unit in The Hague stating that Mladic had entered the final phase of his life, after a rapid decline in his health. The minister argued that, under these circumstances, Mladic should be allowed to spend his final days in Serbia. The government has offered to transfer him to Belgrade’s Military Medical Academy and accept restrictions and monitoring imposed by the court.

In last week’s decision rejecting an early release, the IRMCT ruled that Mladic was receiving comprehensive medical care and assistance, as well as an exceptional visitation regime allowing meaningful contact with his family. It said that his condition alone did not justify humanitarian early release, given the gravity of his genocide conviction and life sentence. The court stressed that it would continue to protect Mladic’s fundamental rights and dignity.

This is not the first time that Mladic’s defence has sought his release on humanitarian grounds. During his time in custody in the Netherlands, Mladic has had several serious medical problems and has suffered two strokes and a heart attack.

In June 2025, Mladic’s lawyers made an urgent request to the IRMCT for his release after he was transferred to palliative care, saying he had only has months to live. His defence again sought his immediate release in May this year after a serious medical episode, arguing that he was approaching the end of his life.

Mladic has been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011. He is serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The court confirmed his conviction and sentence after an appeal in 2021.

World.title: European Court Orders Turkey to Release Osman Kavala Immediately, Again
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights, ECHR, on Tuesday ruled for a second time that Turkey should release the jailed philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala. Judges found that his detention and conviction violated multiple provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights.

“The respondent State was required to secure the applicant’s release at the earliest possible date,” the Court said, adding that Turkey must eliminate the consequences of the measures taken against him. It said Kavala’s criminal conviction should be regarded as “null and void” under the Convention’s provisions.

Kavala is a prominent civil society figure and former board member of the Open Society Foundations in Turkey. He has been in custody since October 2017, facing charges in connection with the 2013 Gezi Park protests and the failed coup attempt of July 2016.

An Istanbul court sentenced Kavala to “aggravated life imprisonment” – without the possibility of release – in April 2022. He was convicted of attempting to overthrow the government through his support for the Gezi Park protests. The months of demonstrations constituted the largest popular uprising against the authoritarian leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Two appeal courts upheld Kavala’s conviction in December 2022 and September 2023.

In its latest ruling, the ECHR found violations of several provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights, including freedom of expression and assembly, the right to a fair trial and the right to liberty and security. It also found that Kavala’s aggravated life sentence without the possibility of release violated Article 3, which explicitly prohibits “torture [and] inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

Judges concluded that a desire to silence Kavala was behind the criminal proceedings, his conviction and his continued detention. The Turkish authorities aimed to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender.

The judgment follows years of pressure over Turkey’s failure to implement previous ECHR rulings concerning Kavala. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers eventually launched infringement proceedings against Turkey in 2022. That process could ultimately lead to sanctions, including the suspension of voting rights or even membership.

The Court also ordered Turkey to pay Kavala 70,000 euros in non-pecuniary damages and 43,342.57 euros in costs and expenses.

World.title: Kosovo Starts Countdown on KLA Leaders War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Countdown monitor installed at Pristina city center photographed on August 24, 2026. Photo: BIRN/ Islam Berisha

The clock is ticking in Ferizaj/Urosevac. Kosovo’s third-largest city now has installed a countdown timer on Monday, which will reach zero on the day that former president Hashim Thaci is due to learn his fate. The capital, Pristina, has a similar installation, with other cities due to follow suit.

Along with three other former senior leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), Thaci is accused of committing crimes against humanity – including murder, torture and illegal detention – during the Kosovo conflict in the late 1990s. Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague are calling for a 45-year prison sentence.

But as far as Ferizaj/Urosevac’s mayor Agim Aliu is concerned, Thaci and his co-defendants – Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi – are heroes of Kosovo’s independence struggle. And he believes the newly-installed timer in the city’s main square is counting down the days to what should be a massive celebration.

“Ferizaj and the entire Kosovo [will] experience September 16 as a new date of freedom,” he says, adding that he expects a “historic verdict” reflecting “the sacrifice” the four defendants made for Kosovo’s freedom.

On Monday, Ferizaj/Urosevac became the second municipality to receive a countdown clock, courtesy of the initiative “Freedom Has a Name” (Liria Ka Emer). It plans to install similar timers in other municipalities around Kosovo.

One of the initiative’s leaders is Eliza Hoxha, an MP representing Thaci’s former party, the PDK (Democratic Party of Kosovo), which is currently in opposition. She says she believes in the four defendants’ innocence.

“Kosovo is waiting, we are all waiting. We will count down hours, minutes, seconds until September 16. Kosovo waits for Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi to once again stamp our right to be free and independent.”

The charges facing the four men are serious. Prosecutors accuse them of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania. Those include more than one hundred murders.

The charges cover the period during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. As prime minister in 2014, Hashim Thaci signed an agreement with the European Union to establish the court.

It is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters. Veterans are widely viewed as heroes in Kosovo and the potential for witness intimidation was a serious concern.

During the trial, the prosecution argued that the defendants’ senior roles in the KLA meant they were responsible for subordinates who committed crimes. The defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges. Since then, he and his three co-defendants have been in detention in The Hague, with the trial starting in April 2023. KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the KSC of bias.

Prosecutors brought further charges against Thaci In 2024. He and four others, including former Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci, are accused of obstruction of justice and witness tampering. Prosecutors say Thaci and his co-accused attempted to direct witness testimony in his war crimes trial.

The second case went to trial in February this year, just days after proceedings in Thaci’s first trial concluded. All the accused have pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Billionaires Gather on 200 Million Euro Yacht Near Mljet
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Multiple billionaires have come together on a 200 million euro yacht near the southern Croatian island of Mljet. Jeff Bezos, and Jan Koum are among them.

Poslovni reports that this impressive vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros. Mljet is set to be hosting a meeting of two of the world’s biggest technology billionaires, Jan Koum and Jeff Bezos, over the next few days. They met on Koum’s yacht worth nearly 200 million dollars.

Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp whose wealth is estimated at 17 billion dollars, anchored his superyacht Moonrise near Mljet, and the same day Jeff Bezos, owner of Amazon, arrived in the company of American media mogul Barry Diller. Koum arrived on the Moonrise by helicopter on Monday, and Bezos visited him in the late afternoon hours. The three billionaires, Koum, Bezos and Diller, thus found themselves on the same vessel in the middle of the Adriatic Sea.

Koum is no stranger to the Croatian coast; he has holidayed in our beautiful country before. His superyacht Moonrise was photographed between the islands of Lopud and Šipan back in 2021 and 2024, and it was recorded that on one occasion he arrived for a summer holiday in Croatia with as many as three vessels: in addition to Moonrise he was accompanied by the 74-metre yacht Mogambo and the 55-metre Power Play, which served him as a helipad. The Amazon owner regularly summers on the Mediterranean on his superyacht Koru, where he cruised the Adriatic in the summers of 2023 and 2025, with recorded stays on Hvar, Mljet, Korčula, and a visit to the Šibenik archipelago.

The yacht Moonrise isn’t just an ordinary vessel. It’s a 100-metre superyacht from the Dutch shipyard Feadship, built in 2020. The sophisticated exterior design is by De Voogt, while the interior is the work of French designer Rémi Tessier. The vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros.

World.title: Pula Receives 12 Electric Buses Worth 6.8 Million Euros
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Pula has received 12 electric buses worth a total of 6.8 million euros with an aim of increasing passenger comfort and being more environmentally friendly.

Pulapromet has put another six new electric buses into service, thereby completing the project of acquiring a total of 12 electric vehicles for Pula’s public transport. Index reports that the project was fully financed with funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, and the total value of the purchased buses amounts to 6,763,900 euros. For the project, Pulapromet had been allocated 6,994,998 euros, but after the public procurement procedure the total value was somewhat lower.

Specifically speaking, Pulapromet acquired six MAN and six Iveco electric buses. Director Tomislav Josipović said that this is an important step in modernising the vehicle fleet and raising the quality of public transport.

“By putting these new six electric buses into service today, we are completing the project through which Pulapromet has received a total of 12 new electric vehicles,” said Josipović, adding that almost 6.8 million euros of investment has been directed into the development of public transport without any financial burden on Pulapromet. The new buses should reduce emissions of harmful gases and noise while increasing energy efficiency and passenger comfort.

an increase in public transport use in pula

Pula Mayor Peđa Grbin said that the project does not stop at the acquisition of buses. He announced the installation of solar panels on the canopy at the depot (Remiza), for which the City is waiting for the opening of appropriate co-financing tenders. “The goal is for these electric buses to run on electricity that will be produced here, in Pula, from the most ecological possible source, which is solar energy,” said Grbin. He added that since the beginning of the year the use of public city transport has increased by almost 10 percent. According to him, this has also been contributed to by the City of Pula’s decisions on free transport for pupils, students and pensioners.

Istria County Prefect Boris Miletić thanked the City of Pula, Pulapromet, the surrounding municipalities and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure for implementing the project. He emphasised that electric buses, especially if powered by energy from solar sources, can contribute to reducing the impact of traffic on the environment. Miletić also said that Pulapromet first secured the infrastructure and charging stations, and then acquired the vehicles. He assessed that higher-quality public transport could further increase the number of passengers.

World.title: Istria Showcased in Front of Millions of German Viewers
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Gorgeous Istria has been showcased in front of millions of German viewers, shining the spotlight on Croatia’s largest peninsula.

Morski reports that one of the most successful German travel programmes, “Wunderschön”, devoted a full 90 minutes of airtime to Istria, presenting the diversity of the peninsula to a million-strong audience in the German-speaking world – from Kamenjak, Pula and the Brijuni Islands, via Učka, Buzet and Pazin, to Poreč and Rovinj.

The project was realised in cooperation between the Tourist Board of Istria County and its long-standing PR partner ART Redaktionsteam from Salzburg. Viewers are guided through Istria by well-known German television presenter Stephanie Müller-Spirra, under the direction of award-winning journalist and author Stephan Heise. Alongside numerous local protagonists, the programme also features Marko Purišić – Baby Lasagna, Rade Šerbedžija and extreme alpinist Ines Papert. Istria is presented to the audience through a blend of natural and cultural attractions, active holidays, local stories and top-class food and local wine.

The first broadcast of the report reaches around two million viewers, while through further screenings in Germany, Austria and Switzerland the total viewership is expected to exceed five million, making the project one of the most significant television promotions of Istria on its most important outbound market.

World.title: Belišće – The Croatian Town Around Which an Industrial Empire Grew
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Belišće isn’t a name you’ll likely have ever heard if you’re not from Croatia, but this Croatian town had an industrial empire grow out of it.

It’s also unusual because of the fact that it is one of the few Croatian towns whose beginning can be fixed almost like a date of birth. Putni kofer turns the hands of the clock back to the year 1884, and we find ourselves in a place with a pasture-and-arable clearing called Belistje. It sits just beside the banks of the Drava, and the reason a large sawmill that the Gutmann family builds there. Soon after, a railway, workers’ houses, a school, a post office, an electricity network and a water supply all arrive. In just a few decades, the industrial plant thus created an entire settlement around itself, and from it grew today’s town.

the family company that built an entire town

In 1884, two companies belonging to the Gutmann family from Velika Kanjiža bought from the Valpovo landowner the right to a ten-year use of a huge expanse of oak forests. They erected the sawmill on the Belistje clearing, after which the settlement later took its name. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon notes that the Gutmanns further expanded their business by purchasing forests from the Prandau family of Valpovo and that at the beginning of the 20th century they controlled massive swathes of of forest and land. From the very start Belišće was therefore tied to one of the most valuable resources of the area, Slavonian oak.

the biggest and most modern sawmill in europe

According to data from Belišće, the sawmill was one of the most modern of its time and probably the largest in Europe for cutting oak timber. Large-scale production also needed a good transport link, so already in 1884 the first kilometres of the forest-industrial railway were laid. Over time the network grew to 335 kilometres and developed into the Slavonia-Podravina Railway with public transport, a station, a locomotive shed and a workshop in Belišće. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon emphasises that this railway also carried passengers and thus compensated for the lack of state railways in this part of Slavonia.

Alongside the sawmill and the railway an industrial colony grew. Official sources state that the first residential houses were soon built and a fire brigade founded; in 1886 a school classroom and a post office were opened, and in 1890 a primary school was constructed. By 1892 the place already had an electricity network and a water supply with sewerage, which was still rare in the surrounding villages at that time. Development was also visible in the architecture. Next to the workers’ houses arose a house for the owners and offices, the officials’ social centre Casino, and in 1905 the Gutmann Palace, known in Belišće as Palej. Up to the First World War the workers’ settlement continued to expand, and some of its parts remained known by the names Five Stars, Green Houses, Mitrovica and Pekmez Street.

workers arrived from across the world

Industry drew workers from the Valpovo and Miholjac areas and from Lika, while specialists arrived from other parts of Austria-Hungary. Among them were many Germans, Hungarians and Czechs. With the newcomers cultural life also developed. The Rosenberg family arrived in 1888, and their son Sigmund spent part of his childhood precisely in Belišće. Later, in the United States under the name Sigmund Romberg, he became a well-known composer of operettas and musicals and dedicated the Belišće March to the place of his childhood.

By the time 1918 rolled around, the company moved its headquarters from Budapest to Belišće, and in 1927 the place became an independent municipality. After 1945 followed the period of the Kombinat, and a new major industrial phase began in 1960 with the opening of factories for semi-cellulose, paper and packaging. The old production lines and the narrow-gauge railways gradually closed down, but their traces still determine the appearance of the town today. The Gutmann Palace has been restored as an interpretation centre of industrial heritage; nearby is a gate from the first sawmill, installed in 1889; the complex of workers’ houses is protected as a monument ensemble; and a train with a locomotive from 1913 has also been preserved. Belišće has thus turned its industrial past, from which it literally arose, into the most recognisable part of its own heritage.
