World.title: Why has Georgia’s government revived debate over Treaty of Georgievsk?
World.content:
In recent days, Georgian government officials have made a series of similar statements about the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the agreement with Russia saved Georgia and the Georgian nation. He argues that it laid the foundations for today’s sovereign state and helped preserve its European prospects.

Several days later, other leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party began speaking about the Treaty of Georgievsk in similar terms. They repeat not only the main conclusion but also the same arguments: Georgia faced the threat of destruction, an agreement with Russia was the only option, and that decision saved the Georgian nation, Christianity and Georgian statehood.

This level of coordination suggests that the discussion has moved beyond a spontaneous debate about history. The positive assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk sounds more like a unified political message from Georgian Dream.

But what is the purpose of this message?

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement under which eastern Georgia (the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti) came under the protection of the Russian Empire. The parties signed the treaty in the summer of 1783 at the fortress of Georgievsk. The treaty protected Georgia from external threats but ultimately led to the complete loss of its independence.

Opposition figures say the government is preparing the public for a possible new agreement with Russia. Former president Mikheil Saakashvili, who is currently in prison, has even referred to specific draft agreements.

Other political commentators see the renewed focus on the treaty as an attempt to divert attention from important current issues. Against the backdrop of what they describe as the Georgian government’s increasingly pro-Russian course and anti-Western rhetoric, the Treaty of Georgievsk is a particularly sensitive issue for politically active Georgians and can easily provoke a strong reaction.

According to this view, the government deliberately sparked a historical debate to draw attention away from corruption within the administration. At the same time, the authorities have intensified the charges against former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili. His case goes beyond the actions of an individual official and raises questions about the scale of systemic corruption itself.

Russian media have already described Kobakhidze’s remarks as another sign that Tbilisi’s attitude towards Moscow is changing.

So why has a treaty signed 243 years ago suddenly become one of the main topics of Georgia’s current political debate?

What Prime Minister Kobakhidze said

Irakli Kobakhidze has made several statements about the Treaty of Georgievsk. His main argument is that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation.

On 18 August, Kobakhidze described the signing of the treaty as a “civilisational choice”. He said Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose fellow Orthodox Russia.

“The fact that today we are an independent, sovereign state based on traditional European values and traditional European culture is precisely the result of this pragmatic decision taken by Erekle II,” the prime minister said.

Kobakhidze has also argued that Erekle II’s decision was not only justified, but the “only correct and only possible” choice at the time. In his account, Russia honoured the terms of the agreement during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end. Almost 20 years passed between the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country was effectively saved.”

Kobakhidze presented Russia’s abolition of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti as a process that became possible only after the Georgian king’s death: “When Erekle II died, unfortunately, events took a different course.”

Georgian Dream leaders have also drawn parallels between this historical episode and modern Georgian-Russian relations.

Kobakhidze compared the Treaty of Georgievsk with the August 2008 war and said that “under Mikheil Saakashvili’s leadership, all the agreements, whether signed or unsigned, were torn up over our heads.”

Other party leaders have expressed similar views. MP David Matikashvili, for example, called the Treaty of Georgievsk a “smart and wise” decision.

“Ultimately, despite the many negative consequences, Georgia and the Georgian people managed to survive physically. The genius of King Erekle is obvious here,” he said.

More about the Treaty of Georgievsk

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783 between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. It was not an agreement between a united Georgia and Russia. At the time, the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia were not parties to the treaty.

Under the agreement, Kartli-Kakheti came under Russian protection. In return, Russia undertook to protect its territorial integrity and the Bagrationi dynasty.

Historian Beka Kobakhidze strongly disputes Kobakhidze’s claim that Russia honoured the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime. He writes that the period from 1783 until Erekle’s death was instead one of the most difficult periods of his reign.

In 1785, an army led by Avar ruler Omar Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti. Beka Kobakhidze says Erekle had warned Russia about the planned attack and requested the assistance provided for under the treaty. Russia did not provide it.

Agha Mohammad Khan’s 1795 campaign had even more devastating consequences. After the Battle of Krtsanisi, his forces captured and looted Tbilisi. Thousands of people were killed or taken captive.

Beka Kobakhidze draws on these facts to write:

“Irakli Kobakhidze is falsifying history. The period from 1783 to 1798, from the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk to Erekle’s death, was the most difficult and destructive period of his reign.”

In 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. The Bagrationi royal family lost power, and some of its members were exiled to Russia. The Russian Empire later conquered and annexed the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia as well.

Was Georgia “on the brink of extinction”?

Another key element of Georgian Dream’s new historical narrative concerns demographic survival. The prime minister says the Georgian nation faced a “real threat of extinction” at the end of the 18th century. MP Matikashvili has also referred to the “physical survival” of the Georgian people.

This view is not new. The Russian imperial narrative, and later the Soviet version of history, often portrayed the annexation of Georgia as a painful but necessary step to save the country.

Historian Giorgi Ugulava wrote in a 2025 article for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that this representation was one of the main products of Russian imperial propaganda. The argument was that Georgia could not survive independently and that Russian protection was the best option available.

Why has Erekle II become a political symbol for Georgian Dream?

Georgian Dream’s political campaign around Erekle II began well before August 2026.

In 2023, literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili criticised Erekle II over the Treaty of Georgievsk. Georgian Dream leaders responded with fierce criticism of the scholar. That same year, the pro-Russian Conservative Movement disrupted one of Berdzenishvili’s lectures. He was later attacked in the street.

At the time, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze said violence was unacceptable. At the same time, however, he accused Berdzenishvili of acting against Georgian identity.

In August 2024, Kobakhidze announced plans to erect a new monument to Erekle II in Tbilisi. The monument opened on 24 September 2025. At the ceremony, Kobakhidze described Erekle II as a symbol of “patriotism”, “love of the homeland” and “pragmatism”.

Kobakhidze also claimed that foreign diplomats had criticised Erekle II during meetings with Georgian Dream representatives. He did not name any of the diplomats or specify which countries they represented. However, according to his account, criticism of Erekle II formed part of coordinated actions by Western diplomats and the Georgian opposition.

Erekle II has therefore gradually evolved from a historical figure into a symbol of the current political confrontation. On one side stands the “pragmatic” king who reached an agreement with Russia. On the other are his critics, whom the government portrays as agents of Western interests.

“A new treaty”: what do pro-Russian forces in Georgia want?

While Georgian Dream highlights the positive historical significance of the old Treaty of Georgievsk, openly operating pro-Russian forces in Georgia are already calling directly for a “new treaty”.

One of the main figures in this campaign is Russian-Georgian citizen Mamuka Pipia, leader of the Solidarity for Peace party.

In July 2025, Pipia called for the signing of a “Treaty of Georgievsk 2” and an alliance treaty with Russia. His proposals included restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and removing Article 78 from Georgia’s Constitution. The article requires constitutional bodies to take all measures to ensure Georgia’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Pipia said: “Given today’s geopolitical situation, Russia and Georgia need to support each other, and they need to formalise an alliance treaty on equal terms.”

In August 2026, Pipia described Kobakhidze’s statements as a success for his own political agenda.

“I am glad that the country’s leadership now recognises the reality that we have been speaking about openly for the past two years,” he said.

Pipia says his idea of a “new Treaty of Georgievsk” means “a completely new, comprehensive and, most importantly, equal treaty with the Russian Federation”.

“We are working in this direction, and Moscow will make an appropriate statement very soon,” he added.

Georgian Dream denies coordinating with pro-Russian groups. However, Pipia’s political network maintains open contacts with Russian officials. He has appeared in public at various times with Russian State Duma deputies and other senior Russian officials.

In May 2025, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who is under US sanctions, was also in Red Square with Pipia. The US Treasury Department has described Partskhaladze as a Georgian-Russian oligarch and said Russia’s FSB used him to influence Georgian society and politics.

How closely do the two narratives align?

Mamuka Pipia’s and Georgian Dream’s ultimate political demands do not currently coincide. Georgian Dream is not officially calling for an alliance treaty with Russia, a “new treaty” or the repeal of Article 78 of the Constitution. This is a significant difference.

However, the similarities in their rhetoric are clear. In both cases, the main arguments for closer relations with Russia are “pragmatism”, peace, security and national interests. In both narratives, the West is increasingly portrayed not as a security partner but as a source of threats or pressure.

The rhetoric around the “deep state” also overlaps. For years, Pipia has spoken about Western forces allegedly trying to use Georgia against Russia. A similar conspiracy theory has become part of Georgian Dream’s official political messaging in recent years.

Now another important element has entered this shared vocabulary: the interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk as an agreement that saved Georgia.

What does the opposition say about a possible new agreement?

Against this backdrop, Georgian opposition figures suspect that the historical debate may serve to prepare public opinion for a more concrete political decision.

Mikheil Saakashvili said that the government was carrying out “ideological preparations for signing a treaty of betrayal”. He claims that Russia has even given ruling-party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili drafts of several agreements.

Saakashvili referred to restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and separate agreements on Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. He also claims that Irakli Kobakhidze is expected to travel to Moscow in the coming weeks.

There is currently no independent confirmation of this information. Neither the Georgian nor the Russian authorities have officially announced preparations for such agreements.

Former diplomat Ghia Japaridze also sees the government’s rhetoric as preparation for possible changes in foreign policy. He says the government is using the Treaty of Georgievsk to “justify a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course”.

What is the Russian media saying?

Irakli Kobakhidze’s statements have also attracted attention in Russia.

On 21 August, the Russian publication Vzglyad published an article headlined “Georgia has taken an important step towards normality”.

The article links several issues: the Georgian government’s campaign against so-called “Russophobia”, accusations against the West and the new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The publication places particular emphasis on the “restoration of respect for the Treaty of Georgievsk — an alliance with Russia that saved Georgia”.

In other words, what Georgian officials present in Tbilisi as a historical interpretation and an assessment of Erekle II’s decision is already being read by Russian media as a sign of changing political attitudes towards modern Russia.

A day earlier, even more far-reaching claims circulated in Russian Telegram channels. INSIDER-T, citing unofficial sources, claimed that Tbilisi had offered Moscow a behind-the-scenes deal: “full geopolitical loyalty” from Georgia in exchange for Russia publicly abandoning the annexation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

These claims are also not supported by reliable evidence.

What matters, however, is the political expectations now emerging in the Russian information space in response to statements by Georgian officials.

A historical dispute or an ongoing political process?

There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence that the Georgian authorities are preparing to sign a “New Treaty of Georgievsk” or another alliance agreement with Russia.

However, it is difficult to describe what is happening as merely a dispute among historians.

On one side is a government that has sharply worsened relations with Georgia’s main Western partners in recent years and has effectively frozen the country’s EU accession process.

On the other are pro-Russian groups openly calling for a political alliance and security ties with Russia. They see the prime minister’s new rhetoric as a victory for their position.

This is accompanied by the reaction of the Russian information space, where Georgian government statements are increasingly seen as a sign that Tbilisi is turning towards the Kremlin.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the Treaty of Georgievsk is no longer confined to the 18th century. The key question now is why the government needs to convince the public that a historical agreement with Russia, which ultimately led to the annexation of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, saved Georgia.

And, more importantly, what modern political choice might this version of history be intended to justify?

Debate over the Treaty of Georgievsk in Georgia

World.title: 750,000 lari bribe and other new allegations against jailed former Georgian PM who turned against the government
World.content:
Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili

New charges have been brought against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili for accepting a large bribe. The charges came shortly after he published open letters accusing the government of persecuting him to prevent his return to politics.

Garibashvili is already serving a five-year sentence for legalising illicit income. The new charges carry a prison sentence of between 11 and 15 years.

🟥 According to the prosecution, then-defence minister Juansher Burchuladze, who is now in prison, illegally transferred 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Garibashvili in cash in several instalments.

What does the prosecution accuse Garibashvili of?

The case concerns the purchase of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to the prosecution, the ministry conducted three secret procurement procedures from late 2022 onwards.

At the time, Juansher Burchuladze served as defence minister, while Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister.

According to investigators, Burchuladze and his relative, Vasil Mcheidze, reached an agreement with a local business and offered it an opportunity to take part in government tenders. With their help, the business was supposed to win the tenders and then pay them 10% of the total contract value.

The businessman demanded additional guarantees.

According to the prosecution, Burchuladze then reached an agreement with Irakli Garibashvili, who was serving as prime minister.

Investigators accuse the former prime minister of protecting the scheme and demanding his share of the proceeds.

According to the indictment, deputy defence minister Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement department head Vladimir Gudushauri then created non-competitive conditions. This allowed selected companies to win the tenders at predetermined prices.

The prosecution says the companies supplied the ministry with goods worth 18,484,960 lari (about $7.5 million). However, the actual value of the goods was 11,499,705 lari (about $4.5 million).

The prosecution estimates the damage to the state at 6,985,255 lari (about $2.6 million).

How was the 1.9 million lari divided?

According to the investigation, the businessman ultimately transferred 1.9 million lari (about $730,000) to Vasil Mcheidze in several instalments. The amount represented roughly 10% of the total value of the contracts.

Vasil Mcheidze kept 400,000 lari (about $155,000);

he transferred 1.5 million lari (about $580,000) to Juansher Burchuladze;

Burchuladze kept 750,000 lari (about $290,000);

he transferred the remaining 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Irakli Garibashvili.

Prosecutors have charged the former prime minister under Article 338 of the Criminal Code. The article covers accepting a particularly large bribe by a public or political official as part of a group.

At this stage, the prosecution is asking the court to schedule a preliminary hearing. It is not seeking a new pre-trial measure because Garibashvili is already in custody.

Who gave investigators new testimony?

According to the prosecution, Vasil Mcheidze decided to cooperate with investigators on 12 August. He provided the authorities with information in his possession.

Juansher Burchuladze is also cooperating with the investigation. The prosecution is relying on their testimony to establish Garibashvili’s role in the new case.

Burchuladze was arrested in September 2025. On 23 April 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison for abuse of power and legalising illicit income.

Burchuladze’s former deputy, Giorgi Khaindrava, and Vasil Mcheidze each received eight-year prison sentences in the same case. Gudushauri reached a plea agreement with the prosecution.

Why does the timing of the new charges against Garibashvili matter?

Just days before prosecutors brought the new charges, Garibashvili made three statements from prison. They were published on 17, 18 and 20 August.

The former prime minister said the ruling party was demanding that he admit to additional acts of corruption. He said the government feared his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said he had received a letter from prominent Georgian Dream representative Mamuka Mdinaradze. According to Garibashvili, a close friend of Mdinaradze delivered the letter to a member of his family.

“You sent me to prison for five years because of false assumptions, fantasies, envy, fears and suspicions created by a certain group within the party,” Garibashvili wrote.

He said the demand that he admit to the new allegations came with a hint that authorities could arrest his father.

“I am not fighting anyone. I am only defending myself and my family. That is why I will have no choice but to respond in kind to everything you do,” Garibashvili said.

The new charges have given the former prime minister’s statements added significance. However, his account has not been investigated or independently verified.

What does Georgian Dream say?

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze suggested that Garibashvili may have had information about the ongoing investigation. In his view, the former prime minister’s statements were pre-emptive.

“Former politicians often use this method, and legal issues are sometimes brought into the political sphere,” Kaladze said.

He said Garibashvili’s safety and rights were protected.

Mamuka Mdinaradze denies Garibashvili’s allegations. He considers the current case against the former prime minister part of the government’s fight against corruption.

Garibashvili family’s response

Garibashvili’s wife’s brother, Alexander Tamazashvili, published an extract from the public registry after prosecutors brought the new charges. He said the document showed a property transaction involving Zurab Tukvadze, a businessman and one of the prosecution’s witnesses.

The prosecution’s public statement does not name the businessman. However, Tamazashvili claims that Tukvadze transferred a country house in the Tskneti settlement to Vasil Mcheidze in 2023. Tamazashvili suggested that the property transfer amounted to a bribe.

The statement can also be seen as an ironic rebuttal of the allegations. However, the published property transaction neither proves nor disproves that anyone may have given cash to Garibashvili.

Garibashvili himself has not publicly responded to the details of the new charges.

Opposition raises two possible concerns

Opposition representatives have highlighted two issues in the case.

The first is possible corruption in defence procurement.

The second is the suspicion that the law may serve as a tool of political pressure.

Levan Samushia, a member of the opposition Strong Georgia – Lelo party, said Garibashvili’s earlier statements give grounds for such suspicions.

“Is the law not being used in this case to exert pressure based on clan interests? Otherwise, how could Garibashvili have known in advance that he might face charges?” Samushia said.

Zurab Japaridze, leader of Girchi – More Freedom, drew attention to the scheme described in the indictment. He linked Garibashvili’s alleged receipt of cash to his previous case.

“He artificially inflated the price, received his share in cash in lari, then exchanged it for dollars and gold and kept the bundles in a safe,” Japaridze wrote.

Garibashvili’s first case

Garibashvili first faced corruption charges in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to the prosecution, Garibashvili provided false information in his property declarations. In doing so, he allegedly attempted to give illegally obtained income a legitimate appearance.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a deal with the prosecution. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

Garibashvili has not pleaded guilty in the new case. The main grounds for the charges are testimony from Burchuladze and Mcheidze. The court will have to assess the credibility of their statements, along with the other evidence.

The case now brings together two parallel questions.

One concerns possible corruption in secret Defence Ministry procurement procedures.

The other concerns Garibashvili’s claim that the government demanded that he admit guilt in advance.

Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

World.title: Uzbekistan, China discuss expanding cooperation across key sectors
World.content:
Photo: telegram channel of the Head of the Presidential Administration

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Uzbekistan and China discussed strengthening bilateral relations and expanding cooperation in transport, trade, education and culture.

This was reflected in the statement posted by the Head of the Presidential Administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, on her social media account, following a meeting between Uzbek officials and Zhao Leji, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress.

According to information, the talks focused primarily on the sustainable development of relations between Uzbekistan and China, which have strengthened in recent years against the backdrop of closer dialogue between the leaders of the two nations.

The sides also highlighted the growing role of interparliamentary cooperation in advancing bilateral ties.

Uzbekistan welcomed China’s continued support and its readiness to work jointly on concrete projects across several sectors, including transportation, trade, education and culture.

“We value China’s support and readiness to work together on concrete projects in transport, trade, education and culture,” Mirziyoyeva said.

The meeting also emphasized the importance of turning the countries’ broad range of plans and agreements into practical results through consistent implementation.

The Uzbek side thanked Zhao for what it described as an open and substantive discussion, underscoring the importance of continued high-level political and parliamentary dialogue in supporting the countries’ growing partnership.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Initial public offerings (IPOs) are expected to gain further momentum in Azerbaijan in the coming years, Chairman of the Executive Board and CEO of the Baku Stock Exchange (BSE), Ruslan Khalilov, told Trend.

World.title: Fitch names Azerbaijan as key alternative route for Kazakh uranium exports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor) through Azerbaijan and Georgia is the main alternative route for Kazatomprom to export uranium from Kazakhstan.

This was stated in a press release by international rating agency Fitch Ratings.

The agency noted that Kazatomprom remains exposed to geopolitical risks, as its primary export route to western customers, accounting for more than half of its uranium shipments, runs through the Russian port of St. Petersburg.

"There are no current restrictions on exporting uranium from Russia, but we believe potential sanctions, if introduced, might disrupt shipments. The main alternative is the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route through Azerbaijan and Georgia, where Kazatomprom shipped 48% of its deliveries to western customers in 2025. The company also has the option of swaps for foreign inventories," Fitch said.

Fitch Ratings has affirmed the Long-Term Issuer Default Rating (IDR) of Kazatomprom at "BBB", with a Stable Outlook.

The Middle Corridor is a transport and trade route connecting Asia with Europe through several countries in the region. It serves as an alternative to the traditional Northern and Southern corridors.

The route starts in China and runs through Central Asian countries before crossing the Caspian Sea and continuing through Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye to Europe. The Middle Corridor is a multimodal land-based route that provides a link between eastern parts of Asia, including China, and Europe, avoiding longer maritime routes.

World.title: Uzbekistan urges stronger investment in land restoration at COP17
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Uzbekistan has called for stronger international financing and the development of new regional investment mechanisms to address desertification, land degradation and drought.

This was stated in a statement by Uzbekistan’s National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, released following the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) in Ulaanbaatar.

According to the National Committee, the high-level segment brought together heads of state and government officials, ministers, representatives of international organizations, and other participants. The segment was opened by Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khürelsükh and also featured remarks by UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed and UNCCD Executive Secretary Yasmine Fouad.

The discussions focused on accelerating land restoration, strengthening resilience to drought, improving sustainable pasture management and expanding financing for the restoration of land and ecosystems.

A central issue was the global financing gap. According to figures presented at COP17, the annual funding shortfall for addressing desertification, land degradation and drought is estimated at $278 billion, while the annual economic cost of inaction stands at approximately $878 billion.

Speaking at a ministerial dialogue on innovative financing mechanisms, Aziz Abdukhakimov, adviser to the President of Uzbekistan on environmental issues and chairman of the National Committee for Ecology and Climate Change, noted that land degradation and drought pose both environmental and socioeconomic challenges for Uzbekistan.

“For Uzbekistan, land degradation, desertification and drought are not only environmental challenges, but also social and economic ones, directly affecting food and water security, the resilience of rural communities and long-term economic development,” Abdukhakimov said.

Uzbekistan covers about 45 million hectares, with roughly 30 million hectares consisting of desert and arid landscapes. More than 11 million hectares are classified as degraded, while about 70% of the country’s territory faces desertification risks. Pastures cover approximately 26 million hectares, with about 60% experiencing declining productivity.

The country has expanded restoration efforts, including in the Aral Sea region, where protective vegetation has been established across more than 2 million hectares of the dried seabed to help reduce dust storms and improve regional resilience.

Uzbekistan also highlighted the $153 million RESILAND Uzbekistan project financed by the World Bank, as well as more than $32 million in grants mobilized in 2025 for environmental stabilization in the Aral Sea region.

However, Abdukhakimov stressed that international financing remains insufficient and presented several proposals aimed at mobilizing investment in Central Asia.

One proposal calls for establishing a Drylands Project Lab under the Regional Research Institute for Combating Desertification and Developing Desert Economies at Green University. The platform would turn scientific research and tested solutions into investment-ready projects, while a proposed Central Asian Land Project Preparation Center would provide grants and technical assistance. Uzbekistan aims to develop the region’s first portfolio of such projects by 2027.

Uzbekistan also proposed creating a dedicated Central Asia financing window under the UNCCD and its Global Mechanism to support land restoration, drought resilience and measures against sand and dust storms through blended-finance mechanisms.

Another proposal calls for establishing a Central Asian Pasture Data Processing Center, with financing linked to independently verified environmental and socioeconomic outcomes.

Uzbekistan further proposed working with the UNCCD, UNFCCC, and relevant international standard-setting organizations to develop a specialized Carbon Standard for Drylands to measure, report, and verify carbon sequestration in deserts and other arid ecosystems.

The proposals reflect Uzbekistan’s push to shift international financing for land restoration from funding individual activities toward investment tied to measurable environmental and socioeconomic results.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Turkestan region to launch phosphate processing plant
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. A plant for deep processing of phosphate ore is being constructed in Kazakhstan's Turkestan region, with investment totaling 150 billion tenge ($327.2 million), the regional akimat said.

The project is being implemented by Sozak Phosphate LLP in the Sozak district and envisages the creation of a full-cycle production complex covering the extraction, beneficiation and deep processing of phosphate ore.

Once operational, the plant is expected to process 2 million tons of phosphate ore annually and produce 1.6 million tons of sulfuric acid, 600,000 tons of phosphoric acid, 600,000 tons of diammonium phosphate (DAP), 600,000 tons of monoammonium phosphate (MAP) and 350,000 tons of synthetic ammonia. The products are expected to be supplied to the domestic market and exported to China, India and neighboring countries.

Turkestan Region Akim Nuralhan Kusherov discussed the project's progress and further plans with Sinopec leadership.

"The phosphate ore processing plant being implemented in the Sozak district is one of the strategically important major projects not only for the region, but also for the industrial and economic development of the entire country. The project is expected to create around 1,000 jobs," Kusherov said.

He stressed the importance of ensuring high construction quality, compliance with deadlines, industrial safety and environmental requirements.

The project has been included in Kazakhstan's Industrialization Map. According to the State Fund commission's findings, the phosphate ore reserves at the deposit amount to about 1 billion tons, with phosphorus content ranging from approximately 20% to 30%.

An EPC contract for the technological part of the project has been signed with China's Sinopec Nanjing Engineering Co., Ltd. Specialists are currently conducting additional studies of the production site and deposit, including core drilling and ore sampling, while refining raw material characteristics and verifying technological solutions.

The feasibility study is scheduled for completion in October 2026. The project will then proceed to design, construction of engineering infrastructure, railway and water and power supply facilities, equipment procurement and plant construction.

The full-scale implementation of the project is expected to create a new high-value-added chemical production chain in the region. Local deep processing of phosphate ore will enable the production of mineral fertilizers and chemical products, reduce import dependence and increase Kazakhstan's export potential.

The project is expected to generate about 43.3 billion tenge ($94.3 million) in tax revenues for the state budget over 10 years. The plant is scheduled to be launched in 2028.

Currency conversion: $1 = 458.48 tenge as of August 26, 2026.

World.title: Citynet subscribers to earn cashback with every payment
World.content:
The country’s leading internet provider, citynet, is introducing a new “Loyalty Program” to offer additional benefits to its customers. Subscribers using the citynet mobile app will now earn cashback when paying their service fees.

Under the “Loyalty Program,” subscribers will receive different cashback rates depending on the payment period. Users who pay their monthly subscription fee on time will receive cashback equal to 5% of the payment amount, while subscribers who pay for a minimum of six months of service in advance will receive cashback equal to 10% of the total amount paid.

The cashback amount and its transaction history are displayed in the Wallet section of the citynet mobile app. The funds accumulated in the Wallet can, at the user’s choice, be used to pay the next citynet subscription fee or transferred to their Pulz account.

To take advantage of the offer, users simply need to download the citynet mobile app. The app is available on both iOS and Android platforms.

The “Loyalty Program” provides citynet subscribers with additional benefits when using and paying for services. Managing the entire process through the mobile app makes earning and using cashback more convenient and accessible for subscribers.

In addition to high-speed internet services, citynet offers exclusive TV solutions. Ctv also gives users access to selected TV channels such as Digiturk, Setanta Sports, Dizi Channel, and FilmBox, alongside popular streaming and entertainment platforms including YouTube, Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Spotify.

World.title: An Australian among hundreds missing in deadly Nepal floods
World.content:
At least one Australian is missing after a deadly flash flood hit the Tibet-Nepal border, according to local authorities.

The torrent of water swept through the Himalayan border region on Wednesday morning, local time, killing at least nine people in Nepal so far.

Nepal's tourism board said at least 384 travellers, including 291 foreign nationals, had been reported missing.

The list of foreigners unaccounted for, which has been seen by the ABC, includes one Australian.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has yet to respond to the ABC's questions.

Nepal's foreign minister said an earthquake caused an avalanche that triggered the flood along the Bhote Koshi river in Rasuwa. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

Nepal's foreign minister said an earthquake caused an avalanche that triggered the flood along the Bhote Koshi river in Rasuwa, according to local media reports.

Broadcast images showed crumbled homes, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away in the Nepal flood waters.

"There could be heavy casualties or loss of property," said district administrator Narendra Pariyar, who urged dwellers on the banks of the Bhote Koshi river to move to higher ground, after reports of villages and project sites being swept up.

Nepal's rescue helicopters would be unable to land in the affected areas until the waters recede, army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said.

On the Tibetan side of the disaster, Chinese officials said they feared "major casualties" in the the county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a land crossing.

President Xi Jinping urged "all-out" search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

Chinese state media said access to the the area was cut off and communication channels were down, but it was expected dozens of people could be killed.

World.title: The home of the Ford Falcon may soon become Australia's AI engine room
World.content:
For more than half a century, Ford's Broadmeadows manufacturing plant was known as the home of the iconic Falcon.

"That was the manufacturing heartland of Australia," said Basem Abdo, the federal member for Calwell in Melbourne.

" I always say that we didn't just make Australian-made products — that site helped make Australia. "

Now, 10 years after the plant shut its doors, there are plans to turn the former Ford site into the engine room of Australia's AI boom.

Zoe and John live across the road from the former Ford factory in Broadmeadow and are worried about a data centre potentially moving into the site. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

The $1.1 billion proposal for a massive data centre by Singaporean digital infrastructure firm Zerra DC — dubbed "Project Dune" — is predicted to draw 336MW of power across six buildings and will take 12 years to build.

Zoe, who lives across the road from the site and is a former employee at the Ford plant, is concerned about having the data centre on her doorstep.

"I had to ask my children what it is," she told 7.30.

"They said something to do with batteries, and they will be working 24 hours a day.

"I don't think it's a good idea. I don't know how long we're going to live but it's still not a good idea for us to live in this area [during the construction] and having all those things in and out every day.

"It's terrible."

Fears of a 'pathway to nowhere'

The final car rolls off the production line at Ford in Broadmeadows in 2016. (Supplied: Ford Australia)

At its height, the Broadmeadows factory — which covered the size of 10 MCGs — employed more than 5,000 local workers who were producing generations of Ford vehicles.

In contrast, Zerra DC said 407 jobs would be created annually during the construction phase and 670 jobs created annually once the data centre was fully operational, boosting the Victorian economy by $158 million.

But Mr Abdo said many residents in his diverse community were concerned about the long-term job prospects from the data centre.

"People need to see that it offers a pathway to employment, a pathway to good, secure, well-paying jobs that offer them a career, which was what this site was about and which is what this site should be about," he told 7.30.

Basem Abdo says people in his community are concerned the data centre will not offer many long-term jobs. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"I will only support a project that is in line with our national standards that we've put forth clearly on a national level.

" At this stage, I'm not satisfied that that proposal meets those standards. "

Mr Abdo said the project was yet to make the case for the same kind of long-term employment pathways that the region's manufacturing industry provided.

"Are they good, secure jobs that provide long-term careers for people in our area?" he asked.

"This must not lead to a pathway to nowhere in terms of jobs and skills."

'Why is it being fast-tracked?'

An artist's impression of part of the proposed Zerra DC data centre. (Supplied)

State governments in Australia, particularly New South Wales and Victoria, are competing to capture billions of dollars in data centre investment.

An Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) report released this week shows the number of Australian data centres in development has more than doubled since 2025, from 97 to 225 this year.

AEMO's report also predicted data centres would account for 13 per cent of the nation's energy consumption by 2035.

But communities are asking whether the speed of approval for these projects is coming at the expense of scrutiny.

Campbellfield resident Anastasia Drapaniotis has taken a leading role in opposing the Project Dune proposal.

Anastasia Drapaniotis is critical of the planning process for the data centre. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

"I think a lot of the residents feel like they can't do anything about it and I think that's really horrible," she told 7.30.

" It's really awful to feel like you don't have a say in what comes to your area. "

She told 7.30 she was not against data centre developments but was critical of the planning process.

"I would have to say … OK, bring these in, sure, but have stricter regulations," she said.

"Why is it being fast-tracked? Why are they being approved so quickly when something like this would ordinarily take a very long time to get approved?"

Community members protest against the proposed data centre in Broadmeadows. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Zerra DC lodged the development application for the Campbellfield project in April directly with the state government under special planning provisions for big projects and expects the "fast-tracked" decision within four months.

Victoria's Environment Protection Authority lodged a formal objection to the proposal with the Department of Transport and Planning, citing "concerns over potential noise risks and the cumulative impacts associated with the overall site layout and development".

Zoe and her husband John received the letter informing them of the proposal four days before the date on which Victoria's planning minister was permitted to decide on the project.

At the bottom of the letter, it said: "The responsible authority will not decide on the application before: 28 July 2026."

The planning minister is yet to announce a decision on the proposal.

"I think we could fight against it, but as far as it stopping, I don't think so," Zoe said.

"Not when you get a big overseas company coming in with billions of dollars."

Company says it engaged with community

A map showing the proposed Zerra DC project in Broadmeadows. (Supplied)

Zerra DC declined an interview with 7.30 but said in a statement: "We understand that a proposal of this scale can raise genuine questions and concerns for nearby residents and businesses, and we recognise that some people feel they have not had enough opportunity to be heard."

The company said it began its community engagement program in late May and distributed information "to approximately 1,080 nearby households and 470 industrial businesses, supported by translated information, a dedicated project website, community survey, telephone and email channels, and direct visits to neighbouring businesses".

Zerra DC said the redevelopment of the former Ford site represented "a highly-productive long-term use of industrial land", adding that it had "carefully reviewed the issues raised through community feedback and lodged a detailed response to submissions with the Department of Transport and Planning on 7 August".

"No amendments to the proposal have been made at this stage," it said.

Victoria's Minister for Planning Sonya Kilkenny. (ABC News: Maddison Cutajar)

Victoria's Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny also declined an interview with 7.30, but a Victorian government spokesperson said in a statement: "Every proposal is considered on its merits — as this proposal is under consideration it would be inappropriate to comment further.

"Submissions from the community and nearby businesses can be provided up until a decision is made."

The proposal bypassed local government and prompted Hume City Council, which includes the suburb of Broadmeadows, to pass a motion calling for a moratorium on data centre approvals in Victoria.

A further three councils, Melton, Brimbank and Maribyrnong, have since joined Hume in calling for a temporary halt on these types of projects.

Attracting data centres to Australia

Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to attract data centres but "maintaining social licence will be essential". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

While state governments court data centre investment, the federal government increasingly has its own expectations for what large data centres will deliver for Australia and the communities they are built in.

In a speech to business leaders yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential".

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained, and locations are appropriate," he said.

Today, the prime minister took his plan to implement national mandatory standards for the industry to National Cabinet.

Under these legislated rules, the biggest facilities will be required to fund and use renewable energy, pay their share of grid and water infrastructure and meet community expectations.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Notes allegedly written by woman accused of killing parents released
World.content:
A woman standing trial accused of murdering her elderly parents allegedly scrawled notes — which a court has released — including a reference to police waiting to see if she would "get cocky and slip up".

Raelene Polymiadis, 65, of Craigmore is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court, after pleading not guilty to murdering her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson, by injecting them with her own insulin in 2022 and 2023.

Prosecutors previously told the jury a set of notes were allegedly found during a search of Ms Polymiadis's house and car and detailed what she should be saying to police when she spoke to them.

Brenda and Lynton Anderson, both aged 94, died a year apart. (Supplied: Nine News)

Supreme Court Justice Sandi McDonald, who is presiding over the trial, approved the release of handwritten notes, which prosecutors alleged were penned by Ms Polymiadis.

One note written on the top corner of a piece of paper said: "What they will do is wait for a few weeks months year to see if I think I got away with it and I get cocky and slip up. Hang on buddy, it could be a long ride."

A handwritten note tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

In another note, the author posed questions to authorities.

"Who are you sorry?" the note read.

"What's this about?

"Are you from the Coroner's office?

"Why only now are you speaking with me and it's only a few days after the funeral!!"

One of the handwritten notes released by the Supreme Court lists questions. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Prosecutors previously told the court Ms Polymiadis wrote to herself to "sob here", saying that matched a point in the police interview where she started sobbing.

One of the notes released by the court discussed events occurring in hospital.

"We went to see dad, they were keeping him warm," part of the note said.

"He was out to it — unconscious I guess but breathing with help of oxygen I 'think' — I'm sorry this is really hard relieving all this — is it absolutely necessary."

Another handwritten note prosecutors allege Raelene Polymiadis wrote. (Supplied: Courts SA)

The note went on to say, "… just holding his hand, talking to him, but I got no response (sob)".

The trial previously heard police listening devices captured Ms Polymiadis in her car praying to God, confessing to the crimes.

Ms Polymiadis's lawyer, Marie Shaw KC, previously told the jury the context of the alleged confession would arise during the trial.

"The issue about the alleged confession is: was my client admitting she was responsible for the deaths or was she telling her god she felt responsible for their deaths because if they died of insulin administration, they must have accessed her insulin?" Ms Shaw said.

Another of the handwritten notes tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Another note made references to Ms Polymiadis's father.

"Then I burst into tears, thinking my God he got into my stuff, it's my fault."

The trial continues.

World.title: Canberra childcare centre ordered to close as provider enters administration
World.content:
The childcare regulator has ordered Edge Early Learning in Charnwood in Canberra's Belconnen area to close for three months.

The notice of suspension, issued by Children's Education and Care Assurance (CECA), comes about a month after an Edge Early Learning centre in nearby Higgins was forced to shut immediately over its response to a serious medical incident involving a child.

The reasons behind the Charnwood centre's notice of suspension remain unknown, with its closure due to begin on September 3.

In a statement, CECA said:

"Edge has the right to appeal the decision and is legally required to communicate the suspension to families. "Under administration, the administrator can also exercise the right to appeal."

The ABC has spoken to parents who said they were unaware that CECA had ordered the Charnwood centre to close for three months from next Thursday.

Edge Early Learning also has a centre operating in Ngunnawal in the Gungahlin area.

The Edge Early Learning centre in the ACT that was forced to close suddenly in July. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Business-as-usual'

It comes as the childcare provider, which runs dozens of childcare centres across South Australia, Queensland and the ACT, went into voluntary administration.

In a statement from Edge Early Learning, it said administrators had been appointed to "review the business and work with key stakeholders to determine the best path forward", and that the process would allow the company "to assess its financial position and consider options for its future".

" We understand that this may be a confusing and stressful development for families who rely upon Edge Early Learning to provide care for their children. "

Canberra childcare centre ordered to close A Canberra mother had concerns for her daughter's safety at Edge Early Learning in Higgins long before the ACT regulator ordered the centre to close.

Edge Early Learning said it was continuing to operate all centres "on a business-as-usual basis".

"There will be no change to your care arrangements, centre opening hours or staffing. Families should continue to attend their centre as normal," it told parents.

"Our immediate focus is to maintain the safe and ongoing operation of each centre while this urgent review is undertaken."

World.title: Body found as police investigate shooting of Melbourne father
World.content:
Homicide detectives have found a body in their search for a Melbourne father who went missing after allegedly being shot.

A desperate search has been underway for Khaled Malas, 37, who has not been seen since he was allegedly attacked at a home in Wildwood, north-west of the city, on August 19.

Police allege he was shot after a dispute, which is understood to involve a significant debt, and there were grave fears for his welfare.

Police last week searched near a waste facility at Sunbury for missing man Khaled Malas. (ABC News)

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, has been charged with intentionally causing serious injury.

On Wednesday afternoon, investigators found human remains covered in grass on Havelock Road in Clarkefield, about 15 kilometres from Wildwood.

The coroner has been notified, and an autopsy is expected to take place.

Victoria Police said it would consider alternative charges upon receiving the results of the autopsy.

The dog squad was involved in the search near the Sunbury landfill site. (ABC News)

Remembered as a loving father

Omar, a long-time friend, said Mr Malas would be remembered as a family man who was deeply respected by his community.

He said Mr Malas, who arrived in Australia 14 years ago, "loved his young family and kids to death".

"We remember him as a hard, honest worker that came to this country ... to achieve a dream," Omar said.

"He was the sole son that was also providing for his parents overseas as well."

He said the community was in shock.

"[They're] in disbelief ... how can a beautiful soul vanish in such [a] horrible way," he said.

World.title: Queensland allowed to use coal, gas for data centres despite renewable push
World.content:
Queensland will be allowed to go its own way using gas or coal to power data centres, despite Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously demanding states use renewables.

State and territory leaders met on Wednesday to settle national standards for data centre construction, but instead agreed to undertake further work.

Queensland Premier Crisafulli had pushed for an energy-agnostic approach and told the ABC the carve out was a "good win" for his state, which owns much of its own electricity infrastructure.

Data centre fight heats up Premiers are heading into national cabinet divided over how Australia should meet the rapidly growing energy demands of AI data centres.

"It shows because we own our assets, both our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board, and that enables us to bring on new energy opportunities," he said.

Premiers and chief ministers met with Mr Albanese in Sydney to discuss issues including AI, domestic violence, bird flu, fuel security and the embattled national gun buyback.

Ahead of the meeting, federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen had insisted the Commonwealth would legislate over the top of states and territories that refused to adopt the renewables standard.

Queensland argued the state-owned nature of its energy infrastructure put it in a position to maintain a technology-agnostic approach, meaning gas or coal could be used to power its data centres.

The Northern Territory also opposed the renewables focus and has indicated it would use gas to power data centre projects.

Following the meeting, Mr Albanese said both jurisdictions were in a "different position" to other states, as he justified the apparent backdown on renewables.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli had argued for a technology-neutral approach. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas rejected suggestions the prime minister had been rolled on the issue.

"What you see emerging from national cabinet is a genuine desire to make sure we work through the issues associated with a rollout of data centres in Australia in a way that has a degree of uniformity," Mr Malinauskas told 7.30.

"And I think today's discussion was very much an example of us all being aligned on the best way to do that."

Mr Malinauskas said there was unity about the principle that data centres should add to the electricity grid without negatively impacting the national energy market.

"What we agreed upon is that renewables will principally be the form of energy that will power data centres in the future in Australia," he said.

A communique released after national cabinet said the standards would "ensure consistency and clarity for investors, while protecting Australia's economy, strengthening our sovereignty and securing benefits in line with our national interests".

The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

The prime minister said the new standards, which would also include rules on water usage and community consultation, would be legislated early next year.

"We have buy-in on Australia's first national AI laws," he said.

Ongoing discussions are expected to include ensuring data centres do not raise power prices for households and other businesses.

Mr Bowen has consistently argued renewables were the cheapest form of energy to ensure this did not happen.

But Mr Crisafulli has rejected this and insisted his state would be able to keep power prices low even where other energy sources were used.

"We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix even with those data centres on," he said.

Citizenship a condition of holding gun licence

The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence, though the prime minister indicated there would be some exceptions.

Albanese to override Queensland on data centres Queensland's rejection of rules tying data centre construction to new renewables projects means the federal government will be forced to legislate to override the state.

There was little movement on a national gun buyback scheme, which the federal government tried to roll out following the Bondi terrorist attack in December last year.

Queensland had refused to take part, while others including Victoria and South Australia are yet to sign up.

Mr Albanese said the offer was "still there", though jurisdictions were "responsible for their own decisions".

He said the new firearm agreement would allow the sharing of Commonwealth criminal intelligence with the states and territories.

"This is about improving our laws following the horrific antisemitic attack in Bondi last year," Mr Albanese said.

GST distribution was largely off the agenda after Mr Albanese declared on Tuesday he would not meddle with Western Australia's portion of the carve-up while he was prime minister, despite opposition from other jurisdictions.

Cabinet also heard a report from Australia's head vet as the federal government prepares to tip an additional $125 million to protect the nation from bird flu, which has now been detected in all six states.

World.title: Wife of key figure in ICAC probe paid $254k for three months of work
World.content:
The NSW corruption watchdog has heard that the wife of a key figure in an inquiry was paid $254,666 for three months of consulting.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations that prohibited political donations were funnelled through third parties to support the Liberal-aligned, right-wing faction known as the NSW Reformers and advance the interests of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

Anita Perrottet is the wife of Charles Perrottet, a Reformers member and the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Charles is a brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet. (Supplied: Facebook)

ICAC is investigating payments made to Ms Perrottet's company, Macquarie Consulting, by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood's businesses Beckington and JPG Advisory, and whether those payments were for genuine consulting work or used to disguise money allegedly intended for Charles Perrottet.

The commission heard Ms Perrottet was paid $254,666 for three months of consulting work in 2022, despite telling the inquiry she mainly provided verbal marketing and strategic advice and could recall little documentation of the work.

Counsel assisting the commission, Peggy Dwyer SC, challenged the scale of the payments, which were made through Mr Greenwood's businesses.

"That's based on a salary of $1 million, Mrs Perrottet … let's get serious," Dr Dwyer said. "You are giving evidence under oath … Do you seriously suggest that the commission should accept that as truthful evidence that you were entitled to charge $254,666 for work that you actually did … providing an oral sounding board or advice to Jeremy Greenwood for that quarter?"

Ms Perrottet insisted the evidence was truthful.

$10,000 monthly retainer

The ICAC is investigating allegations of prohibited political donations. (ABC News)

Ms Perrottet also told the commission she received a $10,000 monthly retainer from Beckington, without a written or signed agreement.

She said her work was primarily delivered through conversations with Mr Greenwood, either in person or by phone.

Dr Dwyer said the commission had found no evidence of phone calls between Ms Perrottet and Mr Greenwood during the relevant periods.

The commission heard Ms Perrottet could remember only one Beckington client, Greyhound Racing NSW, and that she gave Mr Greenwood advice about the client during face-to-face meetings but could not recall when or where those meetings occurred.

"Are you struggling to remember because it actually didn't happen?" Dr Dwyer asked.

The commission was also shown an invoice from Macquarie Consulting for $150,000, covering 12 months of work for Beckington, which was sent by Charles Perrottet.

Ms Perrottet could not remember why the invoice had been issued, why Charles Perrottet sent it or why three lump-sum payments subsequently received from Beckington did not reconcile with the $150,000 invoice.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Ms Perrottet said she could not recall the details of the fee arrangement but maintained she probably discussed it with Mr Greenwood.

The commission also heard evidence that lobbyist Christian Ellis, also a key figure in the inquiry, sent Charles Perrottet instructions about how invoices from Macquarie Consulting should be structured, including the amounts and periods to be billed.

The commission has also ordered Ms Perrottet to provide phone records and messages involving Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis as it tests her account of the consulting work.

Ms Perrottet will continue giving evidence on Friday before her husband takes the stand.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing.

World.title: Hobart council advances ban on full-home short stays
World.content:
A plan to block Hobart property owners from converting their entire homes into short-stay accommodation has passed another milestone, with the local council voting to send the proposal off for final approval.

Council revives bid to curb whole-home short-stays A fresh proposal from the Hobart City Council would block about 90 per cent of the city's homes from being wholly converted into short-stay accommodation.

The proposal, which aims to restrict the creation of new short-stay accommodation in the city, was considered by the Hobart City Council (HCC) at its planning committee meeting on Wednesday.

The tweak to planning rules would block about 20,000 homes from being wholly converted into visitor accommodation, such as Airbnb or Stayz.

"The draft amendment delivers a clear net community benefit through improved housing outcomes while still allowing the visitor economy to be accommodated," council officers wrote.

"The primary purpose of the proposed amendment is to limit the impact of new visitor accommodation use on the availability and affordability of housing for long-term residents in the city.

"It was informed by extensive background analysis, including data on housing and rental markets, tourism trends, existing visitor accommodation supply and planning approvals."

Council officers said the plan delivers a "clear net community benefit" by improving housing outcomes, while still accommodating the visitor economy. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

More than 50 submissions were made while the plan was out for public consultation across June and July, with 15 supporting the amendment while 41 were in opposition.

The representations in support of the amendment focused largely on the impact that whole-home short stays have on the rental market, housing affordability, neighbourhood cohesion and the function of residential zoning.

Those against the amendment highlighted the benefits short stays have on the city's economy and tourism, their role in providing accommodation for workers and families, private property rights, investment certainty and the impact on small business owners.

The planning amendment will now be sent to the Tasmanian Planning Commission (TPC) for final approval, with the council anticipating a public hearing will be held.

Short stay rental host says 'hosting is an economic lifeline'

Merrydith Callegari, who has been a short-stay rental host in Hobart for more than 10 years, addressed the planning committee ahead of the vote.

She was opposed to the amendment and called for an opportunity to work constructively with the council to develop a framework where short-term rental owners and the council could work together.

"Short-term rentals are a vital part of Tasmania's accommodation requirements, hosting is an economic lifeline for many hosts and related industries, they fill gaps that hotels can't, they give visitors a home," Ms Callegari said.

"I believe banning does not give the result you seek … we need to make building easier, to support landlords, not tear them down — after all, if renting is too hard, landlords will stop renting.

" Every host should have the right to host … it allows people to earn an income they never could before. "

Councillors divided on if move will help rental crisis

Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said cities all over the world were dealing with an increase in short-term rentals, while housing stock continued to fall short of demand.

"It's got to the stage where it's having a very significant impact on our rental market," she said.

"We are losing young people to other parts of Hobart because they can't get a rental here.

"This is rental stock that's been basically turned into small hotels in our suburbs."

Anna Reynolds says short-stay accommodation is having a "significant impact" on the city's rental market. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Cr Reynolds said the amendment was a "good compromise" and still allowed for permits in the CBD, while also not removing any existing permits.

Council locks in 1,050 per cent short-stay conversion fee hike A Tasmanian council has pushed through a 1,050 per cent increase in fees for applications to turn a property into short-stay accommodation.

"We have a higher penetration of short stays as a percentage of our rental market than I think any other capital city," she said.

Councillor Ben Lohberger supported the amendment and said whole-home short-stay rentals have filled some streets with "mini hotels".

"It's quite obvious to me that we do need some way to have discretion on whether we approve these and that's what this is about," he said.

"It's not about banning anything that exist, its not about banning every single future application; it's about giving the council the power to decide.

" We are simply trying to respond to a growing issue. "

Ben Lohberger says whole-home short-stays have filled some residential streets with "mini hotels". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Alderman Marti Zucco said property owners should be able to do whatever they wanted with their homes.

"We should be listening to those representations we got and maybe instead sit down and see if we can find another way forward," Cr Zucco said.

" This is not going to solve the rental crisis in Hobart … we've missed that boat. "

Marti Zucco says property owners should be able to do what they like with their homes. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Deputy Lord Mayor Zelinda Sherlock stressed that the amendment was not "about banning anything" and only applied to residential areas.

The restriction would apply to properties zoned as general residential, inner residential or low-density residential, which account for about 90 per cent of dwellings in Hobart.

The historic suburb of Battery Point, which is very popular for tourists, and Hobart's inner CBD would not be affected.

The councillors who voted in support of the proposal included Anna Reynolds, Ryan Posselt, Gemma Kitsos, Bill Harvey, Ben Lohberger, Mike Dutta and Zelinda Sherlock.

Those who voted against were Marti Zucco, Will Coats and Louise Bloomfield, while councillors Louise Elliot and John Kelly were not present.

World.title: How to leak a travel piece
World.content:
“Up early and reading an online story about British pubs by Herald travel expert Ben Groundwater, I was astounded to see two embedded ads for GROUNDWATER DRILLING SERVICES, illustrated with a gushing pipe,” notes Mark Southcott of Thirroul. “By 7.45, news of this vital service had gone – humans may have intervened to challenge the ad-matching computer – but should we warn Ben?”

“I was excited, as a teenager, to be taken to Parramatta RSL with my parents for a rare celebratory meal,” recalls Maureen Partridge of Baulkham Hills. “Just as our main courses arrived, two men approached and told us to ‘eat up as fast as you can and then leave’. Our sin? My World War II veteran father was wearing a collared shirt and jacket but no tie (C8). Sixty years later I still avoid clubs.”

“Seeing reference to needing to wear a tie to get into the Chatswood Charles in the ’60s brought back memories of a liquor licence law where you could only buy a drink after 8pm if you were having a meal,” says Ian Costley of Belrose. “The Charles provided a tiny paper plate with a fish finger, meat ball and minute vegetable item to satisfy the law, at a bargain price. Luckily, there was no requirement to actually eat it.”

“On a morning walk last week I smiled and said good morning to a young woman walking in the opposite direction,” reports Jim Pollitt of Wahroonga. “She also smiled and nodded, then, as she drew level, she said, ‘Do you need a change of clothing?’ Hurriedly checking myself for a possible wardrobe malfunction, I turned to ask her for clarification, only to notice the little ear buds and realise she was talking hands-free on her phone.”

Joe Moore of Blaxland shares his train of thought: “It was reported yesterday that rail passengers were ‘detrained’ after the failure of the Sydney rail network. I assume they were ‘retrained’ when the problems were resolved. Any late passengers would, of course, ‘mistrain’.”

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 8:55pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made its way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. World.title: Australian among hundreds missing after avalanche triggers deadly flash floods in Nepal
World.content:
Hundreds of people, including an Australian tourist, were reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure.

The Nepal Tourism Board reported 384 tourists were missing as a result of the flash flood, including one Australian. The 291 foreign nationals listed also include visitors from India, the United States, the United Kingdom, South Africa and Malaysia.

Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday (around 1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

“We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.
