World.title: Brisbane’s schools are bursting at the seams. It’s only going to get worse
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Brisbane’s schools are bursting at the seams. It’s only going to get worse Dominique Tassell August 26, 2026 — 8:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“It’s just really reactive planning, as opposed to proactive planning.” That’s how a parent at one of Brisbane’s biggest schools describes the government’s approach to our bursting-at-the-seams education system, where large school cohorts are managed by split start times and staggered lunch breaks. Suburban Futures director Ross Elliott agrees the city’s social infrastructure has not been keeping pace with population growth. Pallara State School is the fourth-largest state primary school in Brisbane. John-Paul Langbroek “I think in the last 10 to 20 years, we’ve spent too much time patting ourselves on the back saying how wonderful population growth is for the economy,” Elliott said. “At the same time, [the government] wasn’t looking at the demands on schools, on hospitals – on all infrastructure.”



Pallara State School in Brisbane’s south is the city’s fourth-biggest state primary school and an example of an institution juggling surging demand and limited space. Related Article Schools ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity The split-campus school, which caters to more than 1300 students, was built in 1956 but has had multiple expansions since, most recently a new junior campus for prep and year 1. The school’s senior campus – for years 2 to 6 – is located 2.5 kilometres down the road. Before the new campus opened in January, P&C treasurer Chad Redgwell said the school used demountables for years.



He said it was forced to cancel its athletics carnival in 2024 due to limited space caused by demountables on the oval. When the new junior campus opened, there was no oval, hall, or library for the first term. Pallara State School opened a new junior campus 2.5 kilometres away from the rest of the primary school in January. John-Paul Langbroek “They didn’t want to delay the kids from entering that site because they would have then had to go to the senior school site, spend one term down there, then move the kids down,” Redgwell said. The large student body was previously managed by splitting start and finish times, as well as lunch breaks.



“So you can imagine you had kids in the classroom trying to learn while the other half of the school’s playing outside,” Redgwell said. “Because there wasn’t enough play space for the kids at lunchtime, they were running into each other, they were fighting over the space – there were a lot of fights.” Redgwell said it was his impression that the government was consistently caught off guard by the number of students at the school, and was therefore unprepared for future demand. He said most in the school community were still anticipating the installation of demountables at the junior school in 2028. Brisbane’s population boom is taking a toll, Elliott said.



Almost three-quarters of the city’s state primary schools have an enrolment management plan – meaning they are at or over 80 per cent of their capacity. Enrolments at just under 90 per cent of the state’s high schools are also managed. Seven schools have opened in Brisbane proper this century. Two are private, and only one was opened in the past decade – two if you count the resurrection of Fortitude Valley State School. Just over 20 schools have been built in the past decade, WHERE? while the population almost doubled from 737,000 residents to approximately 1.38 million residents.



During the same period, 11 schools closed in Brisbane proper. The only new school on the horizon for the city is a primary school in Brisbane’s inner west, which is under consideration and unconfirmed.WHERE? Related Article NAPLAN Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results Building new schools is especially difficult because of the scarcity of appropriate sites, Elliott said. Another option is repurposing buildings, such as large stores like Bunnings, or office buildings that are largely unsuitable for housing because of the plumbing. “It’s always the plumbing,” Elliott said. “In a school, you could have the boys’ and girls’ toilets in the central services core, as they are for an office building.



“Then you can have each different level at school, and then you have the tuck shop and the indoor gym. “The question then becomes, ‘well, where do they go for exercise?’ And, like a lot of schools around the world, they get in a bus and go to a shared sporting field. “That’s the model we’re going to have to look at.” Such schools could also have the benefit of being central, and therefore close to public transport, Elliott said. Schools are a big part of Brisbane’s infrastructure challenge, he said.



“It’s certainly not easy, and you can understand why not everyone would be happy with the way it’s going,” he said. “It’s a symptom of the growth, and it’s probably symptomatic of the fact we should have been doing a lot more planning for it many years ago.” Elliott believes we need to get creative with solutions and look at spaces including office buildings, old shopping buildings, and industrial sheds. “It requires a different way of thinking about it because in terms of infill, no one’s spoilt for choice,” he said. “There are no 5-hectare blocks of vacant land. There are no big blocks of land floating around with no one interested in developing them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Retired psychologist loses $180k to deepfake romance scam
World.content:
NationalQueenslandScams Retired psychologist loses $180k to deepfake romance scam Davina Smith August 26, 2026 — 8:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Watching the video call between Michael and Melanie, it’s hard to believe one person isn’t real. The conversation flows back and forth, full of emotion and feelings. Michael, a retired psychologist in his 70s living in far north Queensland, believed he was speaking with Melanie, a softly spoken nurse in South Africa. The pair met over a dating app and courted the old-fashioned way – through words and correspondence, sharing their deepest thoughts, passions and fears. The deepfake image of a woman used to scam retired psychologist Michael out of $180,000. A Current Affair “She said she was only about 50 years of age, and getting somebody interested [in me], it was obviously flattering,” Michael told A Current Affair.



“My head said, this can’t be true, but my heart said I don’t want to abandon her.” It was a whirlwind 12-month long-distance romance, until Michael exposed Melanie as a deepfake: an online persona created through identity theft and artificial intelligence. Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when “Melanie” shared her identity documents. A Current Affair Scammers stole images from the social media profile of an American doctor, who had no knowledge of the scheme, combining them with YouTube videos she had created. Together with voice-cloning technology and the latest face-swapping applications, the fraudsters created a digital mask that they put on every time Michael dialled in to make a video call.



Dr Priyanka Singh, a specialist in digital forensics at the University of Queensland, analysed the final 10-minute break-up video call between the pair. She pointed out slight distortions in the woman’s earrings, and stray hairs as subtle clues that Melanie was not real, as the face-swapping software struggled to keep up with the actual fraudster’s movements. The scammers blamed these visual discrepancies on a poor internet connection. The gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand, which had an extra finger. A Current Affair Singh identified other major red flags, with Melanie’s chair changing shape and position during the call. At one point, it even disappears. For Singh, the gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand. For a fleeting moment, it appeared she had six fingers.



Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when Melanie shared her passport, South African identity card, and nurse registration certificate. He also received an influx of photos, some stolen from the American doctor’s website, and others photoshopped. And when Melanie needed financial help, Michael obliged. “I didn’t question that, and I was just really, probably, falling in love very quickly,” he said. “Being an empath, it’s very hard to look away.” Michael admitted he sent $180,000 to the scammers, despite warnings from his bank and its repeated attempts to block the transactions. “I was aware that I would take a big risk, but I thought, ‘meet the love of my life and my soulmate’,” he said while shedding tears. “It feels like I’ve been so stupid.”



Related Article Scams The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise Singh said rather than scrutinising increasingly sophisticated technology, the best test when meeting someone online was to seek the opinion of loved ones. In Michael’s case, his family, including his daughter, voiced concerns about Melanie very early in the relationship. “He’s lost a lot of dignity, self-respect and self-confidence,” she told A Current Affair. “Even if he wants to get out there again and find a partner, he’s now wary of this online dating world.”



Ultimately for Michael, revenge came when he confronted the scammers while recording a video call with Melanie. She had set up the meeting hoping to get a further $7000 out of the retiree. The 10-minute call is at times agonising to watch, as the fraudster tries to put doubt in Michael’s head, questioning his commitment to the relationship, his love for her, and even questioning if he is a fraud. Singh said it was a masterclass in how these romance scams play on emotions. When Michael accused Melanie of being a scammer and demanded she admit the fraud, the scammer hung up. Michael reported the case to New South Wales police, who conducted an investigation but concluded the scam was based overseas and it was unlikely he would recover the lost money.



As for his future finding love? “I stopped all my internet accounts ... the best way is to meet somebody in person, isn’t it?” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes
World.content:
Exclusive NationalInsects Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes Angus Dalton August 26, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Australian scientists have created insect-robot hybrids for search-and-rescue missions.

The cockroach cyborgs are designed to find people trapped in areas human rescuers can’t reach.

The cyborgs can fire syringes from their backs for emergency treatment.

Other teams have made diving suits for cockroaches so they can operate during floods.

The concept has been trialled in the aftermath of a deadly earthquake in Myanmar.

If you ever find yourself buried beneath the rubble of an earthquake’s aftermath or expiring in a remote cave, salvation may not arrive in the form of a dashing rescuer or detection dog, but of a hulking, hissing, spiky-legged cockroach. Scientists are developing cyborg paramedic cockroaches designed to find people trapped in places human rescuers can’t reach, with the latest recruits capable of delivering medicine by firing syringes from a harpoon system on their backs. A cyborg cockroach armed with a syringe-firing backpack. The University of Queensland The “paraborg” (a portmanteau of paramedic and cyborg) insects are made from giant burrowing cockroaches, which are the world’s heaviest cockroach species and native to north Queensland. “It’s not for everyone,” biorobotics specialist and cyborg creator Dr T. Thang Vo-Doan, from the University of Queensland, said of working with the cockroaches. “But we have very good relationship with them in the lab.”



The glossy arthropods are fashioned into cyborgs by the insertion of electrodes into their antennae, so the cockroaches can be remote-controlled with a joystick. Antennae detect obstacles, so when the left one is stimulated, the cockroaches bear right, and vice versa. Other electrodes in the “cerci” – sensory appendages at the back of the insect – allow researchers to accelerate or stop the cyborg roaches. Scientists eventually want to make fully robotic, insect-inspired rescue devices but Vo-Doan said robots aren’t small, agile or efficient enough yet to operate in disaster zones. Cockroaches, however, are ready to rumble.



“The insect can climb and run, even carry heavy loads in different orientations in a complex environment,” Vo-Doan said. “You already have everything from nature. It simplifies our system a lot in terms of design and engineering.” PhD student Hai Nhan Le remotely controls “paraborg” cockroaches. The University of Queensland He believes more lives can be saved now by harnessing the insects, with agility and efficiency honed by evolution, to carry devices including cameras and sensors into collapsed buildings. While small robots are restricted by limited battery life, cockroaches can go for days, powered simply by gum leaves and apple slices. There’s no requirement for scientists to obtain ethical approval for research with insects. But the cockroaches are anaesthetised for the insertion of electrodes, and electronic systems are carefully removed after experiments.



Vo-Doan said the cyborg recruits seem to live as long and well as their civilian counterparts. The latest study, published in Advanced Science, focused on the “rescue” part of search and rescue. If a swarm of cyborg cockroaches discovered a victim buried beneath rubble who was suffering from sepsis, what happens next? Cyborg cockroaches can traverse complex, rubble-strewn environments better than robots. The University of Queensland Enter the medic class. The researchers created and tested needle-firing cyborgs and showed they could successfully navigate to a target and deliver a jab in 72 per cent of proof-of-concept trials. When cockroaches came within 15 centimetres of a mock target, the hit rate was 95 per cent.



“A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them,” said PhD candidate and first author of the research Hai Nhan Le. “But if you’re trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death.” The idea, eventually, is to create a “fully autonomous paramedic team composed of terrestrial cyborg insects” that can independently search for victims, relay information and deliver medication, the researchers write. The concept might seem far-fetched but other international teams are taking the same approach and have been trialling it in the field.



Ten cyborg Madagascan hissing cockroaches fitted with infrared cameras and sensors were deployed alongside Singapore’s Operation Lionheart rescue team in the aftermath of a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar that killed at least 3600 people. (The cockroach squad didn’t detect any survivors but researchers said the mission yielded valuable lessons to improve the cyborgs.) Other researchers have made 3D-printed diving suits for cyborg cockroaches that could help in flood rescues. NTU Singapore Meanwhile, in June, another team of researchers introduced the aquatic class. They designed flexible cockroach diving suits 3D-printed from resin. Cockroaches wearing the suits could operate underwater for three hours despite being a terrestrial species, the researchers reported in Nature. The amphibious cyborgs could one day carry out missions in flooded areas or help explore the deep ocean – or other planets. “The ultimate goal is to [take this technology to] space,” lead author Professor Hirotaka Sato told New Scientist. “Exploration over the Mars surface, for example.”



Related Article Analysis

China relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics So when might we see cyborg cockroaches rolled out to disaster zones? Perhaps five years, perhaps 20, depending on the level of support the idea gains, Vo-Doan said. Experts such as Superintendent Tim Hassiotis, from Fire & Rescue NSW, are open to the concept if the cyborgs prove effective in real emergencies. “If cyborg insects can safely enter spaces we can’t, locate casualties and ultimately help deliver emergency care, they could become another valuable tool in the future of urban search and rescue,” Hassiotis said. World.title: How to leak a travel piece
World.content:
“Up early and reading an online story about British pubs by Herald travel expert Ben Groundwater, I was astounded to see two embedded ads for GROUNDWATER DRILLING SERVICES, illustrated with a gushing pipe,” notes Mark Southcott of Thirroul. “By 7.45, news of this vital service had gone – humans may have intervened to challenge the ad-matching computer – but should we warn Ben?”

“I was excited, as a teenager, to be taken to Parramatta RSL with my parents for a rare celebratory meal,” recalls Maureen Partridge of Baulkham Hills. “Just as our main courses arrived, two men approached and told us to ‘eat up as fast as you can and then leave’. Our sin? My World War II veteran father was wearing a collared shirt and jacket but no tie (C8). Sixty years later I still avoid clubs.”

“Seeing reference to needing to wear a tie to get into the Chatswood Charles in the ’60s brought back memories of a liquor licence law where you could only buy a drink after 8pm if you were having a meal,” says Ian Costley of Belrose. “The Charles provided a tiny paper plate with a fish finger, meat ball and minute vegetable item to satisfy the law, at a bargain price. Luckily, there was no requirement to actually eat it.”

“On a morning walk last week I smiled and said good morning to a young woman walking in the opposite direction,” reports Jim Pollitt of Wahroonga. “She also smiled and nodded, then, as she drew level, she said, ‘Do you need a change of clothing?’ Hurriedly checking myself for a possible wardrobe malfunction, I turned to ask her for clarification, only to notice the little ear buds and realise she was talking hands-free on her phone.”

Joe Moore of Blaxland shares his train of thought: “It was reported yesterday that rail passengers were ‘detrained’ after the failure of the Sydney rail network. I assume they were ‘retrained’ when the problems were resolved. Any late passengers would, of course, ‘mistrain’.”

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made its way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising. “The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Watching the video call between Michael and Melanie, it’s hard to believe one person isn’t real. The conversation flows back and forth, full of emotion and feelings. Michael, a retired psychologist in his 70s living in far north Queensland, believed he was speaking with Melanie, a softly spoken nurse in South Africa. The pair met over a dating app and courted the old-fashioned way – through words and correspondence, sharing their deepest thoughts, passions and fears. The deepfake image of a woman used to scam retired psychologist Michael out of $180,000. A Current Affair “She said she was only about 50 years of age, and getting somebody interested [in me], it was obviously flattering,” Michael told A Current Affair.



“My head said, this can’t be true, but my heart said I don’t want to abandon her.” It was a whirlwind 12-month long-distance romance, until Michael exposed Melanie as a deepfake: an online persona created through identity theft and artificial intelligence. Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when “Melanie” shared her identity documents. A Current Affair Scammers stole images from the social media profile of an American doctor, who had no knowledge of the scheme, combining them with YouTube videos she had created. Together with voice-cloning technology and the latest face-swapping applications, the fraudsters created a digital mask that they put on every time Michael dialled in to make a video call.



Dr Priyanka Singh, a specialist in digital forensics at the University of Queensland, analysed the final 10-minute break-up video call between the pair. She pointed out slight distortions in the woman’s earrings, and stray hairs as subtle clues that Melanie was not real, as the face-swapping software struggled to keep up with the actual fraudster’s movements. The scammers blamed these visual discrepancies on a poor internet connection. The gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand, which had an extra finger. A Current Affair Singh identified other major red flags, with Melanie’s chair changing shape and position during the call. At one point, it even disappears. For Singh, the gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand. For a fleeting moment, it appeared she had six fingers.



Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when Melanie shared her passport, South African identity card, and nurse registration certificate. He also received an influx of photos, some stolen from the American doctor’s website, and others photoshopped. And when Melanie needed financial help, Michael obliged. “I didn’t question that, and I was just really, probably, falling in love very quickly,” he said. “Being an empath, it’s very hard to look away.” Michael admitted he sent $180,000 to the scammers, despite warnings from his bank and its repeated attempts to block the transactions. “I was aware that I would take a big risk, but I thought, ‘meet the love of my life and my soulmate’,” he said while shedding tears. “It feels like I’ve been so stupid.”



Related Article Scams The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise Singh said rather than scrutinising increasingly sophisticated technology, the best test when meeting someone online was to seek the opinion of loved ones. In Michael’s case, his family, including his daughter, voiced concerns about Melanie very early in the relationship. “He’s lost a lot of dignity, self-respect and self-confidence,” she told A Current Affair. “Even if he wants to get out there again and find a partner, he’s now wary of this online dating world.”



Ultimately for Michael, revenge came when he confronted the scammers while recording a video call with Melanie. She had set up the meeting hoping to get a further $7000 out of the retiree. The 10-minute call is at times agonising to watch, as the fraudster tries to put doubt in Michael’s head, questioning his commitment to the relationship, his love for her, and even questioning if he is a fraud. Singh said it was a masterclass in how these romance scams play on emotions. When Michael accused Melanie of being a scammer and demanded she admit the fraud, the scammer hung up. Michael reported the case to New South Wales police, who conducted an investigation but concluded the scam was based overseas and it was unlikely he would recover the lost money.



As for his future finding love? “I stopped all my internet accounts ... the best way is to meet somebody in person, isn’t it?” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Dolly Parton, singer, songwriter, humanitarian, loved by all
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Dolly Parton, singer, songwriter, humanitarian, loved by all August 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. A bright light has gone out with the sad news of the death of one-of-a-kind exemplary musician and humanitarian Dolly Parton. And like many of her adoring fans worldwide, I have my favourite Parton tunes that thrum in my head when they’re played on the radio.

Notably, Parton leaves behind more than her formidable legacy of musicianship (and leading by example musical genre crossover for other musicians to follow her path), but what she gave back to her beloved community of humble origin, children (ie reading books) and to marginalised communities (ie LGBQTI and black) through some of the profits she turned with her hits.

Not to mention that Parton was one of the early atypical feminist role models in life, as in in fiction (9 to 5), demonstrating that women can be many things and need not ever ″⁣shrink″⁣ themselves to fit in any one prescribed box.

Needless to say, many people worldwide will always love Dolly Parton, as do I.

Jelena Rosic, Mornington Joining the great gig in the sky

Dolly Parton, you were the greatest. The essence of country music is ″⁣the cry in the voice″⁣, and you had it to perfection. Enjoy your reunion with all the other greats in Heaven. What a gig that will be.

Robert Scheffer, Bayswater North She was the real thing

In a world of egos and celebrities who are manufactured, Dolly Parton’s authenticity, philanthropy and, more importantly, her music and extraordinary songwriting united everyone.

Pam Papadopoulos, South Yarra



A light has faded in the world

I never thought that I would ever agree with a Donald Trump directive, but I stand corrected. I can certainly get behind his order for the American flag to be lowered across the United States for the next week in honour of Dolly Parton. There is a little less shine in the world now the legendary musician, singer, songwriter, actor, author and philanthropist has left us.

Rest in power, Dolly Parton. We shall not see the likes of you again.

Caryn Auld, Point Cook Inspiration for children to read

Dolly Parton was not just a great singer. She also helped children’s education and inspired millions to read with her book program. What an inspiration.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Success is measured in what is given back

It is difficult to think of many people who have combined extraordinary musical talent with such genuine generosity and humanity as Dolly Parton.

From humble beginnings, she built a remarkable career, yet fame and fortune have never seemed to diminish her warmth nor her concern for others.

Through her philanthropy, most notably her Imagination Library, Parton has helped put books into the hands of millions of children, quietly demonstrating that giving can be every bit as powerful as performing.

Her songs have touched generations. 9 to 5 gave working people an anthem with a smile, while Coat of Many Colours offered something far more profound – a reminder that love, dignity and family can be worth more than material wealth.

Dolly Parton has given us music, laughter and countless reasons to smile, but perhaps her greatest legacy is the goodness she has spread beyond the stage. In an age when celebrity can too often be measured in wealth, outrage and self-promotion, she reminds us that success is better measured by what we give back.

Long may she sing, and long may her generosity inspire us all.

Darren Grindrod, Glenroy THE FORUM Simply, madness

After five Sydney Swans players were stood down for the rest of the AFL season, one would have thought that ″⁣mad Monday″⁣ shenanigans would be suitably modified.

Unfortunately, it seems that was a false hope. Now there have been Richmond players behaving in a disgraceful way in public, including ″⁣appearing to urinate″⁣ against a fence (″⁣Tigers deny antics referenced Swans″⁣, 26/8).

But, hey, they’re footballers, so the commentary will no doubt be along the lines of ″⁣boys will be boys″⁣. Trouble is, they are not boys, they are adults who must know that their actions on this day, would be seen.

Columnist Jenna Price (Comment, 26/8) writes it always seems to be women who have to point out bad behaviour, and men who fail to recognise that there is any kind of problem. Sadly, it seems that not much has changed.

Ruth Hudspeth, Burwood



Not so wise

The Richmond Tigers players’ actions on “mad Monday” remind me of Lord Chesterfield’s statement to his son: “Young men are apt to think themselves wise enough; just as drunken men are apt to think themselves sober enough.“

Howard Hutchins, Wantirna Unreal v real

Reported experiences such as “melding”, “embeddedness”, “boundlessness” of people taking hallucinogens such as psilocybin are not new (“What brain does on magic mushrooms”, 26/8). But they should be reminders these types of mind-altering drugs don’t play well in the real world.

In the real world, psychological and physical boundaries exist between oneself and other people and other objects and for very good reason.

To fail to adhere to the many boundaries that exist can lead to harm (for example, physical such as not keeping to the speed limit when driving a car) or other potential offences (psychological such as various forms of disinhibited behaviours or “boundary violations” in social or intimate settings).

So while medical researchers continue to explore potential therapeutic benefits of hallucinogens, their dangers in real world usage should not be minimised at all or overlooked.

Dr Larry Hermann, consultant psychiatrist, South Yarra Wrong housing approach

I generally admire Shane Wright’s economic analyses. However, his news article, “Warning slump in house prices will drag on until 2028” (26/8), says everything about what’s wrong with our current approach to housing.

Surely, the best thing for correcting the current inequity in access to housing – a basic human right – would be if the current “slump” continued for some time.

Perhaps a better headline would be, “Lower house prices to persist until at least 2028”, with an article highlighting the benefits of lower prices for social cohesion to follow. Vivienne Kane, Hawthorn

Queue around the bloc

I don’t know anyone my age (60+) who would be happy waiting in a long queue to buy something or wait for a restaurant table. This is a generational trait. However, the article, “Brands tap into psychology of queue culture” (24/8), took me back to a very different time and place in communist Hungary when queueing, shortages and black markets were a normal part of life. When visiting, I, too, jumped in queues for who knows what?

On one occasion, word had got out that Cuban oranges had arrived in the small country town I was in and so it was queue to buy this rarity or go without.

In those days, consumer sovereignty didn’t rule and there wasn’t an abundance of popular, trendy goods, except in the Dollar shops.

So, while queueing today is seen as social, fun and on trend by some, back then in Eastern bloc countries, it was one of the few ways (other than black markets) to get necessities and desirable goods in short supply. Queues draw us in, but in a different time and place, for very different reasons.

Marg Wilson, Brighton Help the birds more

As Cathy Wilcox’s cartoon powerfully demonstrates (25/8), it is distressing to see wild birds and a seal already dead from bird flu (“First mainland mammal dies from bird flu”, 24/8). This virus has devastated wildlife across the globe, wiping out more than 50 per cent of some bird populations and hundreds of thousands of marine mammals.

Here in Australia, where BirdLife Australia reports that one in six bird species are threatened, scientists warn that H5N1 could have extinction-level impacts.

We have known for years that the H5N1 virus would eventually reach our shores (“Bird flu threat sparks urgent wildlife vaccine push as virus keeps spreading”, 16/8). And our wildlife is already under pressure from habitat destruction and climate change.

Could the Albanese government be investing more to give our precious wildlife a fighting chance?

Karin Ruff, Yanakie Right to protest

Melbourne Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece is worried that people aren’t coming into the city because of protest activity (″⁣Lord Mayor says one in three graffiti reports ‘antisemitic’ ″⁣, 25/8) . He is no doubt concerned about lost revenue to business. We need to remember that the protests are peaceful, and, importantly, people have the right to protest in a democracy.

And we need to remember the reasons for these protests. The people who turn out to support Palestine are protesting against civilian deaths, crimes against humanity, the deplorable treatment of prisoners and the destruction of homes, olive groves and hospitals. How can we weigh people’s right to shop against the fact that according to the Gaza Ministry of Health, Israeli operations in Gaza have killed 1286 people since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year?

Elizabeth O’Connor, Ivanhoe East



China shows off

I fail to grasp the point of the so-called robot humanoid ″⁣Games″⁣ in Beijing other than an opportunity for China to display to the world how incredibly advanced their freaky robots have become.

That one of them ran 100 metres faster than Olympic champion Usain Bolt is just China showing-off. Bolt shouldn’t feel badly; he’s still got his gold medals.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Trade off and lose

Ross Gittins explains, in an understandable way, something many of us thought was always suspect (“Labor’s carbon credit scheme fails to stack up”, 26/8). Allowing firms to obtain carbon credits was probably well intentioned, but was always going to be open to self-interested manipulation by business.

Similarly, “safeguard mechanisms” which cap emissions of large polluters: If they breach these, they have to buy a “carbon offset” to compensate.

What all this means, of course, is that polluting emissions can continue if you have enough wealth to buy credits.

This is not a meaningful way to reduce emissions.

This trade-off is now even more important to consider, given that we are witnessing firms jostling to build data centres, usually in areas too close to populations (“Environmental watchdog challenges data centre over noise fears”, 26/8). Apart from noise pollution, these centres consume huge amounts of electricity and water. Once again, there are meant to be safeguards, but already citizen rights are being ignored because the Planning Minister, Sonya Kilkenny, makes the ultimate decision without having to take account of bodies such as the Environment Protection Authority. What sort of world are we entering into?

Jan Marshall, Brighton Obstacle to progress

Columnist Ross Gittins’ critique of carbon credit and offset systems is on the money (“Labor’s carbon credit scheme fails to stack up”, 26/8). Real climate action requires slashing pollution from coal, oil and gas, ending land clearing, and restoring carbon-rich ecosystems — all at the same time.

Offsetting burnt coal and gas by protecting a tree is at best problematic and at worst a dangerous crutch undermining progress. When will the Albanese government strengthen the Safeguard Mechanism climate policy and ensure carbon accounting reflects reality rather than wishful thinking?

Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn Assumptions made

Ross Gittins’ column reminds me of a joke my mother used to tell about an engineer and an economist who fall down a mine shaft. The engineer fossicks around for materials to build a ladder. The economist says: “Let’s assume there is a ladder.“

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha An elongated idea

A great idea from your correspondent that if Elon Musk invented a car that returned itself to its owner after it’s been stolen, it could be called “the Homer” (Letters, 26/8). And if it took a really, really, really long time to find its way back, it could be called “the Odysseus”.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East



Decentralise option

Building up or out should not be the question. Whatever happened to decentralisation? Regional cities have decent public transport to Melbourne. Bendigo, Ballarat and Geelong, for example, have better access to the airport than many suburbs. Good planning for industry, education, immigration, health and other infrastructure ought to include the rest of Victoria, not just Melbourne.

Pete Dunne, Highett Such iconography

Thanks to your correspondent (Letters, 26/8) for his iconic letter bemoaning the fact that he cannot find anything that is not iconic. It’s certainly a legendary observation – quintessential, really.

Geoff Allen, Parkdale Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Data

As the world warms, increasing the demands on water and power, who or what gets priority access

to cooling: people or data centres (″⁣EPA’s data centre warning″⁣, 26/8)?

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hills



Be it a gold rush or data centre rush, it’s a sure thing the environment comes out worse. More power to the Environment Protection Authority’s arm.

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton I don’t understand what artificial intelligence is and what data centres do. I do, though, have a bad feeling about all of it.

John Rawson, Mernda I asked AI whether huge data centres would create environmental problems but was reassured all would be OK.

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West Robot games! What next, Russian robot soldiers, fighting Ukrainian robot soldiers? Hang on, that might not be such a bad thing.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East AFL

That’s it for me. Swans, now Tiges. No more interest in the AFL. I’ll follow and watch the women’s competition, but not the men’s games. Bonus is that I’ll have less gambling promos to ignore.

Barry Greer, Balnarring Beach



Mark McVeigh proposes to get all the Essendon supporters – an ″⁣armada″⁣ – behind the club. I thought a group of a ships is an armada whereas a group of bombers is a squadron?

Lindsay Donahoo, Wattle Glen Furthermore

Bravo Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney (″⁣Trump’s bulldozer approach no match for Canada’s stance″⁣, 25/8). Give Carney a special peace prize for anti-bullying.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff I have been a rusted-on Labor supporter since the Vietnam War days. The proposal to reduce the rebate on private health insurance cover for over-65s means my vote will be going elsewhere for the first time in 60 years. Kevin Drinan, Bentleigh A song lyric goes, ″⁣Well, hello, Dolly″⁣. Sadly, it is now ″⁣goodbye, Dolly″⁣.

Gerry Lonergan, Reservoir

World.title: Person assaulted, vehicle shot at after car crash between Toyota and Volkswagen
World.content:
A person has been seriously assaulted and a vehicle shot at following a crash in South Auckland, police say.

They said a Toyota and a Volkswagen crashed about 5.10pm on Ronwood Road in Manukau.

Senior Sergeant Aji Basra said an occupant of the Toyota was then reportedly assaulted by occupants of the Volkswagen.

Police believed a firearm was also discharged, damaging the Toyota.

"Two people received minor injuries, one of which required medical attention and has self-transported to hospital.

"The victims are understandably shaken by the incident, and we are providing them with support."

The offenders left the area in the Volkswagen before police arrived, and in tandem with a Nissan, Basra said.

The Volkswagen was found abandoned on Cavendish Drive, and police believe the offenders continued on in the Nissan.

Their enquiries were continuing.

Serious injuries after Far North crash

Meanwhile, Far North police said it appeared there were serious injuries after a two-vehicle crash in the rural locality of Peria.

Emergency services were called to Oruru Road, near Jason Road, about 8pm.

World.title: Landlord not aware of any issues with pool's gate before child's death
World.content:
The landlord of an Auckland property where toddler drowned says he was not aware of any issues with a pool's gate prior to the child's death.

River Albert-Wihone had only recently turned one when he was found in the backyard pool at his family's Lynfield home. He was taken to Starship Children's Hospital where he died in his mother's arms 12 days later.

The property's landlord Vinesh Natali gave evidence to Coroner Alison Mills at Auckland District Court on Wednesday.

The court was told Natali mostly lived overseas while property management company Crockers looked after the home for the majority of the family's tenancy. However, a different agent took over in the months leading up to River's death.

Natali was questioned by a lawyer assisting the coroner, and also by counsel representing River's grandmother Christine Robinson, who was the main tenant of the home used by multiple generations of the family.

Wednesday's hearing focused on the events of January 2022, when Natali - through Crockers - arranged for fences to be built around the pool in order to comply with new regulations.

Natali said that during conversations with Robinson around the time the pool fence was put up in January 2022, he was not made aware of her concerns about the gate.

"She said poor workmanship and so on. I don't think it was specific to the gate opening or closing, or which direction it was opening or closing," Natali said.

He said he told Robinson that Crockers managed the project and any workmanship concerns should be left with the contractors who carried out the work.

The conversation ended there, he said.

Natali said that after construction was completed the fence passed Auckland Council compliance checks in February 2022.

Earlier, the inquest heard that the pool had failed compliance inspections over a period of four years prior to the family moving there in 2020.

A man from a fencing company who examined the pool fence gave evidence that the tragedy could have been avoided if the gate had been installed with better quality hinges and latches.

Natali was questioned by lawyer Danielle Kelly about whether he'd had any input into the products selected for the job.

"Do you have any comment about concern to keep the cost down? Were you concerned to keep the cost as low as possible?" Kelly asked.

"No, I think as long as the costs were reasonable," Natali replied.

"I don't think I set a clear budget for it either, it was what the cost came in, it looked reasonable."

Lawyer Lucy Wright, acting for River's grandmother, asked Natali about a message he had sent to her client about the construction of the pool fence, in which he had said: "Whatever is cheaper."

"Whichever is cheaper doesn't mean it's cheap cheap," Natali said.

"It's a cost benefit as well, it doesn't mean because it's supposed to be cheap, you go and do the cheapest element. We would obviously look at what would be the most cost effective option that was going to be put in," he explained.

Asked about the pool's history of non-compliance, Natali said Crockers started managing his property in 2015, and that they would tell him if any repairs over $200 were required.

River's grandmother Christine Robinson earlier told the inquest she had raised concerns about the pool fence in January 2022, including an intermittent fault with the gate.

Robinson said she had raised this with the builder, with Crockers and with Natali, but she felt that her concerns fell on deaf ears.

Natali was asked if he knew about landlords' obligation to ensure the safety of the swimming pools even if after they've passed compliance checks.

"I would've relied on Crockers to continue to check it in every visit or whatever that they did at the time," he replied.

Natali was asked if, with the benefit of hindsight, he thought he had an obligation to test the pool gate during an inspection he did in October 2023, a month before River's death.

"Possibly," Natali replied.

After Wednesday's hearing, Natali released a statement to RNZ:

World.title: National and Labour spar over how to help struggling NZers get ahead
World.content:
National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds have sparred over their approaches to help struggling New Zealanders get ahead.

The finance spokespeople were speaking at the Politik election summit on Wednesday.

Politik editor Richard Harman had asked Willis and Edmonds to lay out their economic vision, and what they saw as the context for the election campaign.

The pair agreed the economy was not where they wanted it to be, and their challenge was to create the economic conditions to help "mum and dad" get ahead.

Edmonds spoke about her own electorate of Mana, where she said people could no longer afford the "slap up meal" of mince on toast, with prices rising excessively.

Willis said it was irresponsible of Edmonds to say she was focused on the price of mince, "unless you have a policy to address the price of mince, and I haven't heard that from the Labour Party".

National's approach to help people get ahead was to control inflation, she said.

Edmonds said that did not cut it.

"When you know what it's like to only have $8 in your hand and you are sweating when you take your car to get a warrant of fitness ... It is really difficult to speak to people and say, 'well, we're going to work on the economy here, and eventually that'll help trickle down'."

Edmonds said Labour was focused on making other things cheaper for people, pointing to its policies to cap public transport fares and offer three free GP visits.

She also referenced the former Labour government's pay equity scheme, "which was to help our lowest paid women who look after our babies, look after our grandparents in the retirement homes, who are the plunket nurses, who are the midwives."

The National-led government tightened the scheme considerably, making it harder for people in female-dominated workforces to apply to be paid on par with men doing similar jobs.

The debate descended over that, with Willis and Edmonds speaking over each other to get their points across.

"The fact now that they cannot apply for a pay equity claim to help lift their wages, that's terrible," said Edmonds.

Willis said that was not true, and women could still apply.

"Good luck finding the $11 billion (to pay for the scheme)," she said.

"We don't think it's the government's job to fund pay settlement for private sector businesses ... your position is that the taxpayer in Porirua who can't afford mince on toast should be paying more tax so that Ryman Healthcare can get a pay equity subsidy."

Edmonds responded: "Those Ryman Healthcare workers, if the market was working, why are they on the minimum wage?"

They also had a tit-for-tat over Labour's campaign policy to slim down the government's Investment Boost, which allows businesses to deduct 20 percent of the cost of a new asset, over depreciation.

Labour would target it to small businesses only.

Willis said Edmonds had supported Investment Boost, and suggested the Labour finance spokesperson had lost an argument with leader Chris Hipkins over the policy.

Edmonds said there was no debate between her and Hipkins about repurposing Investment Boost.

"Yes, it's a good policy, but my policy is better, so that's where we've left it," she said.

But Willis said it had been a "frustrating debate" and a "phony war" with Labour which she said had continued attacking the government but not offered up its own fixes.

However Willis said that war ended on Sunday when Labour "finally" announced its fiscal strategy to increase spending to 33 percent, which she calculated would see every New Zealander pay $100 more in taxes each week.

World.title: 'It's extraordinary how things change' - NZ election strategies dissected at summit
World.content:
For Labour to have a shot at government, it needs Opportunity to get five or zero percent at November's election, the party's campaign chair says.

Kieran McAnulty says anything between that would mean the Opportunities vote is distributed amongst parties that do make it into parliament.

The comments were made at a conference today, alongside a wider discussion by pollsters on where voters are at a little more than 2 months out from the election, and come after the most recent RNZ Reid Research poll had the Opportunity party as kingmaker.

The conference also featured prominent political figures involved in previous coalition negotiations, offering insights into how they are planned and executed, including the selection of biscuits and how not to disrespect New Zealand First leader Winston Peters.

The 'Politik Election Summit 2026: Navigating a Disrupted Electorate' took place in Wellington on Wednesday.

It featured a range of speakers including political strategists and politicians as well as a keynote from Kosmos Samara, an Australian lobbyist and pollster who described the political landscape across the ditch with the rise of One Nation.

He said One Nation was tapping into voters' concerns about the cost of living, and particularly with Generation X - those born between 1965 and 1980 - while younger, more diverse and more educated voters were more likely to steer clear of the party.

He also discussed how anybody consuming Australian news media might think immigration was a key issue, but said "it just isn't".

He described how the conservative parties - who were losing votes to One Nation - thought immigration was the issue and were doubling down on that narrative.

"They are creating a problem and responding to a problem that doesn't exist."

Polling

Tim Hurdle, a former National senior adviser, consultant and director of several companies, and David Talbot, a pollster and director at Talbot Mills Research both presented polling information heading into the election.

Hurdle, using polling information from Freshwater, showed how parties had been faring since the last election, with National on a downward trajectory after a post-election lift, the rise of New Zealand First and a "redemption arc" for Labour.

His take on the rise of Opportunity was that their vote was coming "a bit" out of Labour.

Talbot - using Talbot Mills Research data, who poll for the Labour party - also spoke about the state of the electorate.

Talbot said on his numbers, Opportunity holds the balance of power. He said the left bloc was dominant in 2025 with a centre-right block in 2026, "although overwhelmingly driven by Winston's rise rather than any strength in the national vote".

His prediction was that Opportunity was going to "get there" in terms of reaching the threshold, and their vote was coming "pretty equally off the left and the right blocks".

"After 10 days of media coverage, our tracking had them well above five really quickly.

"They will probably continue to get attention in the campaign, and that will help them drive that momentum," he said later.

Both Hurdle and Talbot were also asked about National's strategy of attacking Labour on tax.

Hurdle said National had gone "very aggressive very early", which he said was a risky tactic.

"You can only use the same message so much, and it starts to wear off."

Campaign plans

National Party campaign chair Simeon Brown also spoke at the conference too describing National's strategy and reiterating the well-practiced line of "fixing the basics and building the future".

He also took another opportunity to attack Labour with the notion of "nine new taxes".

Brown said tax was going to be a "key issue" this election. Asked whether the party had gone too early on the attack, Brown said New Zealanders wanted clarity on where National stood.

He getting the Prime Minister out and about for public meetings was another key strategy.

When asked about Luxon's lower favourability ratings and whether the party would adjust their strategy due to that, Brown said Luxon was "absolutely central" to the campaign, but that there was a "great team of ministers" who would also play a role.

Meanwhile, Labour's Kieran McAnulty began by saying "unexpectedly, we've got a genuine shot here" about Labour's chances at the election.

He acknowledged that "currently" both the left and right blocs required Opportunity to be able to govern, and it would be "fascinating" to see if that remained the case throughout the campaign.

McAnulty addressed the National party's tax attacks, saying "the traditional attacks on a capital gains tax haven't landed, and so they're moving into that sort of territory".

Asked about Opportunity, he said Labour either needed them to receive enough votes to enter parliament, or no votes at all.

Ultimately, he said Labour would have to play the cards its dealt.

"A three-party coalition is only three years ago unprecedented, and now it's probably the preferred option. It's extraordinary how things change."

Coalition negotiations

Three experienced political advisors and strategists also presented their experience when it came to coalition negotiations.

Long-time National Party chief of staff Wayne Eagleson - who served Sir John Key, Sir Bill English and Don Brash - spoke alongside Neale Jones, who was chief of staff to Labour leader Jacinda Ardern and former leader Andrew Little, and Stuart Wilson who was specialist ministerial adviser to Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour.

Discussing how negotiations begin once the numbers are in after an election, Eagleson said he would be "staggered" if parties were not doing the legwork already.

During the 2011, 2014 and 2017 elections, Eagleson said National was "wargaming it" as early as six months before the election.

That included being clear on what National wanted to achieve and watching carefully what potential coalition partners or confidence and supply partners were after.

"Bottom lines are a massive pain in the arse.

"I understand why people like talking about it, but inside political parties, I think there's a lot less talk about about that."

He described needing to stick to your values, but also being aware of things "you're prepared to trade".

"You don't want to get yourself boxed in the corner."

He discussed the political landscape being different, "we never really seriously looked at coalitions" during his time, but the numbers were different now he said, "with the fragmentation, and that does change it".

Eagleson said National had a pretty good sense of what NZ First and Peters wanted in 2017, because work had been done ahead of time and because: "Winston has been a remarkably consistent political figure for a long period of time."

Jones described the time in 2017 where Jacinda Ardern took over, changing Labour's fortunes. But once Labour got to the negotiating table, Jones described Peters' not wanting to hear the Greens' name mentioned.

"We were not to tell them what we were negotiating, and they had to sign on to it. We had to say to the Greens, 'we are signing an agreement with New Zealand First that you must adhere to, and you have to trust us'."

Jones said building that level of trust through opposition meant they were able to have not just the personal, but also the professional working relationships.

"Had we not done that, we may not have got it across the line."

Jones said Peters was in charge of the 2017 negotiations "on both sides." Jones confirmed that considerations about the type of biscuits were important.

"He [Peters] dictated where we met, when we met, and I vaguely recall the biscuits and the catering him having a strong view on."

Eagleson echoed this, saying because Peters could go "either way" he "drove the room".

"He drove the layout of the room, he largely drove the agenda. He certainly, I'm sure he did drive the biscuits and the opportunity for a 10-minute break to duck out every now and again," he said, to laughs in the room.

Jones also said they were "always careful not to be disrespectful of Winston Peters", and not getting on his bad side.

Jones said even on a Sunday afternoon, "we'd be showing up with a suit and tie, because we knew that we didn't want to blow the coalition negotiations because Winston thought we looked scruffy".

Wilson added that minor parties did not like to be called minor parties.

He said Peters reacted badly in negotiations when he felt he was been disrespected.

"That's probably the same with Seymour, just a different way."

He then discussed the key elements of keeping the coalition together for a three year period was relationships and structures, and what sanctions can be applied as a minor party to the major party to keep those in line, as well as the sanctions the prime minister could apply to the minor party leader and their ministers

World.title: ACT MP Mark Cameron concedes he's 'stuffed' due to health issues in his valedictory speech
World.content:
An ACT MP who is leaving Parliament due to ill health said he's conceded he's "stuffed", and urged MPs to continue fighting for farmers.

Mark Cameron and former Health Minister Dr Shane Reti delivered their valedictory speeches at Parliament on Wednesday.

Cameron was leaving Parliament after six years, saying kidney failure, acute heart failure, and his son's death to suicide had taken their toll.

"We all have our s..., as we say in rural New Zealand, and I have certainly had my fill," he said.

Cameron recalled deciding he was going to "carry the world on his shoulders" despite his poor health.

"I remember fairly recently sitting in the chamber, house duty, nauseous, kidneys at 8 percent - most of you wouldn't have known this - bugger all left," he said.

"I conceded that I was stuffed."

But Parliament and farmers had given him a purpose, he said.

"I needed to carry on, so I did dialysis in my flat, and I went back to bloody work."

That was despite knowing his time as an MP would be cut short eventually, he said.

"We agreed farmers needed to be kept out of the ETS, methane limits reduced, private freshwater assets managed better and in the hands of owners, and stupid winter grazing rules fixed," Cameron said.

"At 8 percent kidney function, I could be a passenger in this reality, or a proponent for better outcomes and change. So here I am."

Cameron urged MPs to believe in rural people.

"They're worth fighting for, they are the economic spine of this country.

"And remember this, it is always hard to argue that fact when your mouth is full of their food."

He thanked his party leader David Seymour - a "bloody legend" - and its deputy Nicole McKee, "an awesome sister, the one I wished I'd always had".

Reti's speech followed after.

Dr Shane Reti. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He was the MP for Whangārei - the first Māori to win the seat - and had been in Parliament since 2014.

Reti served as National's deputy leader under Judith Collins, and was health minister this term, before being demoted in January last year - replaced by Simeon Brown - when health became an increasingly problematic area for the government.

Reti detailed his highlights throughout the years, and most recently as Health Minister, which included the medical school at Waikato hospital, "the biggest funding increase ever in cancer drugs", and extending the breast cancer screening age group from 70 to 74.

But he had unfinished business, too, he said.

"To the fizzy drinks industry, I was coming for you, and you knew it."

Reti said he had been working on a policy to stop the industry adding more sugar to their drinks in New Zealand, versus Australia which had 40 to 50 percent less sugar.

"I say to the fizzy drink industry: Please explain why you have been deliberately sugaring up New Zealanders, and then reformulate to at least the baseline in Australia."

Reti said serving the people of Whangārei had been a privilege, and thanked his colleagues and family.

World.title: Flu vaccine to be free for all under fives
World.content:
The flu vaccine will be free to all under fives from next year.

Doctors had been calling for the vaccine to be fully funded, with this year's influenza strain causing a big spike in infections.

Children under five had by far the biggest rates of hospitalisation, particularly Māori and Pasifika tamariki.

Pharmac chief pharmaceuticals advisor Adrienne Martin said the change meant next winter about 260,000 more children would be eligible from aged six months until their fifth birthday.

"This will help protect young children and their whānau against influenza and will reduce the impact of seasonal flu on our communities, and the wider health system," she said.

Currently flu vaccines were only free for under fives if they had been hospitalised with respiratory illnesses or had other diseases like diabetes, asthma or a heart condition.

The change would not be in time for this year's flu season.

Martin said that was because it would take time to get the supplies.

"Ordering and manufacturing flu vaccine happens many months before the start of the flu season," she said.

"Vaccines take a long time to make and ship to New Zealand, so manufacturers can't always make more product during the flu season if demand is higher than forecast."

Martin said two new influenza vaccines were being funded for the first time, a cell-based vaccine and an adjuvanted vaccine, and will provide increased protection compared with the currently funded egg-based influenza vaccines.

"We are also widening access to a pneumococcal vaccine to help prevent people who have already had a serious infection from getting it again.

"This will give the 700 people who will be eligible for this vaccine each year much needed reassurance and protection."

The Ministry of Health's Dr Andrew Old, said the influenza vaccine changes will help strengthen the country's defences against flu next season.

"I would also encourage those who haven't had a flu vaccine this season to consider getting vaccinated. Flu cases are on the rise and this year's vaccine still offers the best available protection against current strains for people, their friends and families this winter."

The influenza vaccine changes come into effect from the start of next year's influenza season on 1 April 2027. Changes to meningococcal, pneumococcal and all other vaccines take effect from 1 July.

National Hauora Coalition clinical director Dr Nina Bevin told Checkpoint changes to flu vaccinations were needed a year ago, before this year's flu season started.

Under fives to be eligible for free flu vaccines next year Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Bevin said the 59 practices across the coalition's network were all under the pump.

"I was talking to one GP working in South Auckland, and she said Monday was their biggest day in history. She said they were slammed with 146 walk-ins and 89 people waiting for phone triage, and that's on top of their normal booked patients."

Bevin said they are "reaching the limits" of clinical safety.

GP colleagues had written a letter on behalf of the Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners asking Health New Zealand to immediately fund access to flu vaccines, especially for tamariki under five, she said.

World.title: NZ First candidate steps down after earlier shopping himself around to other parties
World.content:
A NZ First candidate has stepped down just a month after being announced as a candidate, after confirming he had earlier shopped himself around to other parties.

George Ngatai was announced as New Zealand First's Papakura candidate in July, but has said "after careful consideration" he had decided to step down.

He admitted that he had communicated with other parties, but no meetings took place.

"Earlier this year there was a period of considerable uncertainty about whether I would have the opportunity to stand as a candidate," his statement said.

"It was personally disappointing and, during that period, I considered what other options might exist."

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live on Thursday morning purportedly show "Uncle George Ngatai" referring to the party as "Winston Peters first and then Shane first," and another discussing whether to run for ACT.

"ACT have 2 MPs not returning. They have 11 MPs and expect to get 10 in this year. We need to be in the top 10. If I get the nod then I will start and support. Then my role is to prep you to replace me after a term."

"See if David will consider list for a strong Maori who is more pakeha than pakeha in thinking," another message said.

Other messages show Ngatai being introduced to ACT leader David Seymour and Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong.

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live. Screenshot

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live. Screenshot

Seymour told reporters on Wednesday he remembered getting a message, but did not think it went anywhere.

"If you want to stand for the ACT Party, it's almost like trying to get into the SAS these days, and I don't think he would have made it," he said.

"We test our candidates on what they believe, and it sounds like this guy just believed anything as long as it got him into Parliament."

Ngatai's statement said "a member of his team" Martel Wikeepa had made contact with people outside New Zealand First, and while some private communications occurred about "possible alternatives," it never developed into a meeting or commitment by Ngatai to another political party.

Wikeepa runs the Shubz Live account.

On Wednesday, Radio Aotearoa - a station owned by Ngatai and his wife Raewyn Bhana - announced an "indefinite stand-down" of Shubz's show.

New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones referred questions on what he described as "the woes of George Ngatai" to the party.

"It's a tad above the Matua's paygrade. But it sounds as if he bought the same parachute as Mr Stu Nash."

RNZ has contacted New Zealand First for a response.

World.title: 'Modern day slavery': Gloriavale leavers file $40m lost wages and entitlements claim against Overseeing Shepherd
World.content:
A group of 61 Gloriavale leavers has filed Employment Relations Authority claims against the Christian community's Overseeing Shepherd for lost wages, entitlements, compensation and damages totalling almost $40 million for work they say amounted to modern day slavery.

In applications lodged on Wednesday, the former Gloriavale members said the Overseeing Shepherd failed to provide them with minimum basic employment entitlements including wages, holiday pay, compulsory KiwiSaver contributions, parental leave and written individual employment agreements.

They want compensation for breach of the statutory duty of good faith and breach of contract and have sought leave to raise personal grievances out of time because of a lack of knowledge about their employment rights and the failure of the Labour Inspectorate.

Lawyers Brian Henry (L) and Stephen Patterson (R), who represent former members of the Gloriavale Christian Community. LOUIS DUNHAM / RNZ

"For applicants work conditions amounted to modern day slavery, including forced child labour, forced labour and servitude in breach of the Employment Relations Act and New Zealand's international human rights treaty obligations," the documents said.

"For most of their working life in Gloriavale the applicants were trapped.

"The applicants did not enjoy a good faith employment relationship but were in a sustained exploitative employment environment."

The legal action followed two landmark Employment Court rulings in 2022 and 2023 that found three men and six women were Gloriavale employees, rather than volunteers, working in factories, on farms or on the community's domestic teams.

Former Gloriavale member Ruby Trust at a press conference on Wednesday.

The court found the women were required to work from a young age, work was effectively assigned from birth and they had no real choice about working on the teams in Gloriavale's commercial-sized kitchen and laundry.

They were required to obey male leaders in a patriarchal community with a strict hierarchy and worked "extremely hard" under "punishing conditions", leaving "deep scars", the court said.

In the men's case, the court found that they were employees from the age of six until they left Gloriavale, ready access to child labour was a significant factor in the success of the community's business model and none of them had a choice as to if and where they worked.

They were subjected to rigorous, sometimes violent supervision in their work and were hit if they were not working hard or fast enough, with some children denied food and publicly shamed.

The nine former members previously lodged claims for lost wages and compensation totalling $5.2 million.

Documents filed with the authority on behalf of the other 61 leavers said they lived in the same controlled, authoritarian environment that did not permit dissenting voices and compelled obedience through fear, including the requirement to work from an early age.

As children they were required to leave school to work and worked hard over excessively long hours without statutory rest and meal breaks, the applications said.

Gloriavale leaver Anna Courage. RNZ/LouisDunham

They worked in an environment that was dangerous for many, where serious accidents happened, were subjected to an emotional and psychological discipline regime and depended on the community for accommodation, food and other necessities of life.

The documents said the former members were taught from an early age that if they did not work they did not eat and disobedience could result in a feared Shepherds and Servants disciplinary meeting.

At the age of 16 they were required to join Gloriavale's Christian Partners and were told where, when and for whom they would work.

"They received money into their bank account (which they had no control over) for labour services provided, from which it would immediately be taken out and put into the Gloriavale sharing account," the documents said.

The applications said the former members were Gloriavale employees who worked under coercion, did not receive remuneration, annual leave entitlements, rest breaks, compulsory employer KiwiSaver contributions or an employment agreement and worked on public holidays.

They have asked the Employment Relations Authority to order payment for lost wages, with deductions for board and food, holiday pay, KiwiSaver contributions, compensation for failing to provide rest and meal breaks, parental leave, a written individual employment agreement, breach of the statutory duty of good faith, breach of contract and hurt and humiliation under personal grievance claims.

The leavers were also seeking exemplary damages because of the "flagrancy" of the conduct and interest on wage arrears.

Barrister Brian Henry said the leavers were Gloriavale employees and were entitled to wages.

"They were denied wages, denied holidays, worked horrific hours and this is the consequence of someone who creates a business model based on child labour. Eventually it catches up with them," he said.

"There is millions and millions of dollars worth of free labour that this organisation has enjoyed and that was illegal."

'Treated like a slave'

Leaver Ruby Trust said she was treated like a slave.

"They say we had a choice but what choice do you get from being born in there with no knowledge of whether or no we were allowed to say yes? We were always taught from a young age that if we didn't work, we would go to hell, we were sinning, we were going against God.

"It was drilled into us from a very young age. What other than slavery is that? They didn't actually give us a choice."

Barrister Stephen Patterson said he calculated that 41 per cent of the men involved in the claims had a debilitating, life-long injuries, including hands crushed in machines, amputated fingers and scalded arms and legs, while many women suffered back problems.

"That's a ratio that should not be occurring in New Zealand in a workplace," he said.

Gloriavale has been contacted for comment.

In May the Employment Court ruled that the clock started ticking on the statutory six-year time limit for wage arrears claims when the nine men and women found to have been Gloriavale employees left the community and experienced the outside world and employment law norms.

While the former members were outside the 90-day timeframe for raising a personal grievance, chief judge Christina Inglis noted they were entitled to apply for leave to do so out of time, with their age and Gloriavale's "uniquely prohibitive circumstances" of potential relevance.

In separate court proceedings, the nine leavers were also seeking damages and declarations of slavery and servitude following an August ruling that the Labour Inspectorate made legal errors in two employment investigations in 2017 and 2021.

Inglis found the Labour Inspectorate misunderstood its jurisdiction and failed to consider children.

"The context of this case involves forced child labour, workplace abuse and servitude," she said.

The inspectorate's 2017 "desktop inquiry" noted that if Gloriavale members were considered employees "there would inevitably be many serious breaches of employment law".

In 2023 Gloriavale members told the Employment Court the community could not afford to pay everyone wages and employment relationships would destroy their Christian way of life.

World.title: Live: Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney head to ring for world title eliminator
World.content:
Both men exchange a couple of shots that rattle the heads of the man in front of them.

Wells is holding the power well, and the poise despite the brutal shots to the body.

BANG! There's a left hook to the body.

TWO MORE! Oh my word! Wells looks like a classical god, so conditioned is he, but those sorts of shots would surely even break granite.

Wells is taking those shots so well given the power with which they are coming in, Peters is having a big of a break.

More solid shot to the body with the left.

And two more.

Peters sits down on a shot but gets countered nicely by Wells, who is leaning back against the ropes.

Two head shots precede a body shot that rocks the foundations of the sky scrapers that surround us here on the Gold Coast.

Wow, the brutality of those shots is fearsome. Sickening.

Wells is a warrior for withstanding them.

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.
