Tech.title: Witcher 3 Remastered Will Be Free in September With New Expansion Coming in 2027
Tech.content:
Gamescom 2026 kicked off on Tuesday with Opening Night Live, the trailer showcase for some of the games coming out later this year and next. Europe’s major gaming event of the year, based in Cologne, Germany, it showed off a bunch of new games, but it was the remaster and expansion for the 11-year-old The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt that stole the show.

Developer CD Projekt Red revealed during the show that The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered will launch on Sept. 29 as a free upgrade for anyone who owns the game on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. Along with this updated version of the game, next year, a new expansion called Songs of the Past will arrive as the swan song for the series protagonist, Geralt of Rivia. The Witcher 4 is expected in 2028, and will focus on his adopted daughter and fellow Witcher, Ciri.

The Witcher 3 Remastered will feature a slew of improvements to the 2015 game. They include smoother combat, UI enhancements, a revamped skill tree, an expanded photo mode, new finishing moves and plenty of graphic upgrades to the textures, lighting, ray tracing and more. The remastered game will also make its debut on the Nintendo Switch 2 and Battle.net the same day.

Not only will Witcher 3 owners get the free upgrade in September, but CD Projekt Red is also making the game’s two expansions free starting Tuesday. Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine came out in the year following the release of The Witcher 3 and added new content, including a drawn-out story and a huge new region.

As for the new expansion, Songs of the Past will come out in 2027, and it will feature a new land for Geralt to explore. Letten is a region with its own identity that’s filled with questions, monsters and a dark secret. Players will fight off never-before-seen enemies and make use of new weapons in what could be the last adventure for Geralt.

The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt is out now on multiple platforms, but the free upgrade will only be available for PC, PS5 and Xbox Series consoles. Songs of the Past is currently slated for release only on PC and Xbox Series consoles, according to the game’s website, though this could change closer to release.

Tech.title: A Robot Gave Me a Vision Test in 90 Seconds. Is It the Future of Vision Care?
Tech.content:
Before you cancel your next eye doctor appointment, there are several things you should keep in mind. Eyebot/Viva Tung/CNET

Getting a prescription for glasses has always been the same: You schedule an appointment with an eye doctor, sit in an exam room while someone flips the lenses and asks you which is best, and wait at least a week for your new glasses to arrive. Not to mention paying out of pocket if you don’t have vision insurance.

Eyebot, a health tech company, wants to make that process optional and vision tests more accessible. The company announced on Thursday that it has partnered with eyewear brand Quay to do just that, and it is currently available at Quay’s Irvine Spectrum and Victoria Gardens locations in Southern California.

The Boston-based startup has built a kiosk that delivers a doctor-reviewed prescription for glasses in under 90 seconds with no appointment or insurance required. I got to test it out, and the experience was much more seamless than I expected.

What is Eyebot?

Simply put, Eyebot is a kiosk that offers non-invasive vision tests on a touchscreen. The process starts with an intake that asks whether you currently wear glasses or have any existing vision conditions. Those with certain eye conditions, such as glaucoma or cataracts, are directed to seek in-person care.

Then, you’ll see letters on a screen, and you type out what letters you see, the same as when you go for an in-person exam. After, the bot conducts the vision scan using a contactless eye scanner that collects refraction (identifies the exact lens prescription needed to correct your vision), lensometry (if you already use glasses, it scans your glasses and measures the power of your existing eyeglasses) and visual acuity (measures how clearly you see) information.

“The Eyebot is a vision testing solution that lets you get a vision exam in four simple steps, similar to what you would experience at an eyeglass clinic,” Matthias Hofmann, CEO at Eyebot, told CNET. The four steps are: intake survey, visual acuity test, tele-doctor review and prescription.

The entire process takes about 90 seconds. Your results are then sent to a licensed optometrist for review. Prescriptions are available within 24 hours after the test. I got mine in about 30 minutes.

However, Eyebot isn’t a replacement for your optometrist. It’s designed to serve the millions of people who can’t access one due to lack of accessibility or affordability.

My first impression of the Eyebot

When I first walked up to the Eyebot kiosk, which I was invited to test at a PR office, I was a little skeptical. It looks like a sleek ATM crossed with a photobooth. While I went in with doubts, I came out pretty impressed. It felt like it was straight out of a futuristic movie, but beyond that, the process was straightforward and intuitive enough that even someone who isn’t well-versed in technology could use the device without issue.

I followed the instructions on the screen, and I saw the bot scanning my eyes. Everything was done within 2 minutes. About 30 minutes later, I received an email with my prescription.

After receiving my results, I went online to The Framery at 1-800 Contacts, ordered glasses with my new prescription and received them in about five business days. All in all, the experience was quick and seamless.

I compared my prescription with the one I got during my in-person vision exam last year, and they were very similar. My optometrist’s prescription from last year showed mild nearsightedness and astigmatism in both eyes. Eyebot read my vision as effectively neutral — a discrepancy worth flagging. Since the nearsightedness and astigmatism are minimal and the prescription the optometrist reviewed after using Eyebot included a small amount of vision correction, I don’t notice any difference between my old and new glasses. I also didn’t have my glasses with me. Eyebot can scan your current glasses and identify your prescription, but I couldn’t test that feature.

Last year’s prescription, on the left, shows mild nearsightedness and astigmatism. On the right is Eyebot’s prescription. *Doctor names, license numbers and signatures have been removed from the image for privacy. Nasha Addarich Martínez/CNET

How much does it cost to get a vision exam with Eyebot?

The vision test itself can cost up to $25 at most locations. At Walmart Vision Centers, a visit to an Eyebot kiosk includes a $25 administrative fee. For Sam’s Club members, the service is covered under a membership ($60 or more per year) at participating clubs. That’s a significant contrast to a traditional in-person vision exam, which typically runs between $100 to $200 without insurance.

When asked how much Eyebot will cost at its new Quay locations, a representative said the price is at the retailer’s discretion.

“Half of Americans don’t even have vision insurance, so if we can get the retailers to subsidize the cost, that’s even better for consumers,” Hofmann says.

Eyebot

Getting a prescription is half the battle, as you still need the glasses. Eyebot partnered with The Framery at 1-800 Contacts to create a one-stop shop experience. Once you create an account with The Framery using the same email you used at Eyebot, you can automatically see your prescription and order glasses on the website.

Prescription glasses at The Framery range from $69 to $129, depending on the frame you choose.

Where to find an Eyebot

Eyebot kiosks are popping up at different locations, including Walmart Vision Centers and Sam’s Club Optical Centers in Pennsylvania, Missouri and Virginia, with plans to expand underway. If you’re interested in finding an Eyebot near you, you can visit the website to view current locations.

What to know before canceling your next eye appointment

Eyebot is worth trying, but not without a few caveats. I think it’s best for adults who need a routine prescription update and don’t have a complex vision history. The Eyebot can’t screen for glaucoma, cataracts, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy or other eye conditions as a comprehensive eye exam with a doctor can. Those conditions don’t always come with obvious symptoms, and a 90-second kiosk test won’t catch them, so it’s best to continue visiting your eye doctor for routine exams.

The American Optometric Association has been clear that this kind of technology isn’t a substitute for your yearly eye exam, especially if you haven’t had a comprehensive eye exam in more than a year or have a family history of eye disease.

But for the average person with healthy vision who’s been squinting a little more at their screens lately and can’t get an eye exam appointment, or can’t afford one, Eyebot can fill the gap.

Tech.title: Sony Is Reminding Us (Again) That We Don’t Own Our PlayStation Games
Tech.content:
Some things are too bizarre to make up, and Sony’s inability to read the room is one of them.

Over the last week or so, the media giant has sent emails to PlayStation users with its entire Terms of Service, which includes a reminder that their digital games are “licensed” and not “sold.” The communication comes as gamers continue to protest Sony’s removal of physical media from the PlayStation 6.

As an isolated incident, Sony’s email isn’t really anything untoward. It lets the user know that they have recently accepted the most recent Terms of Service, Code of Conduct, End User License Agreement and Privacy Policy. The company even included full copies of each in the email.

But the timing of Sony’s email appears intentional, not just unfortunate. PlayStation users are furious over the company’s decision to remove the physical disc drive from the PlayStation 6, as well as its announcement that it will stop producing game discs altogether as of January 2028. Sony announced the end of physical discs just a few days after removing several digitally purchased movies from users’ accounts.

The email was spotted by The Verge’s Tom Warren, who posted about it on X over the weekend: “Sony emailing everyone about PlayStation terms of use during a backlash over the end of discs and a lack of digital ownership is certainly a choice.”

The backlash has grown large enough to inspire a PlayStation boycott — starting Sunday — with players pledging not to buy, log in to or play games for a week to protest Sony’s abandonment of physical media for the console.

So, right in the middle of a protest centered on concerns about game ownership, Sony is reminding us we’re merely buying a license to use a game under the company’s terms.

The new normal: Lease, not own

HP printers throw tantrums if you try to use third-party ink cartridges. James Bricknell / CNET

A move like this from another multibillion-dollar company underscores the new normal in gaming and tech, where companies appear to be shifting further away from the idea of ownership. Instead, they ask consumers to retain access to products that may be revoked or restricted at the company’s discretion. These changes didn’t come in one dramatic wave, but in a steady stream of small consumer-facing microaggressions that have built up over time.

Take the recent HP printer controversy, for example. HP programmed its printers to lock users out if third-party ink is detected. That means you can buy an HP printer and own it — but if you don’t fill it with the official (more expensive) ink cartridges, the printer can sass back like an angsty, spoiled teenager and refuse to work.

There are subtler attempts to chip away at our agency (and purchasing power) as consumers. Apple raised MacBook prices this year, then started a program where the company will literally rent you one, presumably because you can’t afford it otherwise. You wouldn’t own the MacBook, so Apple could lock you out of your device if you missed a lease payment.

When it comes to music and movies, streaming has been the norm for years — we’re dutifully reminded every so often that we’re renting the ability to listen or watch something rather than owning it. I’ll never forget a couple of years ago when the entire library from the rock band Coheed and Cambria’s was removed from YouTube Music due to a licensing dispute while I was in the middle of listening.

Sony and other gaming companies are starting to adopt the same lending-access business model in software and digital entertainment: In this brave new world, mega corporations can own everything and make us “purchase” rentals entirely on their terms. That means they can change, restrict, discontinue or shut down access, but we can never keep, lend, sell or pass down a product.

The shift is leaving older generations (millennials like myself included) increasingly nostalgic for a time when buying something meant taking home something tangible — something that belonged to us.

Tech.title: Our Robot Pool Vacuum Tests Show Why Suction Power Matters Less Than You Think
Tech.content:
If you use a robotic pool cleaner every day as I do, you know what matters. Getting as much debris out of the pool as possible is the goal, but pure suction power — quantified as gallons of pool water sucked through the machine per hour — takes a back seat to efficiency.

An efficient robot pool vacuum doesn’t just pick up debris with stronger suction; it does so strategically, so your pool is cleaned faster and you use less battery. When you’re ready to cool off in the pool — like, now — you want the fastest possible cleaning.

This is the first year we’ve tested robots with high-functioning AI, giving them the ability to detect debris using cameras and sensors, change course and suck it up into the basket. These advanced features have upended the traditional formula for robot pool cleaner proficiency (suction power plus battery life).

Key takeaways

Efficiency over power: Pure suction power (measured in gallons per hour) is less critical than the robot’s cleaning efficiency.

Pure suction power (measured in gallons per hour) is less critical than the robot’s cleaning efficiency. Impact of AI: Robotic pool cleaners equipped with AI debris detection (using cameras and sensors) clean more efficiently than those without such features.

Robotic pool cleaners equipped with AI debris detection (using cameras and sensors) clean more efficiently than those without such features. Corded vs. cordless: In general, corded robotic pool cleaners are more efficient than cordless models because they have a consistent power supply and can perform back-to-back cleaning cycles.

In general, corded robotic pool cleaners are more efficient than cordless models because they have a consistent power supply and can perform back-to-back cleaning cycles. The corded Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus (Lab Award winner) was the most efficient of all the recommended models we tested.

(Lab Award winner) was the most efficient of all the recommended models we tested. The Aiper Scuba V3 (Lab Award winner) was the most efficient cordless robotic pool cleaner tested, picking up more debris in less time than more powerful and expensive models.

CNET Lab Awards

Most Efficient (Corded): Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus (Efficiency Score: 58 items picked up per hour)

(Efficiency Score: 58 items picked up per hour) Most Efficient (Cordless): Aiper Scuba V3 (Efficiency Score: 44.64 items picked up per hour)

Pure power isn’t the end-all, be-all for pool robot cleaners

There’s more to consider in robotic pool cleaning than pure power. Aiper/CNET

When shopping for a robot pool cleaner, you might assume more suction power means better overall performance. Suction rates range anywhere from around 4,000 to 8,000 gallons per hour in robots intended for residential use.

In truth, most top pool robot cleaners have enough suction to lift the debris that’s likely to end up in your pool. Leaves, twigs and even small stones are light enough that even robot pool vacuums on the lower end of the GPH spectrum have no trouble clearing them.

The Best Robot Pool Cleaners Out of More Than 20 tested See at CNET

I’ve seen plenty of robot pool cleaners with massive 8,500 GPH suction take on a pile of pebbles and leaves, with success rates similar to those of models with half that power. That got me thinking about efficiency, and so we devised a testing methodology and formula to determine the most efficient robotic pool cleaners.

How we performed the lab tests

We ran all the cordless vacuums at once with a pool full of pebbles. David Watsky/CNET

To measure the efficiency of each robot pool cleaner, we ran it on a full charge in a 14,000-gallon test pool with 100 pebbles and 30 leaves — more debris than you’re ever likely to have in your pool — scattered about the bottom.

(We’d given each robot the repetitions it needed to map the pool using its cameras and ultrasonic sonar or acoustic sensors, if such a feature existed. Not all pool robot vacuums have it.)

We timed how long the robot operated for on a full charge. When it was finished cleaning, we counted how much debris was captured in the basket, aka how much it picked up from the floor and how much was left behind. We then prorated the pickup performance with the time the robot spent cleaning. This efficiency score indicates how many pieces of debris a robotic pool cleaner collects per hour.

Cordless robot pool cleaner efficiency winners

Many of the pool vacuums performed well, but three were in a league of their own in terms of total pickup performance, leaving fewer than 5 total objects, so we separated those from the rest. After the top three, there was a notable drop-off, and the next best model left 12 pieces of debris in the pool.

Among the three elite performers in pickup, the most efficient robot pool cleaner was the Aiper Scuba V3 with AI detection. It left just five pebbles and cleared every leaf from the pool bottom. The Scuba V3 achieved this in an astonishing 2 hours and 48 minutes – nearly 2 hours faster than the larger, more powerful robots. Its efficiency score was 44.64 items spiked up per hour.

The robot vacuum that cleared the most total debris was the Aiper Scuba X1 Pro Max. It left zero pebbles or leaves but required more than 4 hours, resulting in a lower efficiency score of 28.36 items picked up per hour. I noted that at the 3.5-hour mark of cleaning, there were still a few scattered pebbles, though it eventually picked them up.

The Beatbot Aquasense Pro, another powerful pool cleaner with a massive battery, also performed well, clearing all the leaves and leaving only three stones, but it needed 4 hours and 40 minutes to do so, giving it an efficiency score of 27.21 items picked up per hour.

The second most efficient robot pool cleaner was the Polaris Freedom. It picked up a respectable 107 items in its 2 hours and 25 minutes of cleaning, giving it a healthy efficiency score of 44.28 items picked up per hour. But because it left 23 items, including 10 leaves and 13 pebbles, it represented a noticeable dip in performance from the top of the pack.

The Aiper Scuba S1 Pro had a similar result. High efficiency, but left more total debris than we’d like to see in a top performer.

Suction power didn’t matter much, but AI smarts did

AI capability proved more critical to pickup efficiency than suction power. Aiper

Among the cordless test group, three robot pool cleaners stood out by picking up all 30 leaves and at least 95 pebbles. We considered this a perfect or near-perfect performance. (Remember, we littered the pool with far more debris than you’re likely to have at any given time if you use your robot cleaner somewhat regularly).

Of the top three performers in total pickup, the Aiper Scuba V3 trounced the others in its efficiency rating, despite having significantly lower GPH and battery life. It picked up 125 of the 130 pieces of debris in 2 hours and 48 minutes.

What accounted for Aiper Scuba’s dominant efficiency was its ability to detect debris with cameras, sensors, and AI for targeted cleaning. It was fascinating to watch the Scuba V3 move through the pool, stop and turn toward debris when it encountered a leaf or pebble.

Other robots we tested roam the pool either based on their mapping or aimlessly like a screensaver, hoping to run over leaves, bugs and sticks rather than seeking them out.

Robots with big power and battery life deliver, but there’s a price to pay

Big beasts like the Aiper Pro Max have powerful suction and battery life, but they’re more than the average pool owner needs. David Watsky/CNET

The most expensive robot pool cleaners are typically those with the largest motors and batteries. That also makes them the heaviest, with a large lithium-ion battery accounting for most of the weight.

The two robot pool vacuums that beat the Aiper Scuba V3 in overall performance weigh 7 and 16 pounds more, respectively. When you’re pulling a cordless robot from the pool each day for charging, emptying and cleaning, that extra weight matters.

They’re also significantly more expensive, clocking in at $1,800 and $2,199, whereas the Aiper Scuba V3 retails for around $850.

Corded models: Efficiency over convenience

In general, corded models are more efficient than their cordless counterparts. Because they are fed consistent power through an electrical cord, suction never drops or wanes mid-cycle, ensuring heavy debris, sand and leaves are vacuumed. They also run endlessly, so you can trigger back-to-back cycles until your pool is clean.

On the flip side, you can’t swim while a corded robot pool cleaner is working due to the risk of electrical shock. You’ll also need an outlet nearby and manage an unsightly cord running across the deck during operation.

Because of these structural differences, we put corded robot pool cleaners in their own category but used a similar equation to calculate efficiency. Corded robot cleaners often have set runtimes ranging from two to three hours.

Of the three corded models we tested, the Dolphin Nautilus CC with Wi-Fi performed the best, clearing all leaves and all but 14 pebbles during its 2-hour run time, giving it an impressive efficiency score of 58 items picked up per hour. That’s better than the Polaris ERA could manage in its longer cycle of 2 hours and 30 minutes (45 efficiency score). The Dolphin E10 picked up only 108 of the 130 items in 2 hours of cleaning, but managed a solid 54 efficiency score.

My expert buying advice on robotic pool cleaners

We’ve tested nearly two dozen robotic pool cleaners. David Watsky/CNET

If you’re in the market for a robotic pool cleaner, prioritize efficiency and smart debris detection over raw suction power specs, especially for an average-size pool. Our lab data shows that models like the Aiper Scuba V3, which use AI-driven navigation to target debris, deliver more efficient cleaning than more powerful robots, which are often both expensive and heavy.

If you want the fastest cleanup and an easier daily lifting experience, focus on cordless models with advanced sensors. If you have the patience to manage a cord and require continuous cleaning power, a corded model remains the most reliable, high-efficiency workhorse.

The best time to buy is during seasonal shifts or major retail holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, when you can often find significant discounts on these premium units. Given the rapid advancement in AI-enhanced pool cleaning technology, check for sales or brand-specific promotions, as older models are frequently marked down to make way for new releases with improved navigation and sensor suites.
